en: A Lamp for the Lineage of the Conquerors.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
He whose heart is the Great Compassion that has arisen day after day.
For the sake of others' welfare, through birth after birth, he underwent the experience of suffering;
he attained the state of perfect enlightenment step by step, step by step, step by step.
I pay homage to that Conqueror, Conqueror, Conqueror. (The Yamakabandhana)
Having abandoned delight in whatever brings pleasure,
the sage delights only in the Dhamma;
the sage is liberated from all states of existence, from becoming and non-becoming.
I pay homage to him who is honored, who is beneficial, who is the ultimate benefit; (this is a Yamaka-bandhana verse:
those who have drunk the essence of the True Dhamma find no further taste for worldly flavors;
in that field of great merit, they are ever peaceful, ever at peace.
I pay homage to that assembly of the hosts of sages, who have gone forth and are purified by discipline—
the royal swans in the lotus pond of the Conqueror’s feet. (A Yamaka-bandhana)
May the bee-like speech of the Jinorasānas,
which extracts the essence of the true goal with its fresh flavor, enter my very mind.
By this preeminent merit of my prostration,
may the remaining kamma, the fetters, and the obstructions of the formations that have been accumulated through successive births, be utterly destroyed for me.
Let there be no occasion for further praise;
even if gold were fashioned from dross, it would still be unable to describe the beauty of the Victor who is golden-hued.
Even at the end of an eon, one could not reach the limit of the Buddha’s qualities through the practice of *manatta*;
his beautiful form is like refined gold.
The splendor of his ornaments and speech,
as well as his wisdom— which is not shared by others,
inconceivable, and beyond comparison— were revealed.
Where is the play of uncommon form?
Where is the play of uncommon speech?
Where is the play of uncommon wisdom?
Where indeed is there room for the playful arrogance of one like me,
dull-witted and dependent on others,
who am being shattered by envy and pride?
What use have I for praising or censuring those who seek here the faults of others?
I am one who sees the further shore,
praised by the Teacher and the scriptures.
Those virtuous ones who are perfectly tranquil in their excellent qualities alone understand the labor involved in composing this book;
they alone are the authorities here.
Regarding that Victor, born of the lineage of the Sun,
even though [the Dhamma] was taught by the former teachers who were skilled in the arrival of the Teacher, in those [verses]—
In books, the lineage [of the Buddha] is presented in brief;
even by condensing it, it is not possible for those [books] to make known the lineage of the Sugata.
Therefore, with a mind thus encouraged by the exposition of the Perfect Lineage,
and being deeply devoted to the Triple Gem, [I have composed this].
Of noble lineage and illustrious origin, an ornament to his contemporaries,
whose fame and renown are celebrated—
he who shines as the most fortunate one in Laṅkā.
Of that one named Punandu,
who delighted in unceasing generosity, whose wealth was compassion,
and who possessed an extraordinary faith in the Buddha.
And having accepted this request,
for the sake of the listeners and for their welfare,
I shall set forth the instruction of my former teacher for their benefit.
This lamp of the Conqueror’s lineage is correctly composed in the Magadhi language,
accompanied by the oil of faith and the wick of wisdom.
This lamp of the Conqueror’s lineage,
lit by the listeners within the celestial mansions of their minds,
has dispelled the mass of darkness in the island of Dīpoha.
Filled with the excellence of the glorious Jambudīpa,
it descended by day as if under the weight of its own prosperity,
like Amarāvatī, the city of the king of the gods.
In that city there was a town named Marāvatī;
it obstructed the aerial course of both the *vidyādharas* and the birds, causing them to cry out.
In whatever city the Conqueror of Enemies [established] his wheel,
like a circular wall around the world-system (cakravāḷa),
there the dust was kissed by the moisture of his splendor.
With its moats of beautiful, deep-yellow water,
the eastern side of the city wall bore the appearance of a golden girdle upon its hips.
The royal capital, illuminated by the luster of rubies, sapphires, and emeralds day and night,
was bound [on all sides] by the unceasing rainbow of the lord of the gods.
Where the orb of the moon was treated with contempt by the lotus-faces of the women,
who displayed their brilliance against the surface of the sky.
With her radiance, she made the sapphire archway appear darkened by grief and discolored,
like a lotus within a jeweled palace.
In that city, the womenfolk, delightful to the people,
extended their hands in apprehension toward the orb of the full moon, as if it were a face being kissed.
Where the lotus-faces of women,
reflected in mirror-walls,
became a source of distress for the bees.
Out of compassion for those who have taken refuge in his eyes,
from the mountains that are the bearers of the earth,
streams of the rut of perfect rightness flow forth.
With the dust shaken off by the hooves of your horses,
you are as if agitated by a garland of waves;
with your lute set aside and your jeweled anklets [silent],...
Where, finding its opportunity, would the sweet-sounding swarm of intoxicated bees not adorn the feet with soft hands of playful women?
That city, during the night, [was filled] with the cranes that were the breasts of the women, with the lotus-faces burdened by the collyrium of their eyes,
and with the ripples of their smiles.
She shone like a lake of lotuses in full bloom;
the moonlight kissed the moonstone,
the crystal, and the moonbeams.
Those garlands upon the faces of the fierce ones,
which served to allay their exhaustion—
those very garlands that were bound above and below on his full form...
The series of jeweled pavilions bore the splendor of canopies and coverings smeared with red chalk-paste.
Abounding in the wealth of the seven grains— gold, pearls, gems,
bamboo-colored [crystal], coral, silver, and diamonds.
Ah! Like a woman of noble birth who is wealthy, she has been spread out toward the faces of many directions, filled with various garments, ornaments, and the like.
(The Binding of the Silesas)
Where the market-stalls surpassed the wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) by accomplishing the goals desired by the world;
where the people were devoted to others and intoxicated with drinking honey-wine.
Where the ponds have their banks thick with dark-blue lotus-stalks,
where swans dwell, and which are delightful with five-colored lotuses—
just like those who indulge in sensual pleasures; (The Bond of Slime).
In the eastern quarter, where darkness was dispelled by the continuous streams of radiance from heaps of jewels,
and which was graced by the blossoming of jasmine and lotuses;
The world distinguishes between night and day by that [sound] which possesses a deep resonance like the ringing of a bell from a herd of clouds and elephants.
In that city where, even at an improper time, the intoxicated peacock-crested goddesses— fearless—
performed their unbroken play with his lotus feet.
The blooming *kokāsana* flower,
with its head bound by anklets worn by the newlywed bride,
surpassed the remaining lotuses of the night-lily pond.
The netherworld (Rasātala) is covered by the hoods of serpents;
the vault of heaven (Nabhotala) is covered by streaks of lightning;
and that which is covered by gold of various forms—
The capital city was named Dhajāvati;
it possessed various essential materials, was adorned with well-proportioned elements,
was worthy of praise, and was delightful to the multitudes of living beings.
That city was like a verse adorned with poetic figures (*silesa*),
full of flavor and possessing the excellence of ornaments;
in that city dwelt the treasury of compassion.
In the lineage of the Brahmin Sāra,
the Buddhaṅkura arose in the past, measured by four hundred thousand incalculable eons (asaṅkhya-kappa).
Now, at the auspicious rising of the majesty of the merit of Ekadivākara in the lineage of the Bhovādis,
Jambudīpa has indeed been born.
He plundered the play of the auspicious abode;
at the moment of his birth,
by the fragrance and beauty arising from his body, his own dwelling was [perfumed].
The sandalwood-oil lamps, their radiance extinguished,
could be recognized by their shapes alone,
for they were free from defects and well-maintained.
Nourished by nurses with breasts as large as jars, the prince,
whose body was exceedingly delicate, passed some days.
Then, while the Great Festival was being celebrated by learned scholars who were masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
those fathers caused the nectar to be prepared.
The name "Sumedha" possesses the essence of its literal meaning;
as the prince grew up endowed with such sublime fortune,
his mother could never have enough of him.
Kissing his lotus-face,
whose eyes were like blue lotuses,
the prince’s limbs became thrilled with bliss.
Upon the jeweled ground of the celestial mansion,
he shone like his parents as he moved along on his pair of golden knees, making his supplication.
Possessing a beautiful form like a golden bimba fruit,
he moved along supported by his nurse’s arms,
with clusters of toes on his feet that were clearly discernible.
He graced his dwelling with grace,
and by his own splendor he touched the world of living beings from beginning to end with glory.
Having eclipsed the splendor of the sun and moon,
that wise one, well-born on both sides,
increased [in glory] as far as his seventh ancestor.
Though you were born into a womb of lowly origin,
you are one whose fame is purified by the ages;
do not speak of birth, for even one who is cast down and despised may become most excellent.
He mastered the Veda along with its glossaries and treatises,
the science of phonology together with its rules of accentuation and analysis of syllables,
and the science of history along with its duties and sacred traditions.
He was one who knew the Vedas along with the Vedāṅgas, a teacher of the scriptures,
a reciter of the mantras, and skilled in the arts,
in worldly sciences, and in the characteristics of omens.
You are the one who fulfills the desires of poets,
a grammarian, and a leader of the assembly;
[you are the wind] that is the column of smoke from the fire of the pride of Kandappa.
His own face, resting in playful charm with its cheeks not merely tender,
soiled the mind of even a woman with its impurity.
O ocean of the sense-sphere of forms,
you are the boat for men to cross over the craving for form;
O Pāyāsi, you have drunk [the water] of the sense-sphere of the eye with those who are dear.
The twice-born one of excellent wisdom and perfectly purified intellect, having reached the end of his parents' lives,
became a guide for his own mind across the interval [of existence].
One day, while sitting on the terrace of his palace, he experienced the pleasures of sense-desire while living as a householder,
which were produced by the power of his merit.
Having taken his seat in the cross-legged posture while alone in seclusion,
he who contemplates the true nature of things reflected: "Rebirth and the breaking up of the body are suffering."
I am born; therefore, I am a phenomenon subject to birth, aging, and disease.
Thus, I am empty of the suffering of existence, which is eternal, unborn, ageless, and healthy.
"It is right to seek out Nibbāna," just as when there is suffering there is the pleasure of its relief,
and when there is other heat there is coolness.
When existence exists, non-existence likewise exists;
when the three fires exist, Nirvana exists;
when blameworthy states are found here [in this world].
"O sir, blameless dhamma exists;
there is non-arising when there is arising"—
thus did he who sought his own welfare reflect.
Seeing a pond filled with excrement,
one would neither blame it nor cross over it; so too,
while the Deathless exists, one does not cleanse away the defilements.
Likewise, one should not associate with that [evil person];
there is no fault in him. When the path of safety exists, it is no fault if one avoids evil, nor would one abandon happiness.
If one does not proceed along the path of safety when it exists because of being obstructed by evil, there is no fault in that person;
just as a man with a grievous disease [does not recover] even though a physician is present. (The Yamakabandhana)
It is not his fault that he does not obtain treatment, when there exists the Buddha-physician for one afflicted by the diseases of lust and the like;
who would find fault in him if he does not desire the medicine of the Dhamma?
Just as one who wanders freely, having cast off a corpse tied around his neck,
goes wherever he pleases,
so too is this loathsome, putrid body.
What if I were now to go away,
leaving this place of excrement, disregarded by people,
having made my dung like that which they carry away?
Likewise, this body is filled with putrefying corpses;
what if I were now to go away, having abandoned it,
just as one leaves a worn-out boat behind on the waters?
Just as a driver avoids a leaking cart,
so too should one avoid this body with its nine gates of leakage;
what if I were now to go forth, having abandoned it?
Just as a wise man, fearing legal prosecution, would flee from the core of a city to a safe town,
so too should one protect the body that brings about skillful states.
What if I were now to go forth, abandoning the world,
intent upon renunciation and beyond comparison with others,
remembering that very same heroic one?
Having struck the shoreless, essence-less threefold existence,
he dwelt with a weary mind;
[desiring] gold, pearls, gems, silver, and the like—
Then Rāsivaḍḍha opened the treasuries and storehouses filled with wealth and grain, and showed them to him.
In this world, the wealth of grandfathers,
great-grandfathers, and parents is indeed not small, O younger sister.
O wise one of excellent intelligence, you shine forth;
having dispelled the mass of non-existence, you have made manifest the wheel of the lineage down to the seventh generation.
One who perceives the measure of both the acquisition and the loss of wealth,
and practices this way of life for the sake of his family—
"Like a god among sensual pleasures,
enjoy yourself according to your desire"—
thus did Rāsivaḍḍha entice him.
Having gathered this great heap of wealth and grain,
he did not take even a single kahāpaṇa for his mother and father— oh, how strange!
They have gone hence to their respective destinations according to their karma;
then there remains the essence of beings, which is peaceful through relinquishment and exceedingly heroic in grasping the core of that very state.
Having reported this matter to the king,
he caused a drum to be sounded throughout his own city;
with the fragrance of the drum’s roar, he satisfied [the people].
Born under the constellation Maghā,
the Lord of the Helpless, who was addressed as "Bho," enjoyed for seven days various riches such as honey and other gems.
Because of the downpour of rain from the water-bearing clouds of that supreme sacrificial hall,
the great multitude’s craving for further objects of existence increased.
The banks of the lakes of the mind were broken;
having abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires,
Sumedha then went forth from his home, well-established in happiness.
Having plunged into the Himalayas,
Dhammaka performed the ascetic practice of the "Dhamma-cloak"; then,
having understood his thoughts, the King of the Devas [spoke].
Vissakamma was employed to measure out a secluded dwelling-place suitable for one who endures solitude,
as well as a delightful area for walking meditation.
Having approached that empty hermitage, which was deserted by those who had gone forth, and having entered the privy,
he saw the letters inscribed within it.
He looked upon the burden of the cart’s equipment;
he avoided, again and again, that which was to be avoided, seeing the fault in the cloth that had been newly worn and possessed of fresh defects.
It was draped with a rug of mind-born flowers and bark-cloth,
and was beautiful with a rug of *punnāga* flowers.
Placing a fragment of deerskin upon his shoulder,
having fashioned a circle of matted locks upon his body,
and then taking up a triple-curved staff and a water-pot;
The wise one, with his many-armed serpent-like body,
took hold of the tip of a support-staff and thus assumed the guise of an ascetic.
With a mind detached from both non-existence and existence,
he descended from the walkway and sat upon a stone slab during the day.
Having entered in the evening,
he dwelt in the leaf-hut and lay down on a bed spread with wood-shavings;
at the time of dawn, he awoke.
"Having reflected on the circumstances of my arrival,
I thought: 'For me, who desires solitude, dwelling here may as well be like living at home.'"
Indeed, its leaf-canopy was as dark as a dove's foot,
with the color of ripe *veluva* fruit;
even the ground and the walls were as bright as silver.
The bed is covered with fine cloth,
and my leaf-hut is beautiful and pleasing;
yet this hut is fraught with danger and difficult to maintain.
The search for exquisite alms-food is the root of suffering;
there is no measure or charm [to prevent it].
Having rejected the perception of "home," [one should dwell in seclusion].
Having abandoned that house of family leaves with its eight defects,
he resorts to the root of a tree common to all beings,
which has ten qualities, and subsists on whatever fruit or alms-food he may obtain.
For seven days, the wise Sumedha exerted himself in the Great Struggle;
the wise one reached the further shore of mastery in the higher knowledges.
He experienced every bliss of meditative attainment;
at that moment, the joyful sound of "Excellent! was proclaimed by the deities of the forest.
He has risen up together with his glory through the excellence of his purified knowledge and conduct;
the masters of vidyā chant verses illuminating his virtues.
Now the Himalaya mountain,
as if dancing and singing songs with its cymbals,
lutes, and drums, trembled all over.
With his head’s sprout-like crest being fanned by hundreds of mountain peaks as arms and by the chowries of their waterfalls,
he has shaken off all evil.
Even the great lakes, as if their offerings had been accepted,
were stirred by the thundering of unseasonable clouds,
while the throngs of rutting peacocks were set to clamor like the sounding of kettledrums.
As he dwelt in the midst of the forest grove,
the earth trembled with the rhythmic dance of his unbroken strides,
while the gentle breeze served as the support for his powerful arms.
The Lord of the Sāla trees, embraced by the slender-bodied women who were like sunīla-sakhāmaṇi fans,
caused even the steadfast one to tremble slightly.
Kapītanā, Aśoka, Tamāla, Nīpa; Kapītanā, Aśoka,
Tamāla, Nīpa— (this is the great Yamaka on the complete practice of pādas)—
Kapītanā, Aśoka, Tamāla, Nīpa.
Kapītanās, Aśokas, Tamālas, and Nīpas;
are not the Velalītās, Pasavakas, and Avataṃsas, as well as the canopies of creepers and the Sālīs with rows of honey, [ornaments]?
Are these not like creepers forming a canopy, frequented by swarms of bees,
entwined with blossoming *punnāga* flowers as their ornaments, and adorned with rows of flowers,
*kandalī* stalks, and *pāṭala* blooms? (This is a *samuggabhedayamaka*).
That dark-blue forest row was thick with blossoms,
its beauty like a *pāṭala* flower,
resembling a magnificent dark-blue streak of collyrium; (it was bound with a half-gem-like cord).
With head bowed from the intoxication of the *mañjarī* flower,
and with hands joined in reverence,
you shine like one who has been delighted by being bound in a beautiful forest.
Having removed the painful blow of the binding cord (the foot-fetters),
they scattered dust while bowing down among the creepers,
like women scattering parched grain as they bend low.
The twice-born, dwelling in the forest,
were like elephants trapped by a canopy of creepers; though they exerted themselves, those lords of elephants could not break free from the bond of the net of verses,
which was like a tangled web of cow-urine.
Having bowed at the feet of him whose abode is the lamp of wisdom—
pure, radiant, and flourishing with the fruits [of attainment] on the most excellent foothills of the Himalayan mountain range— (the wheel of the womb named Kabba).
Like the hooded serpent, the Lord of Snakes, he bore the parasol of loving-kindness upon his head;
thus self-controlled, he moved about,
like a protector providing some aid to those who were weak.
Nanda, for wisdom, firm in speech, in safety;

(The *gabbhacakra* of the poet's name) Not from those who are not wise, nor from fear, nor from lack of joy, nor from one who is not seeking welfare, nor from one who does not dwell in giving; (A reverse *yamaka* concerning the first half of the verse)
This body is indeed a dwelling place, neither desirable, nor lovely, nor dear;
it is a source of suffering, empty, void, and insubstantial. (The bond is auspicious in every way.
Controlled by compassion, he lived in the forest for seven months.
I dwelt for a long time, delighting in the sacrifice, as a swan dwelling in the midst of the waters—
amidst the humming of honey-bees intoxicated by nectar,
and amidst the breezes fragrant with sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
In the Himalayas, upon every blooming lotus,

he dwells experiencing supreme bliss at his own will. (The *pādānta-yamaka*) Thus ends the "Illumination of the Deeds of the Brahmin Sumedha," which serves as the distant cause for the Lamp of the Conqueror’s Lineage— a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, the source of joy for the hearts of all poets.
The First Heaven.
(Slowly approaching: The splendor of the city of the gods, the essence of all prosperity, resembling the pericarp of a lotus in Jambudvīpa, which is peerless.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara— the ten-powered one, the sole lamp for the entire world, who had reached the further shore of the perfections— was in the delightful city called Ramma,
the best of cities. There, his heart was stirred by a woman of vast compassion.
Surrounded by various monks whose taints were destroyed,
wandering on his journey and gradually turning the wheel of Dhamma with great skill,
he eventually arrived and resided in that monastery known as Soṇassana.
Having heard the report of the fame of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara,
which had spread abroad as "He is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One, an Arahant," and so forth,
the citizens quickly procured robes, medicinal requisites, and drinks.
With joyful minds, they carried perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
Having approached the lion-like Dīpaṅkara Buddha and honored him with perfumes,
garlands, and the like, they sat to one side with palms joined in reverent salutation.
Having heard the Dhamma, which is so auspicious to hear,
and having made a formal request to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, they, with joyful hearts, prepared a fragrant bath for him.
On the following day, those virtuous people, having adorned the hall of offerings, [prepared for the ceremony].
Raising up flagstaffs like palm trees and placing full water-jars,
they remained thus, adorning the city for her arrival by scattering white jasmine flowers and offering oblations of parched grain.
Then, having ascended high above the Himalayas, that ascetic Sumedha,
traveling through the air over them while shaking his bark garment,
saw them purifying their path with hearts filled with joy and gladness.
"Shining like a twilight cloud, you alone are the bearer of the sun;
why do you adorn this path as you cleanse the place of mire and unevenness, this heap of refuse? he asked.
Venerable Sir, now, relying on the excellent Dīpaṅkara mountain,
he dwells as a Buddha, proclaiming the great drum of the Dhamma.
That Fully Awakened One, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, from whom we...
"They say that even entering a village field is an adornment for one's hair and beard;
how much more so the arising of a Buddha! The sound of 'Buddha' is even rarer to hear.
Thinking thus, you desire to adorn yourself and have set out upon the path.
"His person shines with the armor of jhāna and higher knowledge;
he is like a mountain peak in his unwavering faith—a powerful ascetic possessed of psychic power.
Having thus observed him, [he crossed] that difficult section of the path, which was as uneven as a mire.
The joyful virtuous ones immediately prepared for him,
having gathered various flowers— both aquatic and terrestrial— from the forest,
and having brought *kovidāra* and other blossoms from the abodes of the gods and asuras.
Having brought full blue lotuses from the abode of the serpents and having prepared the path by means of my psychic power, saying "I am clever," I shall cause my heart,
thus made unclouded, to blossom with joy. Therefore—
Having arranged for physical service with a clear and discerning mind,
the wise one thought, "Today I shall accumulate abundant merit," and began to cleanse the straight path from the turbidity of the mud.
As he passed through the mud, his stainless eyes shone like flashes of lightning amidst the womb of clouds; and as people cried out, "A Buddha!
A Buddha!", the wise one held up his own hands like two empty baskets.
Having offered earth and scattering sand as white as silver,
at that spot which was stirred up and not yet well-adorned,
the supreme Lord Dīpaṅkara stood together with many who had destroyed the taints.
Having attained the state of Brahmā, among immortals, humans, nāgas, siddhas, and vidyādharas,
he manifested vast and sublime miracles; his beautiful face,
adorned with the marks of excellence, was like a golden lotus.
The Teacher, whose secondary characteristics shone with coolness and who was adorned with a garland of rays,
was emitting radiance in every direction like a rutting king of elephants upon a jeweled surface as he approached directly toward him.
Having looked with stainless eyes like blue lotuses smeared with sandalwood paste,
and having opened his back as if treading upon a jeweled slab, he—
having cast off various outflows— did not tread upon the mire.
"May this Fully Awakened One go forth for my long-term welfare"— having reflected thus,
he cast off his coarse antelope skin, matted hair, and bark garments,
and having removed his hair, he spread out his body upon the uneven mud.
Having built a bridge and made a supreme aspiration,
he whose heart was urged on by his consort lay down with his head toward the east, possessing the jewel-gems of the five supernormal powers.
Having heard even a single line of verse, my defilement is no longer heavy for me.
If I wish to reach the supreme city after having shattered [the enemy],
while infinite suffering beings exist within the abode of the three realms of existence,
how could I, being alone, consider myself worthy to attain the Dharma?
Now, may I, delighting in the welfare of others, attain perfect enlightenment;
and having boarded the supreme ship of the Dhamma,
may I ferry all people across the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra to the excellent city of peace.
"Later, just as the Sage Dīpaṅkara attained final Nibbāna,"—
thus did he, having brought together the eight factors of the path,
become for all beings like a great bridge for crossing over from saṃsāra.
With matted locks bound upon his head and palms joined in reverence,
he lay upon the muddy ground and made a solemn aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One for the sake of supreme enlightenment. Immediately,
the Blessed One, from the top of his head, emitted a radiance of five colors.
Opening his pair of eyes, which resembled blooming blue lotuses,
he beheld the excellent seer like a lattice window made of sapphire gems,
as the sage raised his lotus-like face from the surface of the mud.
Thinking, "I shall attain enlightenment in this [life]," this aspiration is the knowledge of the future;
having correctly directed [his mind] from here for more than a hundred thousand eons,
he looked back and perceived the four incalculable eons above.
"Having attained enlightenment, may there be a Buddha named Gotama like me;
look upon you [all]!"— having spoken thus in the midst of the Saṅgha,
that King of Dhamma, bestowing a gift like a lotus, [spoke].
O Queen Māyā, from the dwelling place named Kapilapura,
where the sprouts of her lower lip were slightly reddened by betel, which had not yet arrived,
and whose hundred words were marked with the seal of wisdom and contained within them a message of inquiry; (she sends this).
Your mother will be Queen Suddhodanā, your father King Adiccavamso,
and your beloved wife Bimbā, who possesses a bimba-like complexion,
will be as charming as a golden image. At that time, Rāhula shall become your jewel of a son.
Exulting were those first and second disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna,
born of brahmin families and endowed with vast wisdom and supernormal powers;
and the ascetic named Ānanda was the chief attendant of the female disciples.
The Elder Nun Khemā and the most excellent Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā—
both of you were confident like the branches of the *assattha* tree. You, O one called Gotamī,
having departed from your own home, practiced for six years.
"Having partaken of the supreme milk-rice given by Sujātā,
O you who will surely awaken to enlightenment, sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree!"—
thus [addressed], the Teacher, like a flash of lightning released from a mass of evening clouds, [shone forth].
Having displayed her own creeper-like arm from within her robe,
she emitted a deep sound like the roar of a rain-cloud,
and sent forth six-colored rays of light like a celestial rainbow.
Thinking, "We have not awakened to the teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara;
may we attain the Dhamma of liberation right here before you," at that very moment,
gods and humans, having reached the state free from the stake of craving, attained it.
Having worshipped him with lotus-like hands upon his footstool—
the Buddha whose lotus-feet are kissed by the heads of Brahmās, gods, and men— he,
having fully honored him with eight handfuls of flowers from that place, [departed].
He set forth, treading steps that caused the forest of beautiful lotuses to raise its heads,
while his gait was as captivating as a golden mountain peak,
scattering handfuls of flowers over every delightful spot on the earth, thereby honoring the matted-hair ascetics.
The hosts of those who had conquered their taints and were free from defilements departed toward the south;
the gods, like unto gods, performed salutations, honors, and worship,
and having followed the Island-Born Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, they turned back.
When he had left that place and the people were seated,
the deities who had come from his field of birth [to that assembly] saw him upon the lion-throne,
which was covered with flowers offered by gods and men; they perceived this matter.
They announced [this] with their hands folded like clusters of blossoms:
"In the past, when the sprouts of the Buddhas had ascended the flower-thrones, now,
at this very time, you likewise ascend the throne."
"A thousandfold world-system, consisting of a thousand times ten thousand worlds, will ceaselessly undergo dissolution;
by that [merit] you shall become a Buddha.
Having heard these words of the deities, sweet to the ear, he reflected upon them.
With even greater energy born of his mind, his body suffused with rapture,
that wise one reflected upon how many factors conducive to enlightenment he had previously cultivated through association with the Supreme Being,
so as to realize the element of Dhamma together with its cause.
O wise one, having struck the ground and placed a full water-jar there,
after all the water has been poured out, what indeed could one bring back?
Even so, having given away wealth, children, wife, limbs, and even life—
"May I not become disenchanted," he thus resolved upon the first perfection;
disregarding it as if it were his own life, he wandered about protecting the yak-tail fan that shone with the luster of the moon, as if guarding his very life.
Thus, O steadfast one, you of pure virtue, having been entreated,
took up this second perfection as a guardian of the gate to the city of supreme peace;
you who were moved with awe while dwelling for a long time in that terrible prison-house.
Just as he brought about liberation from that [bondage] so that he might be intent on renunciation,
even so you should become disenchanted with this prison-like existence.
Thus entreated, for a third time he set out toward the further shore, walking alone.
Just as a mendicant monk, wandering for alms from house to house among families high and low,
does not long remain established in restraint; so too, for the sake of full enlightenment,
associate with those who are capable and wise, and ask them questions when you are in doubt.
"You were requested for the fourth perfection, O wise one;
like a lion roaming its own domain, ever courageous, so do you, O Sumedha,
abide in standing, walking, lying down, and sitting."
"Exertion"—he who was slack in energy for the sake of enlightenment urged himself on;
he, possessing firm energy, fulfilled the fifth perfection.
Like the earth, O Lord, toward all that is desirable and undesirable, and toward every honor and dishonor...
"Without falling into mental distress, being patient and forbearing,
may you be one who endures those who would harm others for the sake of perfect enlightenment"— thus did he, the Preacher of Patience,
who delighted in the welfare of others, entreat [the Bodhisatta] regarding the sixth perfection.
Just as the medicinal star does not overstep its course, its fixed law,
so too, O wise one, you who are well-practiced in the highest truth,
do not at any time transgress it, for you desire perfect awakening.
He who spoke the truth thus requested the seventh perfection;
though he strove with great force from that place toward the forest,
he remained there for an eon, as immovable as a mountain firmly established on level ground.
"Stand firm, just as you have resolved, in these dharmas of determination!
Thus he spoke, like one who has descended [into the water]; and he fulfilled the eighth perfection (*pāramitā*) toward those submerged in the lake of existence, whether lowly or noble.
Just as coolness spreads equally through water, so too,
with a mind of loving-kindness, he cultivated it toward all beings within the three realms of existence;
thus, with a heart full of mettā, he fulfilled the ninth perfection.
When desirable and undesirable objects have been encountered,
just as this daughter-in-law of Vasumatī remains neutral toward both suffering and pleasure, so too,
O friend, be one who possesses a balanced scale— a peaceful one who looks with equanimity.
The one of great wisdom fulfilled the tenth perfection; shaking the ocean of perfections as far as the realm of the Thirty-Three, that Lord of Beings,
possessed of sharp intelligence, stood firm upon the mountain of knowledge.
The Earth, the consort of Vasu, gave a cry of "Well done!
as it trembled at that moment due to the power of the Dharma of the mindful one;
we are terrified, for this vast earth has shaken violently.
Having reached the vicinity of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, who dwelt in Ramma, they questioned him;
the earth trembled violently—what was the cause of that?
Having reflected, the Sage understood it and explained the matter to them.
Free from doubt, the citizens of that city again approached him and worshipped his pair of feet with perfumes,
garlands, and other offerings; having formed their hands into lotuses in añjali, they [honored] the Lord Dīpaṅkara.
That man of supreme strength rose from his seated place:
"May no disease befall you, may there be no fear or trembling;
may your intention, your highest aspiration, be swiftly fulfilled."
Thus, having reached the field of his birth,
the aged ascetics honored that Jaṭila with hundreds of words of praise and with flowers and other offerings; then,
ascending the path of the forest, they delighted the minds of the deities.
While that ascetic had reached his own hermitage on Mount Himavat,
the sun, garlanded with rays, arrived at the Mountain of the Setting Sun;
having caused the forest of lotuses to close and withdrawn its web of beams.
The delightful dwelling place of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, named Rammavatī;
his two parents, Sudeva and Sumedhā; and his two chief attendant monks, Sāgata and Maṅgala.
Tissocā were the first and second disciples of that elder-nāga;
surrounded by various ones whose taints were exhausted,
Nandā and Sunandā were his first and second female disciples, the foremost among them.
The Bodhi tree named Pipphali stood fifty ratanas in height;
for a hundred thousand years it remained there, delivering the multitude of people.
Then, after a long time, appeared the Teacher named Dīpaṅkara, a lamp illuminating the refuge for gods and men.
Like a lamp, he dwelt as a lamp of Dhamma within the mansion of the three worlds, dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
like a mass of fire, he shone forth and then attained Parinibbāna.
Though his taints were exhausted, the noble disciples—like lamps whose oil is spent and whose flames have gone out—were likewise extinguished.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Establishment of the Foundation for the Ascetic Sumedha," in the *Jitavaṃsadīpa*— the cause of joy for the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda,
which is a distant foundation [for the lineage]. Then the Blessed One named Koṇḍañña, like a moon awakening a bed of night-lotuses, awakened the world.
Then, having been born as Varamati, King Vijitāvin possessed the perfect Wheel-Treasure and became a wheel-turning monarch;
he gave a magnificent gift to the Sangha headed by the Buddha.
Having given [the gift] and made a vow for supreme enlightenment,
he renounced his kingdom, entered the teaching of the Conqueror,
and attained the meditative absorptions (jhānas) as a result of that excellent gift.
His city was named Rammavatī;
Sunanda was his father and Sujātā his mother;
Bhadda and Subhadda were his excellent disciples.
The three excellent female lay disciples of the ascetic Tissāpatissa—
Lakkhāyukā, Vijayabodhi, and Visālasālā—
and the one named Kalyāṇī, as well as Anuruddha, attended upon him.
Her body measured eighty cubits;
she had three assemblies of noble disciples.
After that, at another time, here in this world, occurred the breaking of her limbs.
The Victor Maṅgalajina was born for the sake of the world’s welfare;
at that time, there was one named Suruci, a most radiant sprout of the Buddhas,
a banner of the twice-born lineage, who dwelt in Avati.
Having given seven gifts to the Conqueror together with his disciples,
he aspired for peerless Enlightenment through the gift of a cow’s drink;
and having been prophesied by the Blessed One, he departed from his existence.
Having gone forth, he experienced the bliss born of concentration.
His father was Uttara, the ruler of that excellent city;
his preceptors were Sudeva and Dhammasena.
His pair of chief disciples were Bhadda and Sāvali,
and his two female disciples were Sivalī and Asokā.
Pālita attended upon that Conqueror for eighty-eight years.
Hattha was his son, whose body was like a diamond;
Bodhi was the Nāga-tree, and the disciples were peaceful;
their lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After that, the Protector Sumana, a treasury of compassion who subdues the mind’s restlessness,
arose in the world; at that time,
he was the incomparable King of Nāgas, a sprout of the Buddhas.
Blazing with a mass of fiery flames and possessing incomparable supernatural power, that Nāga, even while in his own abode,
paid homage to the Buddha and his disciple with celestial musical instruments.
Having given incomparable gifts, he made a vow:
"May you become a Buddha. Thus he spoke, and the Buddha was born.
His father was Sudanta, and the city was named Khema.
The King, the glorious one, was the father of his own disciples;
Saraṇa and Vasi were the foremost among them, having cultivated their own selves.
You, Soṇā, were the foremost female ascetic (samaṇī) among them, likewise well-disciplined (upasoṇā).
His Bodhi tree was the Nāgataru;
his founding Elder was Udena Thera.
His lifespan was ninety thousand years, and his body measured ninety cubits in height.
There were three assemblies of noble disciples;
thereafter, there arose here on earth one named Revata,
a god among gods whose feet are worshipped by the gods and others.
Then there will be one named Atideva, the best among beings,
an ornament to the lineage of those who address others as "Bho," a knower of the four Vedas;
with palms joined at his head, he shall listen to the discourse on the Dhamma.
Having gone to that supreme refuge, the most excellent, and having given,
she then aspired for the ocean of happiness; "O Great Seer,
you will soon become a Buddha," thus Visākhā spoke.
His mother was Mahesī Vipulā, whose city was named Dhaññavatī;
his father was Vipula, who,
in the midst of the Saṅgha, became like Brahmā, Varuṇa, and the best of gods.
Bhaddā and the pair of Bhaddās—these two types of Subhaddās;
Sambhava dwelt there and served him.
Nāgabodhi was the tree, and his own person became the jewel of the sword.
The lifespan was sixty thousand years,
and there were three assemblies of noble disciples;
at another time, there was Janapārijāta.
Then there arose the Victor Sobhita, who had conquered the five Māras;
he was a master of all the Vedas and possessed vast wealth.
He was the sprout of a future Buddha, destined to become one named Ajita.
Having reflected upon the Dhamma and established himself in the refuges,
the wise man gave a magnificent gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and made a solemn aspiration for exertion.
"You shall attain supreme enlightenment," he said, for you are a great Teacher.
His delightful city was called Sudhamma;
the king was Sudhamma, his father, and his mother was Sudhammā.
His pair of chief disciples were the peerless Sunetta and his sister Nakula, Sujātā, the most excellent among women;
the Bodhi tree of this Naga-like Buddha was the Nāgataru. His body was eight cubits in height.
The Elder Tamotama was five cubits in height;
his lifespan was ninety thousand years,
and there were three assemblies of noble disciples.
Not long after that, there arose the Buddha Anomadassi,
whose eyes were as pure as a blooming lotus and as blue as a clear sky;
he was a sprout of Buddhahood who had then conquered the hosts of gods and enemies, O Yakkha.
He will become a general of great psychic power and majesty;
that man, on the path to full enlightenment, made this aspiration:
"May I give a magnificent gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha."
The Victor said, "Having established yourself in the three refuges,
you shall become a Buddha"; for it was indeed possible that [the son] named Candavatī and [the daughter] named Yasodharā [would attain enlightenment].
His mother was Mahesī, his father was the illustrious Janaka,
lord of men; his pair of chief disciples were Nisabha and Atoma,
and Sundarī and Sumanā were his two female attendants.
Bodhi was his Kakudha tree; the Sage’s body measured eighty cubits;
and the elder named Varuṇa served him, his lifespan being one hundred thousand years.
There were three assemblies of noble disciples;
after that, Paduma, the lord of bipeds, was born— one whose mind is awakened like a lotus, a lotus among those who possess wisdom.
Then the lion, whose neck was graced by a mass of beautiful manes and who could split the temples of the finest elephants,
became steadfast as he experienced the bliss of cessation within the Buddha.
Having honored him for seven days with offerings of incense for his eyes,
Sīha— having regained the granting of the boon— spoke once more to the disciples who had returned with their minds full of faith.
His father was King Paduma of Campakapura, and his mother was Asamā;
Sāla and Upasāla were his two excellent disciples.
Rāmā too, his most excellent and peerless wife,
attended upon him by name; Varuṇa was under her control,
and his body measured fifty cubits in height.
Bodhi was also a *soṇa* tree; his lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and there were three assemblies of noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).
After him came the Sage named Nārada, the giver of boons.
Then the sprout of a Buddha arose, terrifying the mass of the darkness of evil;
he was a master of asceticism who had attained all the knowledges and super-knowledges, and lived on fallen fruit.
Having made a sublime aspiration and having given a magnificent gift to the Conqueror together with his disciples,
Muḷāraviro honored him with fragrant yellow sandalwood.
The Teacher also gave a prediction at that time:
"In the city named Dhaññavatī, there was a king named Sumedha;
he was the father, and Anomā was his mother."
The two dwellers at Bhaddasāla, Jita and Mitta, [attained] the path in the interval;
the female ascetic Phagguṇī among the bhikkhunīs;
and the bhikkhu Vāseṭṭha attended upon him, [seeing] his physical body.
His Bodhi tree was the Mahāsīsa-śākhin,
an Aṣṭaśrī-ratna; his lifespan was ninety thousand years,
and there were three assemblies of noble disciples.
After him was born the Dhamma-king Padumuttara,
a lotus among the three worlds, with feet marked by lotuses;
he was wealthy, of magnificent fortune, and a great ruler.
At that time, he who was named Jaṭila became Buddhaṅkura;
having made an aspiration for the conditions necessary for the attainment of perfect enlightenment at the feet of Padumuttara, he performed various acts of service.
Deeply devoted to the Three Jewels, she gave three sets of the triple robe to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha;
for that Victor, there was a city named Haṃsavatī.
Ānandabhupati was his father and Sujātā his mother;
among those dwelling in Devala and Sujāta, these two became the foremost, equal to the best of female ascetics.
A tree named Sumanā, a vast *sāla* tree with a lifespan of a hundred thousand years and possessing the splendor of a *jaya-bodhi*, stood in attendance upon the Sage;
its body measured eighty cubits.
There were three assemblies of the Blessed One’s followers;
later, at another time,
a teacher named Sumedha appeared in the world for the welfare of the world.
It is said that at that time there was another well-born youth named Uttara,
who possessed a fortune of eighty crores;
having distributed that wealth of eighty crores, he—
Having given a gift to this Sugata together with the Saṅgha,
he went forth into homelessness aspiring for supreme enlightenment;
the Sage predicted that his state would not be barren for such a long time.
There was a delightful and beautiful city named Sudassana;
its king was Sudanta, his father, and his mother was Sudattā.
He took refuge in the Saṅghas and lived fulfilling all desires.
The women were supremely beautiful; the Bodhi tree was a *nīpa* tree;
and the elder named Sāgara established [the dispensation] when the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
Her body rose up to eighty cubits,
and she possessed three assemblies of followers who were mindful.
Later, at another time, there was a lamp for the people...
Born as one of noble birth, the Blessed One,
who had conquered the five Māras, became at that time a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa),
a supreme Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin) endowed with the seven treasures.
Rejoicing in the nectar of the Dhamma, the wise one gave away his sovereignty over the four continents along with the seven treasures and his own person to the Two Jewels,
and having made a vow for enlightenment, he went forth into homelessness.
Knowing his state of ignorance, the Great Sage spoke:
"There was a delightful and most auspicious city named Uggata;
the king was my father and my mother was named Pabhāvati."
The Sudassana deities and the Elder Theras were foremost,
as were the Nāgas and the Elder Nāgasamālā who appeared before the assembly;
the sage Nārada, being self-possessed, attended upon them.
The Bodhi tree was made of bamboo and measured fifty cubits;
his lifespan was ninety thousand years,
and there were three assemblies of the faithful for that wise one.
After her, here in this world, there was born one of incomparable beauty, Piyadassi Samantadassi;
the wise one became the brahmin Kassapa, who was different from the others.
Skilled in the three Vedas, he sought what is wholesome;
by means of the *Dhatubhaya* consisting of one million verses,
he [constructed] a great monastery for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Having performed this, he gave it away, having aspired to the state of a Buddha;
the Buddha also spoke thus: "May there be the fulfillment of that aspiration.
His mother was named Candā, and his father was named Pudinna.
There was a king whose city bore an unsurpassed name;
at its head were two pairs of queens:
Sujātā, who gave the Dharma to the assembly, and Pakālitasabbadassī, who looked upon all with clarity.
The ascetic Sotavha attended upon him;
Bodhi was the Piyaṅgu Buddha, eighty cubits in height,
and he stood for ninety thousand years.
There were three assemblies of the wise; later, at another time,
there arose in the world a sage named Atthadassī,
who delighted in accomplishing the welfare of the world.
At that time, there was also a seer named Susīma, the seventh in the lineage of those whose nature is unsurpassable, possessing the power of fire-like psychic potency;
having brought celestial flowers from a divine abode for him—
Having worshipped Mandāravā flowers upon a well-established footstool,
the Teacher made this aspiration:
"In the future, you shall become like me," he said.
His father was King Bhavisāgara, his mother Queen Sudassanā,
and his excellent disciples were the monks Santopa and Santa.
The Dhammas became the most excellent of all, and they were well-spoken;
Abhayo, that sage, attended upon him, and his lifespan reached one hundred thousand years,
with eighty thousand elephants at his command.
Campeyya, Sākhi, and Bodhi, who were the causes for his perfect enlightenment—
these three were known as noble disciples.
After him, Dhammadassi arose here in this world.
That supreme master of the training beyond the boundary, who sees the further shore of existence,
was at that time, it is said, the king of the gods, a Buddha-sprout of great majesty within the realm of the Thirty-three.
He honored with divine perfumes and flowers the state of Buddhahood,
whose lotus-throne consists of broad feet marked with wheels,
as he was engaged in conversation; and he honored it with divine musical instruments.
Thus, aspiring to the state of a silent sage, he spoke of his own nature;
he took refuge in that Sugata as his fixed resort.
The King was his father, named Saraṇa, and Sunandā was his mother.
Padumāvatī was foremost among the goddesses,
Phussadevī and Khemā were foremost among the female monastics, and all those named [after them];
the elder Sunetta, renowned for his wisdom, attended upon him.
Jayabodhi was a hundred thousand years of age,
as was Bimbijāla; his body measured eighty cubits,
and there were three assemblies of noble disciples.
At a later time, he arose as a teacher known by the name Siddhattha, one whose awakening was accomplished; at that time,
he was a sprout of a Buddha, having attained the fire of the immovable jhānas.
The one named Maṅgala lived on fruit provided by the Bhojī;
having brought from the forest a single ripe *jambu* fruit from a noble family tree,
which was endowed with perfect fragrance and flavor, he [lived].
He made a vow for Buddhahood at his feet,
and the Blessed One, having experienced that [vow], prophesied it;
Jayasena by name ascended into the air over the city.
Janaka was his father and Suphassā his mother;
many monks were under his influence, and Sumitta was his dear friend;
Sīvalī and Surāmā were the two excellent nuns among the female renunciants.
That sage Revata arose as a lord of sages;
his Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra, and he, the charioteer of men,
had a life-span of one hundred thousand years and a stature of sixty cubits.
There were three assemblies of noble disciples;
after him, there arose here another teacher named Nissaya, whose conduct was praised and who had crossed over the four floods.
Then the well-born King Sujāta became a sprout of Buddhahood,
his footstool adorned with the crest-jewels of noble kshatriyas;
having abandoned kingship, that steadfast one donned the robes of a sage.
As the Conqueror was proceeding, he honored him with many celestial flowers,
his head becoming radiant like a parasol;
the Teacher also spoke, saying, "May his aspiration be fulfilled."
For King Janaka, whose name signifies the gathering of people, begot Khema— the lotus-like city— amidst his own assembly;
[therein arose] the two renowned Thera-Nāgas, the originators of the Brahma-devas.
Phussā and Aggayugalā were his chief female disciples;
Sambhavā attended upon him, the Lord of the World.
His Bodhi tree was named Asana, and its purpose was fulfilled.
The Great Seer remained for a hundred thousand years by the count of rain-falls;
there were three assemblies of noble disciples.
After that, he saw the shore of the ocean of existence.
The great sage Phussa appeared here in this world; at that time,
the wise one, victorious and having conquered the host of his enemies,
became a king with splendor like that of the lord of the gods.
A man on the path to full enlightenment,
having made his aspiration and renounced a flourishing kingdom, went forth from the world;
having mastered the Three Piṭakas, he preached the Dhamma to the people.
The Blessed One Phussa, like previous Buddhas, made a prophecy for him:
"In the city of Kāsī, there will be a king named Jayasena; he will be your father, and his queen will be Janati Sirimā."
Cālā and Upacālā, who were well-guarded in the Dhamma by the Saṅgha,
offered their finest pairs of garments to the Bodhi tree, the Amalaka tree,
and the Śāla trees that had served as the Buddha’s resting places.
The one named Sabhiya, who was five cubits in height,
lived for ninety thousand years;
there were three assemblies of the disciples for the Blessed One.
After him, the essence of beings among men and gods,
the Teacher Vipassī, the all-seeing one, arose here, possessing great power and majesty through some past karma.
At that time, there was a king of nāgas named Buddhaṅkura;
he offered to Aṅgīrasa a seat made of solid gold,
adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Thus, having sat down there and being requested by Mahī, the Victorious One, Vipassī, the Bodhisatta who aspired to the state of Buddhahood,
gave his prophecy: "His city shall be named Bandhumatī."
Nāmo was his father and Jananī Bandhumatī his mother, the great queen;
Khaṇḍatissa and Vasin were two excellent disciples,
while Candā and Candamittā formed a noble pair of female lay followers.
The Elder Tamasoka established his body upon the Bodhi tree, which had dark branches;
there the Sage dwelt for eighty thousand years.
There were three assemblies of noble disciples;
thereafter, the Teacher Sikhī arose, who was like a branch of the world’s lineage, possessing higher virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Then there was a wise king named Arindama,
full of faith and possessing abundant wealth in the Three Jewels;
he gave alms that were delightful with ornaments of the seven precious gems.
Having recognized the Elephant-Treasure in the Sugata together with the Saṅgha, that essence among beings aspired to the state of Buddhahood;
the Teacher declared: "You shall obtain the supreme state of happiness."
The city of Cāruvatī was the Buddha’s [birthplace];
his mother was Pabhāvatī and his father was the king named Aruṇa;
among the Saṅghas were Abhibhū and Sambhava.
They were the foremost, named Makhila and Upaduma;
Khemaṅkara attended upon the Victor for thirty-seven years.
Vijaya, Bodhi, Puṇḍarīka, and Hatthucchita—these were the names of those who stood supreme.
Thus you were one whose lifespan measured thirty-seven thousand years;
there were three assemblies of his disciples;
and after him, here on earth, Ketumāla arose.
At that time, it is said, the Buddha-sprout named Sudassana was the king known as Vessabhū,
who shone with the radiance of his arms and was a lion among the lordly elephants of rival kings.
Having given an incomparable gift of robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha within the teaching of the Victor,
he went forth into homelessness, aspiring for the enlightenment of omniscience.
"You will certainly become a Buddha," the Teacher said to her.
"Her father will be Anopama-pura, and her mother will be the illustrious Mahesī, the queen."
And Soṇuttarā was among his own male and female disciples,
while Dāmā was supreme in wisdom and psychic power, and Samālā was supreme;
Bodhi, too, shall be his great Sāla tree.
The perfected bhikkhu served him with a sixty-cubit [staff];
the Teacher dwelt for sixty thousand years,
and there were three "thunderbolt-falls" from his chief disciples.
After him, another was born from that same lineage:
the Blessed One named Kakusandha, the Kinsman of those to be trained.
At that time, he was the Buddha-sprout upon the earth, a king of peace.
With his hands thoroughly cleansed by the sprinkling of the water-stream of his continuous acts of giving,
he— having provided food and drink sufficient for the bowl and robes— went from his house to the Conqueror and his disciples.
The King went forth into homelessness having made a vow for enlightenment;
thus the Teacher spoke regarding the fulfillment of that vow.
His father was Aggidatta, and his city was named Khemavatī.
The wise Vipassī was her father, Visākhā her mother;
the Elder Sañjīva and the Elder Vidhura were her two chief brothers, and Sāmā was the eldest of the pair; Campaka was her name.
The Buddha-son Upaṭṭhāka attended upon that Victor;
his body was thirty cubits in measure, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.
His Bodhi tree was glorious, and his life-span was thirty thousand years.
He shall have but a single assembly of disciples; later,
at another time, he will be a treasury of compassion,
a conqueror of the world, with a form as beautiful as the golden mountain.
Then there arose the sage named Pabbata,
a great personage who was a lord of the earth;
he gave a magnificent gift to the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha.
Having given away his most precious and costly robes and garments, he went forth into homelessness, having aspired to the state of a Buddha.
The Teacher said to him: "You shall become a Buddha."
That city shall be renowned by the name Uttarā;
her mother shall be named Avanisurā, her father Yaññadatta,
and her sister Samuddā, a nun who dwells in the higher realms.
Tassa and Uttara were the supreme among the assemblies.
Sotthija attended upon that Jina; he was thirty cubits tall.
Aṅgīrasa became his Bodhi tree, an Udumbara branch.
Thus, you were one whose lifespan measured thirty thousand years,
and you alone were his disciple, the Peaceful One.
After him, O Great Sage, there was another here named Kassapa.
In this world, he appeared like the single horn of a rhinoceros;
at that time, Jotipāla was born upon the earth as a sprout of a Buddha,
skilled in all three Vedas and in every branch of knowledge.
With the virtuous friend as his companion, that young man approached the Sugata;
having heard the Dhamma and its instruction,
he set out to attain omniscience.
The Sage Kassapa also prophesied in the past:
"In the city of Bārāṇasī, there will be two parents named Brahmadatta and Dhanavanta."
Among the monks and among the nuns,
Tissabhāradvāja and Bhaddayugala, as well as Anuruddha and Uruvelā—
Sabbamitta the ascetic attended upon them all.
The Bodhi tree was a Nigrodha with branches twenty cubits in height;
his lifespan was twenty thousand years;
and there was but a single assembly of noble disciples.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Establishment of the Bodhisatta’s Remaining Aspirations," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda— a work that serves as the primary cause for bestowing joy upon the hearts of all poets and contains the distant origins [of the lineage].
Herein lies the great treasure of the aspirations made at Laṅkā at the feet of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara.
The Bodhisatta performed an outpouring of merit numbering four hundred and one lakhs;
in the interval between these, various external objects arose.
That hero, for the sake of the welfare of his people alone, renounced his head, bones, flesh, and blood, as well as his children and wife,
and even his very life, to beggars who were wretched and destitute.
Seeking out those devoted to generosity, he entered [the forest];
having reached the grove of asceticism belonging to the one whose wealth is austerity,
he received for three days a cartload of saltless sour gruel.
When the Brahmin Saṅkha, whose belly was overcome by hunger and thirst, saw the Paccekabuddha Mahiya—
who had set out on a path through the wilderness and carried a bowl—
[he offered him food]. (The Deeds of Akitti)
Touched by the heat of the sun’s rays, he who was intent on his own duty gave an umbrella and sandals with hands well-washed; (this is the *Saṅkhacariya*).
From the fear of oppression by famine in the kingdom of Kaliṅga...

O Dhanañjaya, when that king approached the Nāga king who had come begging, he took his own collyrium with his trunk and offered it as a libation of water for the sake of the funeral rites. (The Practice of the Kurudhamma)
Having been the Great Sudassana, a wheel-turning monarch in the city of Kusāvatī,
day and night, he practiced and caused others to practice the giving of clothing, alms-food, and drink.
To all the beggars who came from every quarter, [he gave]— (The Life of Mahāsudassana)—
he who was the priest of the king ruling over the sevenfold earth,
even though he had received from the kings an entire mass of wealth and grain.
Having renounced his wealth for the sake of those who came as supplicants,
he accumulated a continuous stream of merit for the cause of enlightenment; even the king named Nimi,
following the Dhamma, practiced the life of Mahāgovinda.
He who, having constructed a four-faced palace for Mithilā,
formerly gave gifts of uncut hair, heads, people, birds, and quadrupeds—
he who was the most excellent among givers; (The Life of King Nimi).
He who, having been Prince Canda, the son of a single king,
was going forth among the people for the sake of the head-anointing ceremony,
was moved to renunciation even by the three worlds with all their splendor.
Having established a boundary, he set in motion the wheel of giving; (The Life of Prince Candaka).
He who, though already dissatisfied with grasping for the essence of material things, [sought] even from the Lord of the Earth the one named Sivi, the sovereign of the gods.
Having plucked out his eyes, which were seized by the power of congenital blindness, he obtained divine vision; (this was the conduct of King Śibi.
As for the Wise Hare, who was supremely devoted to generosity:

Having been exhorted by his friends and firmly resolved upon the observance of the Uposatha, he leapt from the charcoal mound, risking his very life, desiring to give his own flesh and body to the bird.
(The Story of the Wise Hare; thus ends the Perfection of Giving.)
He who, devoted to supporting his mother,
rescued her from the blind elephant-tamer’s female elephant,
even though she was firmly seized by its trunk and was not yet struggling free.
Out of fear of breaking his virtue, he did not give way to anger; (The Story of Mātuposaka) He who was the serpent Bhuridatta,
though dwelling in a place devoid of a shell,
maintained his vows and observances, remaining established in concentration, like a snake possessing poison.
When the snake was cast into the basket by the snake-charmer, you abandoned your anger out of fear of violating your virtue; (this is the *Bhuridatta-jātaka*);
you who were rich in virtue, vows, and other perfections, and possessed of blazing supernormal powers.
The serpent named Campeyya, while in the snake-charmer’s basket, roamed at will like a yak-cow among its tail-locks;
he guarded his virtue and did not even become angry when his own slayer approached. (The Story of Campeyya)
And Cūḷabodhi, who was well-known and held in high regard,
having abandoned his virtuous conduct and observances, went to live in the forest out of love for his wife;
and when she had been seized by force by the King of Kāsi—
Devoted to purifying his virtue, he abandoned anger; (The Deeds of Cūḷabodhi)— he who,
though a buffalo of terrifying form, was pure in virtue, patient,
and free from resentment even when Valimukha approached him.
Having rejected the words of the tree-dwelling yakkhas,
he released him from the fear of breaking his virtue,
he who rescued one being swept away by the current of a river.
For the sake of giving his own life to a cow that was about to kill her calf,
the King released the hare-colored deer Ruru from execution without agitation; (this is the story of the conduct of Ruru, the king of deer.)
The sage named Mātaṅga protected the wealth of his virtue,
even though a wrathful matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila) with a mass of matted hair and tooth-sticks had cast a spell upon him.
By the power of the accomplishment of the *sampāta-sāpa* protection;
(The *Mātaṅga-cariya*: the base one who has entered the path, longing for strife, whose two chariot-parts are struck down by the Dhamma-yakkha.)
The King of Dhamma-yakkhas, who indeed protected his virtue and did not allow himself to be consumed by the fire of anger or by sloth,
[practiced] the conduct of the sons of the gods regarding what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma—
[he was] Jayaddisa, who had fallen under the power of a man-eater.
Relying on the king’s promise, Alīnasatta, with his weapons laid aside, approached and tamed the yakkha;
was this not indeed due to the power of his virtue and vows? (The Story of Alīnasatta)
The serpent Saṅkhapāla, whose body was so massive that it could not even bear the weight of the burden of his own coils as he slithered along,
felt compassion for Bhojaputta because of the latter's lack of feet.
Out of fear of breaking his virtue, he was like the heat of a fire; thus [ends] the Saṅkhapāla-jātaka (the Perfection of Virtue).
Yudhañjaya, who saw the nature of conditioned phenomena as momentary and subject to destruction, like the dissolving of a dewdrop—
King Yudhañjaya, the son of the Kuru king renowned for his joyfulness,
having renounced his kingdom while his people were weeping, went forth into homelessness and reached the perfection of renunciation. (The Life of Yudhañjaya)
On account of the words of the immoral Kuṭaja-jaṭila,
having been commanded by the king to carry out an execution and having found an opportunity to kill,
he departed from the kingdom after being instructed; (this was the conduct of Somanassa.)
He who was born as the son of the King of Kāsi, named Ayoghara,
having long been steadfast in his dwelling at Ayoghara,
abandoned the supreme kingdom bestowed by his father.
He who had reached the perfection of renunciation entered the forest; (this is the practice of Ayoghara.
Having rejected even the words of his friends and kinsmen, which were offered because of their concern for the five strands of sensual pleasure, he departed.
Kañcana, whose skin was like refined gold, reached the forest of asceticism and went forth from home with his kinsmen; (this is the account of Bhisacariya:
he was like a piece of raw meat thrown into a fire.
He whose mind turned away from the realm of conditioned phenomena—that wise Soṇa Bhūsura—abandoning his wealth, went to the forest with his retinue to go forth.
(The Story of the Wise Soṇa; thus is the perfection of renunciation.)
The far-sighted Seṇaka, who dwelt within the womb of a quiver,
clearly perceived the serpent, most terrifying,
that had appeared to the mind of Vippassi, which was turbid with delusion.
The wise Senaka, the lord of the wise, who was like Mahosadha in intellect and equal to Ummagga,
Saṃvuta, and Nisagga, fulfilled the perfection of wisdom, O Earth-Minded One.
(This is the life-story of the sage Senaka.)
Just as from the Ummagga [Jātaka], the Lord of Pañcāla released the King of Mithilā along with his army from the enemy;
(this is the Mahosadha Cariyā, thus the Perfection of Wisdom);
and with the vigor of a bull, through his heroism, he [overcame] the terrible...
Like the suffering of saṃsāra, though he was thin and dark-skinned,
that compassionate essence of beings, Kālaka,
constantly strove to drain the waters of the deep ocean. (The Deeds of Kālaka)
The Great King Janaka and others were like moons amidst a field of lotuses;
he who crossed the ocean of profound human existence— that very mine of waters—
was a hero whose valor lay in his noble arms.
In crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, he was like a boat; (this is the Mahājanaka Cariya; thus ends the Perfection of Energy.
He whose heart was full of patience, who spoke with patience and self-restraint—even when his entire body was being cut to pieces—
He sprinkled the water of perfected patience as his ornament upon the king of the forest of reeds that was burning with the fire of malice;
he who was devoted to protecting the Dhamma was indeed a true protector of the Dhamma. (The Life of Khantivādī)
Even when the executioner was commissioned by him, the King fell into the Neighboring Hell;
yet he maintained patience, his sole friend being the virtue of patience. (The Life of Dhammapāla; thus ends the Perfection of Patience.)
He who, having become a king of monkeys, placed his foot upon the head of the terrifying crocodile of the middle of the ocean,
fulfilled the promise he had given— a promise that could not be obtained by any other.
The King of Monkeys, who dwelt facing the opposite bank of the river of existence,
fearless of the unreal, was devoted to the perfection of truth; seeing with truth, he lived at the junction of the earth of truth by means of truth.
In the glorious Jambudīpa, while maintaining harmony among the people, he who was like a young bird whose wings had not yet grown spoke these words to the entire world: (The Life of Saccasavbhaya).
He who was like a fledgling bird with undeveloped wings—
Sleeping in a very small bird’s nest with only one foot,
he extinguished a forest fire with the truth over an area of sixteen karīs,
remaining steadfast until the end of his life. (The Story of Vaṭṭapotaka)
The King of Cranes, though his own kinsmen had become food for vultures, crows, and herons,
liberated them from the parching heat of the summer sun in a waterless lake.
O King of Snakes, by means of truth— which is the condition for the arrival of unseasonable clouds—
you, the noble ascetic Maṇḍabya, tasted the sacrificial offering given by Araṇyadatta,
even though he was unconscious from the force of the venom of the snake’s fang.
Having performed an act of truth out of compassion,
the sage Kaṇhadīpāyana released him from that calamity; (this is the life-story of Kaṇhadīpāyana,) who was once a king named Sutasoma under the sway of a man-eater.
In his kingdom of three hundred leagues, and even for the sake of his own life, did he not guard the truth?
For one devoted to truth is free from despair, fulfilling the mutual agreement between both parties. (The Story of Sutasoma; Thus ends the Perfection of Truth.)
One who has grown weary of the splendors of royalty and,
out of fear of existence, acts like a mute and deaf person among the mutes—
when he was led to the site of the charnel ground to be buried alive—
"O, you have not abandoned us, who were firmly resolved! (The Temiya Jātaka; thus ends the Perfection of Resolution.
He who was devoted to dwelling in loving-kindness for the sake of his blind father, who was exceedingly compassionate and golden-hued,"
Surrounded by wild beasts, dwelling in the forest,
he who was the King of Kāsi, renowned throughout the earth as a sole monarch, fulfilled the perfection known as loving-kindness,
being fearful of evil. (The conduct of one with a golden complexion.)
Accompanied by his wife Mettā, even regarding his own life, he remained undaunted when the hostile king’s royal authority was severed;
through the equal cultivation of loving-kindness, he pervaded him with metta. (The Conduct of the Sole King; thus ends the Perfection of Loving-Kindness.)
He who, though as pure as a swan’s down,
is equal to a scale in his response to honor and dishonor, pleasure and pain,
and who makes his dwelling in the midst of a charnel ground strewn with bones;
Having overcome enmity with non-enmity, he guarded himself with equanimity; (this was the conduct of Lomahaṃsa; thus I have described the various modes of equanimity).
He, firmly intent upon enlightenment, possessed of mature wisdom, was a sprout of a Buddha through the power of the perfections he had accumulated.
He was never born in the world-intervening hells, nor in the hells of Uru or Niraya; he never attained birth as a paṇḍaka,
a neuter, or one of the mute class.
He may not be reborn by birth as one blind from birth, deaf, female, or dull-witted;
nor as a fly, a mosquito, a stinging insect, an ant, or the like; nor even as a worm, a moth, or an elephant.
The scent-elephant did not attain the quality of broadness;
the slender, well-formed partridge did not attain the quality of delicacy;
and the *umdana* and *mammana* birds did not attain the quality of softness.
He did not attain such a state of being even more inferior;
he was not a slayer of his mother, nor a murderer of his father,
nor a schismatic of the Saṅgha, nor a killer of an Arhat.
There was no one with a wicked heart toward the Tathāgata,
nor anyone who caused blood to flow from his body;
those two [actions] were both warded off by the ripening of karma.
They lived adhering to views such as annihilationism,
yet he, being destined for certain enlightenment, never clung to their doctrine,
having faith in karma and its fruit.
Even in that existence where there exists merely the fourfold mental aggregate,
he did not take rebirth-linking among the non-percipient beings for the sake of performing merit,
because it was impossible. Pure—
At times, fearing conceptual proliferation, he remained indifferent to the five sense-pleasures;
at other times, though destined for enlightenment,
the sprout of a Buddha was indifferent even to long-lived existences and their comforts.
Having made this declaration of his resolve in this world of the living,
he was reborn there for the sake of fulfilling the thirty perfections.
Thus, that Bull among Men, at the Bodhi tree which is difficult to enter—
He who, delighting in the welfare of others, produced the collection of perfections and the qualities of Dhamma— acting as a ladder of thirty-two steps for the descent into the palace—
and who endured terrible suffering while wandering for a very long time through saṃsāra; ()

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Practice of Forming the Perfections," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda—a work that serves as the primary cause for bestowing joy upon the hearts of all poets—and which recounts the distant past.
In former times, the city of Jetuttara was endowed with various colored gems and possessed a wealth of meaning, like a path strewn with diverse jewels. (This is a *śleṣa* composition.)
With its moats serving as a girdle and its ramparts bound like a waist-cloth,
that royal capital shone like a bride adorned by her husband;
with the garlands of moonbeams from its jeweled peaks, it bore the splendor of the young moon-god.
In that place, the moon’s orb, together with its circle of rays,
became a source of longing for her; the golden rows of banners,
shimmering in their jeweled palaces— the abode of Lakshmi— caused the peacocks there to dance.
With the ornaments fashioned for the king of elephants,
with his tusks, and with streams of ichor, that city shone like a cloud;
the sky was turned grey by the dust raised by the hooves of the multitude of horses.
She brought the splendor of a canopy that wards off the sun’s heat;
with her dark-blue hair like seaweed, her face like a full-blown lotus,
her eyes like restless blue lilies, and her breasts like the plump bodies of swans.
With its pollen as the juice of its feet, obstructed by the hips of bees, and with the tinkling of its jewel-like swarms of bees, that lotus-pond was like a woman; (this is *śleṣa* [paronomasia]).
That royal capital was called "Kevakala," even without the presence of wish-fulfilling trees.
Like the royal capital of Viśāṇā, abounding in every excellence,
there was once in that city a king, a noble steed among men,
renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Vessantara.
Even while still a prince, devoted to the sport of giving,
he would take even the jewel-ornaments on the bodies of his nurses,
break them into pieces, and distribute them as alms to beggars.
Thus, having pointed out the external objects, he who was eight years old,
having ascended the palace, sat down and reflected:
"I shall give my own head, eyes, flesh, and blood."
The Great Being, cherished by happiness like the moon in its bright fortnight,
protected his subjects with the ten royal virtues after attaining the glory of sovereignty.
Once, while seated alone in the upper palace, that king—
He recollected the defilement of sensual pleasures and their danger, such as separation and so forth;
the king, delighting in renunciation and weary of existence and becoming,
took hold of the essence of prosperity and abandoned the excellence of royal splendor.
Like a noble elephant king from a forest ablaze with fire,
he went forth from the home while his circle of kinsmen wept;
[he departed] from that place beautifully adorned with groves of *campaka*, *asoka*, and *vakula* trees.
A place where peacocks sport in unbroken circles, where cuckoos warble,
a dwelling for many beasts and birds, a refuge for water-fowl,
and where the breeze is scented by the fragrance of blooming flowers.
A lake of lotuses overflowing with bees intoxicated by honey,
a mountain deepened by the roar of cascading waterfalls,
a mountain cave with a curved slope that can be gazed upon from afar.
Having reached the ascetic grove named Vaṅkagiri— a place difficult to enter—
that king, having obtained the renunciation of the sword and possessing a lovely appearance,
spent a long time practicing the holy life.
The chief queen of that king, named Maddī, who had been raised in luxury,
entered that forest of asceticism together with her sons and daughters.
At that time, the Brahmin Pūjaka, who was full of great desire, went to see Bīga.
He approached Vessantara, the essence of the sevenfold sacrifice, [saying]:
"I have need of laborers. To me, who was worn out by old age, he—having encountered that wise and compassionate one—begged for his son and daughter.
Desiring perfect enlightenment for the sake of liberation from the slavery of craving, he placed both the black antelope skin and the alms-bowl,
which contained the weight of his hair and beard,
into the vessel of his joined palms, moistened with water from the right hand.
Having bound her, the pitiless one delivered her away;
