then the King of the Gods, intent on giving and discerning the ripening of karmic results,
approached Maddi, who remained faithful to her husband.
Having washed his hands with the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*),
and having performed that ritual of dedication, the god abandoned the goddess Vippasā.
By the power of his perfections (*pāramitā*), the earth shook seven times.
The Earth, like a bride, as if receiving her approval, exclaimed, "Excellent!
Excellent! Thus did the King of Men, who was bringing the perfections to maturity, dwell in a palace floor adorned with the radiance of jewels.
In that place where nets of five-colored banners were stirred by the very gentle breeze,
which was as delightful as a symphony of the tinkling sounds from clusters of jeweled bells,
and which was made enchanting by divine dances, songs, and instrumental music;
Adorned with pavilions of Kandappa and decorated with theater-pavilions,
the sky was crowded and filled with the rays of their crest-jewels,
as if with hundreds of divine rainbows from the gods and divine kings.
From afar, amidst the winds of beautiful yak-tail fans that dispelled the radiance of the moon,
he was surrounded by Apsarases whose limbs were anointed with sandalwood paste from their breasts;
like a man awakened from sleep, he rejoiced in the Tusita abode of the Thirty-three gods.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn as one named Santusita;
dwelling in the Tusita abode amidst the five divine sensual pleasures,
that sole eye of the world enjoyed the five sense-faculties.
Then, in the ten thousand world-systems,
the deities gathered together in one place, having heard the joyful clamor concerning the Buddha;
they approached him where the Supreme Person was.
Having made their lotus-like faces— the abodes of swarms of bees that were their eyes—
into a gesture of salutation, they joined their hands in the form of a lotus bud before the seat of his feet,
which was illuminated by the spray of rays from his crest-jewel, and paid him homage.
O Noble One, having aspired to the state of a Wheel-turning Monarch,
a Sakka, a Māra, or a Brahmā, you brought the perfections to fulfillment;
desiring perfect enlightenment, you acted as a kinsman to those capable of being trained.
"O worthy one, by her the ten perfections were fulfilled with great difficulty.
For the welfare of the world including the devas, they entreated that steadfast one, supreme in compassion, saying: 'May he be born from the mother's womb.'"
Because below a lifespan of one hundred years and above one million years is an improper time for Buddhas, he foresaw that it was the right time;
because in other continents fully enlightened ones do not arise.
Because they are born in Jambudvīpa, he understood that to be the continent;
because Tathāgatas do not arise in the lands of the barbarians,
but are born in the Middle Country, he understood that to be the region.
Because those who are not born from the womb of a Vessa or a Sudda are born [as such],
and because Buddhas and Brahmins are born from patience, therefore he was Vipassī by clan.
Because the womb of the Perfectly Awakened One’s mother had no other domain, [he was thus named].
Therefore, he beheld his mother by way of determining the limit of her lifespan.
Having thus performed these fivefold observations, the One with Eyes for the Whole World,
his mind filled with compassion, gave them his promise.
While the assembly of devas, their garlands of lotuses kissing their heads, was still gathered there,
the Lord of the Tusita realm descended into the Nandana Grove.
Having passed away from there, he was born into a family endowed with wisdom, generosity, and nobility.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Account of the Propitiation of the Devas, beginning with the Vessantara Jātaka," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda—a supreme gift that bestows joy upon the hearts of all poets—and containing the distant past (dūrenidāna).
This concludes the first section on the Distant Past in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*.
That city, born from the essence of all beings, the glory of Jambudīpa,
a crown jewel among cities like the prosperous Amarāvatī,
and the ground for the lineage of kings of the Solar dynasty—
In former times, the city of Kapilavatthu was the abode of the Lakṣyās;
it was endowed with qualities that were pleasing to the ear like the essence of music,
with forms born of beauty, and with multitudes of meanings joined by ascetics.
The royal capital, which was like a poetic composition (*vasantatilakā*) filled with the footprints of vast multitudes of living beings— [this is] a *śleṣa* construction—
belonged to the maiden Earth, whose arm-like creeper was the eastern direction.
Her circular wall, adorned with a girdle of conchs fastened together, shone like a mountain peak,
appearing like a crown due to its well-prepared plasterwork.
The moat of that city, like the capital of Indra,
shone with the ten beautiful banks whose waters were stirred by the pollen of lotuses, while rows of jewels and pearls were woven together like threads by swarms of bees.
Like a wall stained with red ochre, it was as if its garment had slipped away;
there, rogues intoxicated by the wine of the pride of Love sported beneath a canopy of deep blue creepers stirred by a gentle breeze.
In which [grove], the pleasure garden resembling a drinking hall,
was frequented by intoxicated female elephants, proud of their fresh youth,
as they drank with the cupped hands of their flickering eyes.
That royal capital, with its women whose faces were like the moon and whose thick,
swelling breasts were reflected in the mirrors of the finest gems in the theaters, surpassed the beauty of Lake Mānasa.
In that city, where the family of peacocks dwelling in their homes [was delighted] by the shimmering rays of the intended ornaments,
and by the showers of rut like the downpour of rain from the flocks of cranes that were the [Buddha’s] tusks;
Excellent elephants, like clouds of water,
sported there; outside the circle of the ramparts,
the mass of dust raised by the multitude of horses was struck down by mallets.
He created a moment of terror for the people descending upon the street,
which possessed the splendor of a blazing, spreading mass of fire; in that [moment],
the continuous stream of light from the jewels on the celestial palaces—
The orb of the sun, having been kissed by the moon,
attained a change of color as if overcome by anger,
as if it were being insulted by the lotus-faces of women.
They were occupied by lords of pillars,
beautiful and white as the lofty peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
and were constantly well-maintained with plaster.
In that city, where the dwellings resembled the abodes of Lakṣmī,
and where the tips of pavilions fashioned from sapphires and lapis lazuli were marked by the wandering of rows of golden banners;
At the peak of Mount Jīmūtakūṭa, like a garland of many lightning-flashes,
it produced a playful, sinless [joy] for women separated from their lovers,
with the rays of the jeweled archways glowing with the passion of twilight.
That royal capital, which dispels the mass of darkness for all the citizens and generates lofty joy,
was like a night-blooming lily to the women wandering at night with delight.
Its banks were thickly covered with *sevāla* moss and filaments;
it was filled with blooming red lotuses, blue lotuses, and white water-lilies,
and was delightful with the gathering of rows of swans and cranes.
In that city, where there were lotus-pools of perfectly clear water,
the lotus-faces of noble women vied with great effort to attain an incomparable splendor.
As long as the white-lotus moon and the sun travel on,
as if bound by mutual hostility, in that [city] where gold, silver, and copper-colored bamboo—
The marketplaces were filled with costly items such as pearls,
coral, and cat’s-eye gems, and with various shops abounding in fine silk,
linen, cotton, and garments of silk and fine cloth.
Armed with discuses, swords, bows, spears, maces,
and other weapons, clad in golden armor, they were conquerors of enemy hosts and exceedingly skilled at crossing the ocean of battle.
Where the warriors once provided protection in that foremost of cities,
there now, near the ramparts, the jeweled pavilions have crumbled like rows of autumn clouds white with cotton-wool.
At that moment, bestowing the splendor of a curtain upon her,
she guarded her languor while her lotus-like faces were moistened with honey;
[she was adorned] by well-prepared, overflowing clusters of blossoming creepers.
That place became beautiful, like the netherworld (rasātala),
with heaps of wealth— the lord of riches' own treasures—
overflowing and rising up from every side, as if from the outspread hoods of serpents.
In that city, upon the mirror-like faces of women whose temple-lattice windows were open and whose tresses were soiled by rising dust,
the rays of the moon shone.
The world was reflected like a jewel in its eyes; it possessed a deep,
resonant sound like the roar of a great conch,
and its white mansions were like masses of foam upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
That city, which was like a full ocean of milk with horses for its surging waves,
was adorned by Lakṣmī— though it was soiled by streaks of dust and darkened by the rows of its mansions.
That city was like a forest of blooming lotuses,
where bees were intoxicated by the spring, which was as delightful as a lotus,
frequented by royal swans, and inhabited by the world. (A composition using the *śleṣa* [pun] device.)
In that city, where peacocks radiant with jewels were like the earth oppressed by passion with its rows of open-mouthed birds, and where the clouds,
heavy with water, covered the regions without interval;
The women who have come on this day of the abundant rain; (the bond of slime);
for those people who fear saṃsāra and are devoted to the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, the forest of asceticism is their refuge.
That royal capital became a place of both kinds,
like a drinking ground for the many blind worldlings,
yet it was the site of the sprout of the Buddha, the illuminator of the solar lineage.
O friend, you who formerly dwelt in the excellent lands of Kapilavatthu for the sake of rightly experiencing happiness—
may that city now illuminate the true nature of the Dhamma.
In that city, the capital of the realm,
there was once a king who was skilled in wise policy and possessed of the four means of attraction;

The necks of the full water-jars are established four finger-breadths above her lotus feet,

For those desiring the fruit produced from the field of the body filled with the water of the radiance of his form,

O sir, Duveṇijaṅghā, causing great delight,
stands here with her great arms not bent,
stroking his pair of knees.
He displays the grace of the broad branch of the Bodhi tree that has arisen from his own body;

Entering the treasury of the sheath of the unbroken space [of the heart],
by virtue of its being not shared with others and so forth,

In this body of the one of the Gotama clan,

This mark on the upper body of the Lord of Beasts,

What power does a king possess that he cannot uproot?
Even this man, with his thick roll of flesh,

and whose shoulders are perfectly rounded—
O King, he shines like a cluster of *mutiṅga* fruits; (this is the *śleṣa* ornament.

O Blessed One, for this woman who possesses a row of thirty-two teeth,

The future beauty of his tongue,
which possesses the grace of a string of pure pearls,
flows from this lotus-face perfumed with the fragrance of truth.
O King, this beautiful row of teeth,
perfectly even, shines like a cluster of filaments;

The row of teeth, free from any gaps,
protects her like a continuous vine; in the thicket of her mouth,
it displays the splendor of a series of flower buds.
The moonlight of the face of this speaker of truth, with its row of exceedingly white teeth,
shines forth during his sporting in the lake of the Dhamma.
The garland of swans that carries the stream of his longing has been fashioned;

This voice of his, possessing the eight qualities that are enchanting to the mind,
resounds like a thousand karavīka birds;
to those with ears, it acts as a jeweled earring.
O, upon this peerless abode of the play of beauty, a cluster of blue lotus eyes has been set within a jeweled lion-cage.
Something twofold indeed appears through some skillful means;

Her two eyelashes are like those of a heifer,

She shines with her waist tucked into her garment,
like the orb of the moon when it has lost its spot and stands amidst a dense mass of clouds.
This mark of the turbaned head will bring him sovereignty over a righteous kingdom in the future,

It bears the likeness of a turban and topknot;
O Lord of the Earth, upon his pair of well-placed wheel-marks on the soles of his feet, these two are seen.
The thousand spokes, the hub and the rim,
the threefold lines, the śrīvatsa, and so forth— O Lord,

Shining with the eighty minor marks of physical excellence,

Urged by the detailed discourse of the twice-born man,

In the future, O Brahmin, he will go forth into homelessness;

Then, having departed, those elderly readers of omens said,

Now, while the twice-born elders have passed away,

has undertaken the Great Striving.
Impelled by compassion, he acted after hearing [the plea];

At one time, having reached the further shore of the ocean,
Thinking, "I shall make manifest my great power as I travel through the sky, ruling over these four continents and having conquered the hosts of my enemies," he spoke.
For the purpose of preventing the entry of the prince, who was like a thunderbolt,

he who for a long time had not seen the lotus-face of a son.

carried her own son for nourishment.

Like lamps whose brilliance has faded,

[speaking] repeatedly upon the variegated floor-coverings.
Moving gracefully within the interior of the temple in the Great Forest, upon a floor of jeweled sand,

O Mother! I gazed upon it as it wandered.

Then, having uttered these words with a voice choked with tears,

While engaged in lifting the moon’s orb from the mouth [of the crocodile],

The sky was filled with scattered parched grain and flowers,

The sprout of the Conqueror, possessed of profound wisdom,

With her broad hips clinging to her waist,
that princess surpassed the beauty of the very ground where the god of love was born.
The navel-deep cavity of the noble lady,
whose face was as pure as a lotus and whose line of dark body hair was as soft as a blue water-lily, was deeply kissed by her ample breasts.
Her pair of thighs, more beautiful than a golden plantain tree or the trunk of an elephant,
was like a row of intoxicated bees hovering over a blooming lotus.
I offer the beauty of the pair of pillars consisting of Hari and Maya in the theater of the ocean of milk to Ramā;
I offer the two substances of the form and taste of Madaraya to Tulā.
Her own pair of knees here is equal to the four faces of the Supreme Goddess,
appearing like a pair of coral bowls placed before her downward-turned face.
The mental palace of a young woman,
agitated by sensual thoughts at the approach of Love,
possesses the luster of the neck of a peacock subdued by intoxication.
With shanks as beautiful as the flame of a burning lamp,
her feet were surpassed by women through their soles,
which were radiant with anklets made of jewels.
The lotuses on the faces of the women seem to close their petals,
as it were, under the weight of the bees; they possess the beauty of the tips of the sprouts that are their fingers and toes.
The exceedingly delicate row of her fresh copper-colored nails shone like a flower-offering made for the sake of the Fish-bannered God (Kāma),
resembling the stream of the Yamunā.
Together with his retinue and that woman,
in the area of a pavilion adorned with clusters of jewels,
[he saw] the prince, the banner of the Solar dynasty—
He sat down, seeking permission for his departure;
the prince, surrounded by his kinsmen,
was like the king of the gods among the hosts of deities.
Immediately mounting his chariot drawn by horses,
he set out toward him, shining with glory;
having approached that place, he stood in the pavilion.
As he was being covered with an upper garment, his body,
adorned with ornaments of emeralds,
appeared like the Himalaya mountain shrouded by a mass of snow.
The son of the king, well-adorned with a jeweled crown and clad in Kāsika cloth,
shone like the ocean of milk with the abode of the gods.
Standing as immovable as Mount Sineru of gold,
with a row of star-like pearls shining upon her breast like a cluster of agitated stars in the sky.
The noble king also, with his wide-eyed hands joined in reverence, drank in the essence of her beauty as if it were the nectar of immortality;
on that day, [he saw] the prince at Pubbasela—
By means of the moon-disk of his face, which was the source of supreme splendor,
and by his eyes that were like blue lotuses in bud,
he brought about the awakening of the night-lotus grove of the minds of gods.
A river of dark, radiant beauty with unblinking eyes,
gazing at the youth among the young men,
while beautiful women waved fly-whisks over him.
Like a river abounding with waves trembling in the wind;
like the fresh moonlight of a young maiden amidst the host of stars in the expanse of the sky.
They offered finely wrought gold coins upon the floor of the jeweled pavilion’s railing; then,
having departed, the Brahmin, skilled in all arts—
The host of bards completed all their preliminary duties for the auspicious victory of those [princes];
immediately thereafter, Indra’s rain-cloud poured down.
With his hands like *tāmarasa* lotuses and a water-pot adorned with jewels,
the priest poured auspicious consecration water upon both of them.
Furthermore, for the sake of crushing the enemy's hands,
he mounted his deep and resonant chariot,
which was like a rain-cloud accompanied by the lightning of the gods' bow.
Surrounded by their kinsmen of the Khattiya caste,
they both set out from that city of Kapilapura toward [the prince]; then,
as they entered the midst of the beautifully adorned streets—
The devoted women of Kapila,
standing at the open windows like lion-cages,
adorned the earth with offerings of their unblinking lotus-eyes.
As the people gazed upon the grace of his gait with devotion,
their hands joined in reverence with beautiful hair,
they offered clusters of blossoms from jeweled vases.
He beheld the two rows of trees as if they were fashioned [for him],
while that woman of incomparable beauty was being led by the passionate women to become the target for the sharp arrows of his eyes.
The very arrows of their passion for one who had fallen [from his vows] became the tearing of their hearts, like the fruit thereof;
somehow, they became inhabitants of Kapilavatthu.
On that day, with their lotus-eyes motionless,
they entered Kapilapura like hosts of deities descending from the abode of the Thirty-three,
as if to behold the one pierced by insight.
Just as the noble couple Sujāta and Sujampati returned from the celestial abode named Vejayanta in the city of the Thirty-three Gods,
so too did they return from there to Kapilapura.
Patipatinī went to her own royal palace;
the son of the lord of the earth, having received the consecration of kingship,
went to Kapilapura— among those three abodes.
Together with that bimba-like one whose face was like the lunar orb,
he experienced immeasurable bliss for a very long time;
she who was as sweet-voiced as a blooming lotus and possessed a joyful countenance.
The splendor of her divine body-form in its three stages of youth reached its end through decay and dissolution;
even Queen Bimbā was subject to the inherent nature of conditioned phenomena, O charioteer, O charioteer!

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Occurrence of the Auspicious Marriage Festival," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa* (Lamp of the Conqueror’s Lineage), composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda— the primary cause for bestowing joy upon the hearts of all poets— and which serves as the proximate cause for this [work].
King Guṇamaṇimaṇimā, like the king of the gods, experiencing happiness,
[departed] by means of a horse-drawn carriage...
Once, that beautiful Mālinī descended upon the auspicious grounds of the mango grove,
which was filled with swarms of bees; she did so because the time had arrived for her to awaken to enlightenment.
As the Bodhisatta was proceeding, the sons of the gods,
having fashioned a form resembling an old cart and an ugly, decrepit appearance,
showed him one capable of inspiring detachment from existence.
Thus questioned, "What is this?", he who was overcome by doubt regarding the form of the one who has transcended old age, [Vipassi], whose essence is form, [spoke] to the charioteer,
while his heart-treasure was being urged on by a deity.
He left behind his instruction in the Dhamma like a tiger leaving behind its prey;
it was like a herd of elephants breaking through a grove of auspicious grass on the path to the Mangala garden, facing toward the Himalayas.
In that very way, extreme old age, having become manifest to oneself,
overcomes all the pride of youth; it is like a mouthful of withered lotus fibers,
its beauty lost as the filaments have fallen away.
The row of teeth and bones, broken by the harsh ravages of old age,
became crooked and turned grey; that head, at the consecration of old age, assumed the splendor of a white parasol set upon it.
Those lines on the skin of the one whose form was aged were not sparse;
they arose from the force of his vitality, strength, and the element of heat,
like waves upon the surface of the restless waters of the ocean.
On the shore of the water, which was as restless as the ocean,
where rows of towering waves were driven by the force of the fleeing winds—
there stood upon the path to the grove a woman with crooked breasts, like a branch of a tree.
The wise man beheld that form, which was upright like a younger brother,
yet held a staff upon the ground; it possessed its own youthful charm and,
like a strung bow, brought forth a hundred thousand [arrows] of beauty.
In the enjoyment of the *jiniajagara* (the "victory-snake"), it bears the burden of its worn-out slough;
its skin is like the *tilaka* flower, its sinews are taut with strength,
its thick flesh has vanished, and it is a framework of bones visible through its skin.
Conquer this defilement that is plastered over with skin and bound together by wood-like bones—
a thing devoid of strength, pride, and the like,
leaking from the openings of its wounds the excrement, urine, and other impurities along with blood.
As he beheld that form of one grown old— with cheeks wrinkled and uneven, the head trembling,
and the mind utterly failing— the entire world stood in attendance upon him.
"Blazing now with old age, like a house on fire— this Dhamma is beyond me,
I who am still unliberated," having said this,
he whose heart longed for birth entered the forest of existence.
Furthermore, for the sake of the King’s enjoyment of pleasure as he entered the grove,
[the deity] made him understand: "He is to be avoided by others,
having fallen into a terrible disease."
Furthermore, they showed him another hideous form, the appearance of disease: Visada-mati,
the banner of the Sakya clan, saw it submerged in the mire of excrement and urine, as if it were a worm.
"O you of noble mind, what is this suffering so powerful in its origin, which is dependent on others for its existence?
Having asked "What is this?", he questioned the one who had attained victory;
thus was the excellent Dhamma spoken by that Sūta.
As if drinking nectar with the cupped hands of his ears,
he did not pass beyond the Agamas, for they were subject to the nature of disease; thus,
filled with spiritual urgency, he returned to his own forest abode.
Sometimes, when the Lord was traveling by means of a horse-drawn carriage through that grove-palace,
the deities would fashion it so that it appeared as if it were being devoured by dogs, hawks, vultures, and other such creatures.
In the first [meditation], there is the corpse of a human being, bloated,
the abode of swarms of worms originating from its source, blue-black in color,
with blood trickling from the openings of its wounds.
The charioteer saw the body of Sumati, its eyes pecked by flocks of birds and its limbs smeared with flies; he approached it,
making the charioteer understand the meaning of the word "Bhāratī."
"O friend, even I cannot escape death," having said this, the Śākya king left his palace like the king of beasts entering the forest,
while the beauty of his golden earrings shone upon his own ears.
Furthermore, after some days had passed, that sovereign, accompanied by his retinue, mounted a noble vehicle and departed from the excellent city of Kapilapura,
which was like the abode of the theater of the God of Love.
Then he, as handsome as the five-arrowed god of love, went to that grove,
taking with him a jewel-colored garment adorned with strings of gems,
and having put on a lower robe of the fresh hue of a ripe jackfruit.
On that day, he saw the one of noble mind in the form of an ascetic— created by the deities with unimpaired vision—
just like the form of a Buddha, due to the empowerment of the wise.
Like a charioteer who instructs according to the purpose and the Dhamma,
the Lord of Ascetics spoke to him of the manifold defects in the five sensual pleasures and the benefits of departing from the home life toward the qualities of a recluse.
For the sake of deceiving, flattering, and living by wrong means out of delusion, he was capable of misappropriating the belongings of others; yet, urged on by the perfections,
he fashioned for himself a clay bowl held in his hands.
Having seen Visadamati, he conceived great confidence;
on the road, the splendor of the ascetic’s robes shone like a beautiful *sāla* tree with its blossoming buds.
Placing the burden of the bees of his eyes upon his own mind, the wise one conceived serene confidence in the robe;
[he saw] the mass of diseases revolving in the whirlpool of the suffering of momentary death.
He perceived that they would cross over this fathomless ocean of existence—
which is as formidable as a swarm of sea-monsters, with the force of waves of old age, and which has birth as its shore— just as he himself had done.
"Let a carriage be prepared to go to the pleasure grove,
so that this kunda-flower of a mind, blossomed by the rising of the full moon-like face of the ascetic,
may possess the splendor of the Nandana garden."
On that day, the lord of men spoke to Sandanācāri:
"Surrounded by rows of reeds, palm trees, and *hintāla* trees,
with water cooled by the spray of sandalwood trees and pure and stainless,"
Having entered the grove like Vāsava into Nandana,
the king together with his retinue performed excellent sport for the duration of the day;
the succession of whose fame [shines] upon the sun of a thousand rays—
While the sky was covered by a row of autumn clouds,
the beauty of white parasols rested upon his head,
adorning the shore with the marks of his feet.
With faces like lotuses, with breasts as full as swans, with eyes like blue water-lilies,
with hair as dark as the *nīlikā* flower, and with the sound of anklets resounding from women delighted by the intoxication of wine— of such a harem...
He descended into that delightful pond as if it were the world of men;
(a bond of slush) that pool, its water drawn into the cavities of the deep jar-like navels of beautiful young women, now appeared empty.
Through the union with the broad and firm hips of their beloveds,
the women were filled once more with the intoxication of passion, as if overflowing with the expansion of joy;
for those newly wedded maidens, overcome by natural modesty, were now stirred by the thrill of love.
The stream of water from the king’s pierced elephant trunk,
resembling a net cast in the desire to strike the shoals of fish—
the eyes of those turning away— was stolen for a moment by the one who resembles the god whose banner is a fish.
Her face is a lotus adorned with drops of fresh water;
her firm breasts are like swans amidst it; her hair is dark like seaweed;
and the beautiful shore of her hips is strewn with the ripples of her girdle.
There, you were sporting alone with the king,
who was eager for play; while the waves of the lake gently brushed against the silken garments covering the moon-bright faces of the women.
With the beauty of eyes fashioned [by art], with a navel deep and vast,
you were like a lotus extending from its base to its tip,
adorned with fresh water droplets.
With her firm breasts like playful swans, her dark hair like seaweed,
and her beautiful hips like a shore strewn with waves tossed by her husband,
you were there, like a single restless lake among many lakes.
As she slowly removed her linen garment from her moon-bright face at the king’s command,
the luster of her eyes was formed and her deep navel became visible.
It was as if the lotus-stalks were conversing with the edges of the lotuses;
again, it was as if the moonlight had entered the jar-like breasts of the women, submerged up to their necks.
With her eyes like dark lotuses and her face crowded with a swarm of bees,
she became like a cluster of lotuses filled with swarms of bees intoxicated by honey, while they sang their songs.
Struck by the hundred arms [of the demon], that lotus-pond,
with its drums sounding from the hips of the women, danced with its heads— the lovely lotuses—
while the bees swarmed about; thus it surpassed the hall of divine music.
In the sky above that lake, the creeper-like arms of those women with faces like the moon were as beautiful as streaks of lightning;
they were like rows of blue lotuses amidst a mass of dark clouds.
She shone as she played with peacocks made of precious gems;
she held a full-blown blue lotus in her hand, was surrounded by royal elephants,
enjoyed various kinds of honey, and had transgressed the hour for the religious discourse.
Just as that lord of men, having enjoyed that lotus-eyed courtesan on that day,
attained intense joy; (The Metaphor of the Bond) With its shore agitated by waves following his footsteps.
When the king had abandoned the lake due to the siege,
a gentle and fragrant breeze blew very softly,
its flow choked by the sighs of the women separated from their beloveds.
At that moment, the sun, standing motionless upon the surface of a stone slab, eclipsed the orb of the sun; then,
the lotuses of the wives of the Sarasīs were slightly closed.
Their lotus-like faces were as if filled with grief and dejection;
for there sat the Lord of the Śākyas, surpassing the beauty of a mass of twilight clouds in the dark sky.
Quickly, many barbers approached the king with various garments and diverse ornaments in their hands for the purpose of adorning him;
indeed, he was one who surpassed the glory of the Solar dynasty by his own righteousness.
The Lord of the Gods immediately dispatched his son,
named Vissakamma, saying: "O you who are worthy, adorn him—
the refuge of the three worlds— with divine garments and other such gifts."
Having approached him while wearing the guise of a human,
he bound his head with hundreds of fine cloths and adorned him with ornaments made of jewels and gold.
On that day, the king was like Sakka, the king of the gods;
the eastern quarter was overcome by the burden of the darkness of Mara,
with rows of cloud-like petals of the hundred-fold twilight closing like buds.
The solar orb, possessing the stalk of the Mandārava tree and the support of a lake upon the surface of the sky, assumed the beauty of a budding lotus;
meanwhile, the Lord of Men dispatched a message to him.
Having announced the birth of his own young son, that delighted Bhadda, by looking at the writing-tablet, declared:
"My bondage has been born; Rāhu has been born!"

Then, on that very day, the Lord of Men, his grandfather, having gathered together the entire meaning of the words in accordance with the spoken statements and following the sequence of grammatical treatises, [composed this work].
"O Mamatā, this is Rāhula; his body is honored by the blue lotuses that are the eyes of the forest goddesses.
Having mounted a magnificent vehicle, he approaches."
He was sent forth to enter the assembly hall,
along a street lined with the rows of the pure eyes of the citizens; meanwhile,
the jeweled shutters were opened in the nearby celestial mansions.
She who was the daughter of Pitucchā, whose husband had conquered the wives of the gods,
and who, having drunk in the essence of beauty with the cupped hands of her eyes,
had stilled the thirst for pleasure— she is that Kisāgotamī.
Those who possess such a body, which has conquered the god of love—
his mother too has long since attained Nibbāna, and his father,
the lord of the world, has become cooled and attained Nibbāna.
"Even my own beloved wife has attained Nibbāna"—thus he spoke.
With the defilements within his heart extinguished and stilled, like the Lord of Ascetics, he said: "I am one who has attained Nibbāna."
Having heard this well-sung verse,
so beautifully composed and analyzed through various methods, Varamatī understood its meaning:
"I am that which has been taught as the state of Nibbāna."
Having sent to his palace a brilliant and captivating necklace of beautiful pearls,
which was worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold and weighed heavily for its wearers,
he entered his residence together with his harem.
"May we never experience the cessation of mental disturbances while you are awakening to supreme enlightenment"— thus did they approach you,
O Lord of the Eleven, as if prophesying your attainment of peace.
Furthermore, many clouds of various hues were gathered there,
like an incomparable white parasol adorned with strings of polished pearls,
encircling him upon his royal throne.
Upon the peak of Mount Udaya,
the lunar orb shone with great beauty, surrounded by a multitude of stars;
while the world was still enveloped in the dense darkness of night.
At that moment, the royal capital displayed its utmost splendor;
made lush by the radiating rays of the moon,
it was as if its new renovations had just been completed.
They cause the darkness, severed by the burden of the moon’s rays,
to take on the appearance of streaks of melting gloom,
as they spread over the groves of blooming night-lotuses and the forests of white *asīka* jasmine.
While the swarms of bees, intoxicated by the very sweet honey, were heedless,
he— whose splendor surpassed that of the Lord of the Devas—
was intent on reflecting upon the Dhamma in a place where darkness was dispelled by the light of blazing jewel-lamps.
Not long after he had sat down upon his own glorious golden lion throne,
he became dispassionate toward the five sensual pleasures; instantly,
with hands bearing musical instruments, those whose hair was like dark-blue clouds [approached].
Her eyes are like blue water-lilies, her forehead like the crescent moon,
her waist is encircled by a girdle like a blooming lotus,
her body is slender with lovely breasts, and her thighs and shanks are beautiful and well-rounded.
With cheeks like white water-lilies, with ears adorned by hanging earrings,
with a row of teeth as flawless as a garland of jasmine,
and with a neck bearing the weight of a necklace of gold and gems— she was truly beautiful.
Accompanied by young women skilled in dance and song,
he sat near the lake— clear as a pool, motionless, serene, and tranquil—
seated with a wise mind, endowed with the restraint of guarded sense-doors.
Desiring to delight him— who had abandoned delight in the darkness [of cyclic existence] and yearned for the state of Buddhahood— she descended onto the stage;
by the contact of her feet with the ground made of jewels, [the earth trembled].
A certain woman, uttering a voice like the sound of a golden lute,
moved her fingers with the grace of a trembling sprout and danced along with the melody,
possessing the charm of a golden creeper.
A certain beautiful woman, whose speech has conquered the sweet warbling of the cuckoo,
creates the likeness of the face of the Lord of Men upon the battlefield of the colors of her sharp rays of eyes.
Singing songs pleasant to hear, they shone forth;
even those with sidelong glances played five-fold musical instruments that day, surpassing the women of the gods.
The stage was as if the sky itself during the rainy season,
with the sounds of their lutes— sweet to hear— and the beating of drums;
it was a delight for the noble-minded, possessing the magnificent forms of great beings.
He beheld their dance, which was like a manifestation of the transformations of existence,
within the uneven huts of cyclic existence for those afflicted by the disease of kingship;
he heard their hurried cries, which were like the sound of sweet singing.
Delighting in their dancing and singing, he lay upon an excellent,
glorious couch in the lion’s posture; thus, having been subjected to harassment, they found an opportunity for sleep.
Immediately, those women lay down at the palace of Madana;
he, having awakened from mere sleep along with the night-lotuses,
sat down upon his own glorious couch during the night.
Having spread out the musical instruments he had taken here and there, he beheld the young women overcome by deep sleep:
some, like female monkeys swaying in the wind, were swallowing their own saliva; others... [the text continues].
Some, their cheeks sagging and their teeth exposed, devour with their tusks;
some, their skin fallen away from their vulvas, display them to one another;
and some, garlanded with faltering words, prattle whatever comes to mind.
Some were vomiting, some were coughing; thus, seeing existence in its entirety as full of manifold transformations, devoid of glory,
and lacking essence, she established herself firmly therein.
Like a cemetery strewn with corpses and raw, blackened bones,
or like a house on fire— remembering the three realms of existence as such,
O you who eat by vows, look upon this world as it is truly afflicted!
Thus, uttering this supreme exclamation, that hero among men, through his liberation from it,
generated a state of heroic courage within his mind;
[a state] which had become the dwelling place for the Rākṣasī of the four-fold pleasures of love.
"While the fool is being deluded in the forest of the glorious existence, enough!
Let my dwelling be there no more; come now, having departed from that, I shall seek liberation from the fear of the three realms."
Approaching the door of the celestial mansion, he uncovered the face of Channa,
who was lying on his bed near the threshold; having done so,
he addressed him, saying, "It is not right for you to go there."
The king, together with his ministers, mounted the noble horse Pabalajavabalagga,
whose mindfulness was directed toward the destination; at that very moment,
he departed for the sake of reaching the city of Sakka, intending to fashion a canopy over the horse-stall.
"Agam!"— thus the king of horses, Sahaja-Katthaka,
let out a loud neighing sound, heavy with joy;
having entered the inner chamber where the oil lamp was blazing.
Upon a couch inlaid with jewels and strewn with fragrant flowers,
he beheld his own young son, resembling a golden statue,
reclining upon the earth together with his consort.
If I, having removed the queen from the reach of her hand,
were to place my own young son upon my lap, the queen,
whose face surpasses the lotus, would rise up.
May he prevent my departure for the forest, which is difficult to restrain;
once I have become a Buddha, I shall never again bear the burden of the bees that are the eyes of those whose lotus-faces are my children.
Lifting him up from his dwelling like a hero tossing Mount Meru,
he descended, rescuing Sumariya’s feet— the moon whose eyes are like blue lotus petals and whose radiance is like the orb of the moon.
How did the Lord of Men depart from his palace,
leaving behind Queen Bimbā— who was as beautiful as a golden image and whose full,
heavy breasts were shaped like the wheels of the chariot of the God of Love?
Having abandoned his delicate son named Rāhula, who possessed the radiance of an emerald statue,
was born into the Śākya lineage, had accumulated great merit,
and whose body was covered with the primary and secondary marks of a Great Man.
How did the steadfast one descend? Raising his foot gently,
he stepped down upon that day onto his father, the king of Jambudīpa, the best of kings,
who was like a rutting elephant-king among enemies and now lay in the ocean of grief for his son.
How is it that he, who is compassionate toward friends yet merciless toward us,
cast us down from our abode and dragged us by our feet?
He [has turned] the entire wheel of the path as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa).
Having conquered without a foe on the seventh day, the Lion among Men,
having performed meritorious deeds, though not yet a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti),
how did he descend from there after lifting up his feet?
"Having descended from the celestial chariot, may you deliver me today;
and may I, in turn, deliver you from existence," he said,
and the lord of men mounted that king of steeds.
Kanthaka, the king of horses, whose speed was swift as the wind,
was as white as a polished conch shell and measured by the value of liquid gold;
yet on that day, he made both the sound of his hooves and his neighing heard.
Indeed, that entire city was overwhelmed by him as he went about;
yet on that day, the deities silenced the noise being made,
using the palms of their lotus-like hands which were fashioned by the deities themselves.
The wise man, having mounted the door-panel that had been well-fastened,
quickly reached the enclosure where the tail was hidden,
which was surrounded by walls and doors with firmly fixed panels.
If there had not been the opening of the closed door,
I, taking my excellent horse and the minister Channa,
would have leaped over the city like a lion among men; this was the thought.
At that very moment, the wheel of the city’s ramparts, lofty with its towers and measuring a *rasa-ratana* in height,
as well as the king of horses, the minister Channanāma,
and he who was endowed with the power of valor, all began to deliberate.
Then, being urged by the deity residing there,
he opened the door-panel with a hundred strokes of his fist;
"This one named Siddhattha shall possess my entire realm."
Thinking, "Having overcome him, he will surely awaken to sublime enlightenment," Māra the Evil One,
having emerged from his celestial palace, then remembered [the Buddha] and,
exceedingly enraged, set out along the path to meet him.
At the foot of the Turita Mahī tree, Māra,
the enemy of the foe of Māra, standing in the dark sky,
thus announced: "O Supreme Person, on the seventh day from now..."
Having conquered the world, you will become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin);
having become a wheel-turning monarch, may you dwell at home,
experiencing happiness and turning the wheel for as long as life lasts.
"O Amitamati, do not go forth! Thus Māra instructed him, desiring to prevent his departure;
[the Bodhisatta] listened to those words of lamentation with the cupped hands of his ears.
"Drinking it as if it were poison, you asked, 'Who are you? Standing in the path of the wind,
I replied, 'O best of men, I am the Lord of the deities,
the Wicked One (Pāpimā) who wields power at will.'"
"He is the refuge for gods and men; he is fearless;
he is the one who has generated the jewel of the divine eye;
he is the crusher of the hosts of Māra"—thus did that invincible one, like me, give this reply.
There may be even ten thousand like you;
yet if there were in your mind any reflection such as the faults of sensual desire,
ill-will, and so forth, we would know it at once.
Subject to aversion and looking for some distraction,
he followed him step by step, just like a shadow follows a body; then,
as the full moon approached the month of Āsāḷha, he returned.
When the desire arose to behold the splendor of Kapilapura,
the earth turned on its axis and revealed the site of the cetiya,
situated facing the noble city, to the king of horses.
Instantly, throughout the ten thousand world-systems,
the deities became engaged in the protection of the refuge of the three worlds with lamps made of jewels and gold, and other such offerings.
Some sons of the immortals beheld the path,
adorned with hanging garlands of fragrant flowers, golden water-pots,
white parasols, victory banners, and flags.
Then deities adorned the path leading there,
making the hollow of the world delightful with offerings of flowers;
the sky resounded with the sound of drums and was filled with sixty-eight [celestial beings].
Having entered upon a road strewn with honored, fragrant flowers,
which was radiant with the spreading splendor of four hundred thousand [rays],
he proceeded for as far as thirty yojanas toward the one who was afflicted.
Filled with pure water, strewn with garlands of foam,
possessing rows of blooming lotuses and rows of lofty waves,
its breeze cooled by the moon, and its banks covered with sand.
The heroic one approached the Anoma, the river of the Anomas; having obtained a seat of black stone,
he asked the excellent-minded one, "What is this covered thing called?"— to which she replied, "This is the river Anoma."
“Tamāvatī, if I were to go forth here on this bank,
