I saw the Tathāgata, even when he had passed away and reached rebirth,
as he desired throughout the three worlds— at the very moment of his descent into the womb,
at the moment of his birth, and at the moment of his passing away.
The Tathāgatas attain the state of being objects [of cognition];
the Bull among the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā accepts that the designation [of them as objects] here is permissible by way of figurative usage.
In the Tathāgata who is devoid of substrate and yet not devoid,
in the Tathāgata who has not discarded the sublime,
in the Tathāgata who is both non-beautiful and beautiful.
To those who have fallen into a miserable state or a happy state, he,
having traversed across, above, and below,
beheld the path of wisdom as it truly is. (The Yamaka-bandhana)
And while the Tathāgata was thus established in the jhāna that arises from the super-knowledge of the path of action already perfected,
these [beings] performed unwholesome deeds in three ways.
"These [monks] have performed good deeds in three ways;
they are endowed with the fruits of the Noble Path.
They are not non-monks," thus [he spoke] with the final statement.
By way of denying our virtues, the wicked reviled us,
saying, "There are no virtues in these noble persons," and they were indeed their own enemies.
They praised him for his corresponding virtues:
"These are those who cling to false attainments;
these are those who cling to supreme attainments."
This generation, having accumulated pathways of kamma here and there by way of what has been grasped and acquired,
is falling into the four states of misery, the abyss, and the state of ruin.
"O Sugata, you have gone to a happy state,
a truly happy state," said the ascetic,
who was composed and had mastered his practice, as he stood before him with unblinking eyes. (The Yamaka-bandhana)
For one who is rightly discerning, mindful, and possessed of mindfulness,
by means of which wisdom the great darkness of delusion regarding the future existence of form and formless realms—
arising from causes such as karma— and the sixteenfold doubts concerning the three times, have been brought to an end.
In the second watch of the night, the wisdom that purifies the crossing over of doubt arose.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Attainment and Operation of the Knowledge of Past Lives and the Divine Eye," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*—a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which serves as the primary cause for delighting the hearts of all poets, and which stands not far from its own introductory narrative.
[It is] like a moon in a pool where white lotuses have blossomed.
At dawn, mindfulness gazes toward the western direction;
one should worship the Victor whose face is radiant with moonlight during the final watch of the night.
Afflicted by separation, this bride Night now watches every moment,
her garment of the sky clouded with dark rain-clouds,
as she gazes with the eyes of the four quarters.
He released drops from a mass of spray;
intent on destroying the defilements through concentration,
he drove out that underlying tendency as an ordinary person might.
Thus, by his fame, which cleanses the stain from the world,
the moon, though a treasury of digits, bore its spot;
while in the eastern sky, the scattered stars—
She dispelled the dense darkness of worldly bondage,
possessing the splendor of soft, fresh, deep-blue locks of hair encircled by a necklace radiant with light, like a lady of the night.
The sprout of the Victor, whose inner core has been purified by the power of insight,
is like the moon that whitens the sky with its mass of rays,
removing the stains of evil.
He dispelled the mass of darkness that followed him;
a cool Malaya breeze blew forth intensely,
and the dewdrops of the cold season fell upon the limbs of the quarters.
She wandered upon the earth kissed by the clusters of rays of the moon,
the maker of night— she who was stainless,
free from affliction, and immovable.
When the mind is concentrated, having attained the state of purification through the successive stages of serenity, then, with insight-wisdom,
one should strive for the knowledge that brings about the destruction of the taints.
The wise one, having discerned in due order and even in reverse the wheel of existence together with its three rounds and nine divisions,
attained that noble knowledge and vision.
This is called purity for the sake of purity: he who,
in a single moment, remembers even a thousand-eyed one,
or even a hundred and ten [deities], exactly as they are.
Of Him whose entire interior of the world is adorned by the radiance from the toes of His own feet,
and who dries up the frost of all obscurations without exception;
To one who has attained all knowledge through the arising of samādhi,
and who sees these three worlds as a jujube fruit in the palm of the hand,
nothing remains that has not come within the scope of his wisdom.
The unsurpassed, supreme noble knowledge and vision, never before seen, heard, or known,
is being realized by this ascetic Gotama.
It was extraordinary for one who lacked the service of a spiritual teacher;
yet, by the power of having perfected the virtue of generosity throughout successive existences,
he became one whose bonds of greed were completely disentangled.
May I, having extinguished the fires of aversion and other defilements with the water of the perfection of virtue accompanied by patience,
become one who possesses the perfection of firm wisdom in birth after birth.
Having abandoned all erroneous views by means of serving masters beginning with Vinayaka,
he questioned them and destroyed his delusions and doubts.
In birth after birth, he dispelled [suffering] by honoring the wise,
showing reverence and great respect to his gurus,
and through the practice of serving people.
Pride, conceit, arrogance, and vanity; delight in worldly prosperity from birth to birth,
delight in existence, delight in union with the bodiless one (Kāma),
and delight in beautiful women—
Having gone forth from home and delighting in the homeless life,
he dispelled [defilements] and attained meditative absorption (jhāna) for himself;
in birth after birth, he was possessed of energy and the perfection of truth.
Taking refuge in the supreme wholesome states,
he abandoned the fourfold impurity of verbal misconduct and purified his own heart with diligence.
In birth after birth, having purified the stains of unwholesome mental impurities through the thirty perfections,
he gradually reached the full maturation of his faculties.
The wise one did not desire any other perfection for the sake of the earth; rather,
with his heart impelled by compassion, he made a vow for enlightenment that was indeed beyond counting in every existence.
Then, within themselves, the fourfold attainment of fruits appeared as if they were without interval,
through the power of their own aspiration in birth after birth.
O sir, if one does not accomplish the wholesome state described in three ways—
namely, noble knowledge and vision that has no other person as its object and is free from doubt— how could such a person attain it?

One should wisely contemplate the five aggregates as impermanent due to their arising and passing away; as suffering, both because of their painful nature and because they are uncontrollable and so forth; and as non-self.
Examine it again and again with firm resolve,
by means of the method of the Comprehension of the Aggregates (*kalāpa-sammasana*),
regarding the twelvefold wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) which has no beginning.
In due course, that sprout of the Conqueror brought forth those [seven] aspects within their respective components;
he extracted them by contemplating them as being characterized by impermanence.
Regard that which is called "eternal" as being actually without essence and unconditioned;
contemplate it thoroughly as non-self and as suffering.
Abandon that which is conditioned, which is falsely conceived as happiness.
The one of excellent wisdom gladdened by means of dispassion and revulsion,
having seen through the fading away of delight in the conditioned,
by way of contemplating relinquishment through cessation.
Having thus performed the double contemplation regarding the entire complex of arising and so forth,
and having scrutinized even all that is conditioned from the perspective of name-and-form, he sees it as entirely impermanent.
Furthermore, for the wise one, through the stage of young insight (*taruṇavipassanā*),
these [five aggregates] appeared in twenty-five ways, doubled, according to their causal origin,
moment-by-moment, and in terms of arising and passing away.
"Vipassaka" refers to one who possesses the ten defilements of insight; "bhāvaṃ" is radiance;
"pabhāsati" is the determination of rapture; "sukhī" is happiness;
"ahaṃ" is the absence of agitation; "asamatha-nikanti-upekkhanā" is equanimity toward non-tranquility.
With bodies fully formed and glowing with serene redness,
they have emerged from boundless world-systems;
born of the power of insight, they spread forth.
This path does not possess a radiance tawny like liquid refined gold,
nor does it have as its basis the defilements such as craving (*visattikā*).
As he contemplated the arising and passing away of states, the Path emerged from that [contemplation], which is free from the ten secondary defilements; thus it is said:
"As he thoroughly examined the path and the non-path."
The keen wisdom of insight that has arisen in a wise person who is a young practitioner of vipassanā is called purification by overcoming doubt at the moment of the path.
The Bull among Men, having reached the further shore through knowledge and investigation,
possesses full comprehension and the destruction of higher abandonments;
by means of this full comprehension, he has achieved the perfection of both forms of purification.
Devoted to seeing things as they truly are,
he undertook the investigation of the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering,
and then the characteristic of non-self in all conditioned phenomena.
Not seeing [the aggregates] as they truly are,
he is obstructed by the darkness of the continuity of existence and the paths of conduct;
therefore, purifying his mind regarding arising and passing away, he [should proceed].
Having quickly attained clarity regarding the three characteristics,
one who has merely entered the path of insight acquires the knowledge of the fearfulness of conditioned existence beginning with the knowledge of the dissolution of formations (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa).
Herein, the analysis of the contemplation of the nine successive higher stages for the Self-Become One,
together with the description of its nine qualities,
is set forth as the ninefold development of knowledge.
It is called the purification of the words of the *sapakaṭipada*;
immediately upon the destruction of the darkness that obscures the Four Noble Truths by means of wisdom and intelligence, it becomes firm.
The wise one attained the lineage-consciousness (*gotrabhu*) which has cessation as its domain,
a mind that stands outside the lineage of the ignoble;
it is designated by the name "the lineage-consciousness bestowed by the praiseworthy."
Having uprooted the three defilements along with their roots,
the wise one then attained this primary vision and knowledge, which removes all obstructions, miserable rebirths, and states of ruin.
When the wise say that these [factors] have immediate fruit,
they mean that one should also reflect upon that fruit;
he then attained the second stage once again.
He cultivated insight for its attainment;
he thoroughly cleansed the mire of the suffering of existence,
which is timeless and has diminished the three types of evil deeds.
He attained the second fruit, the unsurpassed,
together with its result and the reviewing knowledge and vision;
then, developing insight once again by himself—
Having uprooted the underlying tendency toward aversion,
he attained the third knowledge and vision, which removes existence, possesses the fruit of reviewal, and is unsurpassed.
One who cultivates the three characteristics with firm intelligence for the sake of attainment will reach the fourth stage above,
like a palm fruit from the top of its trunk.
To those who move having struck down the summit of the defilements,
who have warded off all the delusions of the wheel of existence,
and who have utterly destroyed the immeasurable along with its latent tendencies—
He attained the excellent vision of knowledge whose range is not shared by others,
as well as the reviewing of its fruit; then he attained the vision of knowledge that understands the destruction of the taints.
Purity is said to be the attainment of Arhatship;
at that very moment, the Victor possesses fourteen kinds of Buddha-wisdom and has acquired the fourfold analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*).
The six unique knowledges, the ten powers,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and the fourfold fearlessness, majesty, and influence.
Because he dwells together with those who have attained success,
having himself directly known the states that should be directly known,
and having himself fully understood the states that should be fully understood;
Having abandoned the states that are to be abandoned,
and having personally realized the fruit of the path leading to Nibbāna,
there may be as much further development of the phenomena as can be known.
Granted that his knowledge may have proceeded thus far,
yet through direct higher knowledge he possessed the wisdom of omniscience;
together with his attainment of Arahantship, the Buddha became all-knowing.
The Lord of Sages, awakened by the knowledge of the path that dispels the sleep of great delusion, shines with perfect enlightenment, destroying the host of wicked enemies.
The night-lotus of the palace of Indra laughed aloud;
together with the rising of the Buddha-sun, the dawn became crimsoned by the attainment of the true enlightenment of the Subuddha, like the mountain of the East.
The kinsmen of those to be trained arose together with him;
they awoke from the treasury of deep sleep that had emerged.
Then, a sublime radiance appeared in the field of his birth.
The earth shook with a great upheaval,
and thirty-two auspicious omens appeared throughout the world,
adorned with mountains, rocky peaks, and hills.
At that moment, the Sun, garlanded with rays, arose performing these four functions in the world,
foremost among which is the destruction of the net of darkness.
The Buddha-sun, born from the lineage of the solar dynasty of Riva,
caused the sky to be completely covered by showers of mahīlāja flowers and by fragrant incense banners.
In the world-system of Chaṇhokulā,
which is the abode of great auspiciousness and rests upon a playful support,
for those who have come to perform worship at the lotus of the sun of that time—
The sky, the supportless void, shone with the crests of the gods who stood with hands joined in devotion upon their heads,
made formidable by the radiance of their crest-jewels.
The name "Guṇa" refers to the purity of the continuum of the aggregates;
he is called "Buddha" because of his connection to the pure series of aggregates.
Homage to the Buddha who has realized perfected knowledge!

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Occurrence of the Great Bodhisatta’s Attainment of Perfect Enlightenment through the Knowledge of the Noble Path," within the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda—
a work that serves as the primary cause for bestowing joy upon the hearts of all poets— and which contains the proximate introductory narrative.
In the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, not far from here, is the second section, the Nidānabhāga.
For the sake of the excellent horse Pakkaṅkavara,
his head, eyes, flesh, wife, and children [were sacrificed].
"Having given [it] after a long time, they have performed what is difficult to do"—
thus reflected he whose banner is the Indavaṃsa;
he did not rise from his seat even then.
Having prepared his cross-legged seat and sat down for seven days,
the Sage, his intentions fulfilled,
entered many millions of meditative attainments through higher concentration.
He will not leave his victorious throne;
for whatever task must be done by him still exists,
and even now there is a certain deity present.
"Afflicted by doubt, they were lost in thought";
having understood their state of mind,
he rose up in an instant toward the expanse of the sky.
Displaying this miracle,
he removed the dart of doubt without hesitation;
leaning against this tree as his seat, he sat cross-legged.
Thinking, "I have attained the state of perfect enlightenment," he descended from the place where he had been seated cross-legged,
toward the intermediate direction between the east and the north.
For seven days, he honored the seat of the Victorious Bodhi tree by sprinkling it with the five kinds of precious substances,
which possess beautiful and lovely eyes.
The Conqueror, the sole eye of the world, stood there;
having gone to the space between the place where he had stood and his victory-throne,
he remained for seven days facing the eastern and western directions.
With his lotus-feet marked by the wheel-signs set down [as he walked],
he paced upon a jeweled walkway fashioned for him;
he was between the north and west of the Bodhi tree.
For seven days, the Sage dwelt in right contemplation upon the Abhidhamma within a jeweled pavilion fashioned by the devas from various gems.
Just as Kesava churned the ocean on Mount Mandara,
so the Sage, seated upon that [mountain], churned the fourfold [Abhidhamma] beginning with the *Viññāṇakaṇḍa*— the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
By the power of knowledge, one should not be confused regarding that which is difficult to see:
the analysis of the aggregates and so forth, which is subject to dissolution,
profound, and extremely hard to fathom in its eighteen aspects.
Thus, having conquered Māra, he then agitated the ocean of the Vibhaṅga with the wind of the end of the eon that is knowledge;
the Victor, who understands the emptiness of the elements.
Immediately after that, expanding upon the elements whose intrinsic nature is devoid of a sentient being or a soul,
he established the excellent *Dhātukathā* with its various methods.
"Designations are sixfold by way of the designations of the aggregates and so forth"—
this well-analyzed matrix was taught by the All-Knowing Victor through his wisdom, for the sake of persons...
The Supreme Person, the Lion of Debaters,
shook the conventional designations as he ascended the circle of his own doctrine and rightly [overthrew] the circle of opposing doctrines.
Having compiled the suttas in eighteen thousand sections,
he condensed them with the aid of mnemonic devices; then,
by means of his wisdom, he expanded them for himself.
Although the Protector thoroughly penetrated the subject of discourse—
which is infinite, boundless, supreme,
and not within the sphere of any logicians or any gods— ()
That which, by way of roots, trunks, and so forth, is tenfold according to the order of the summary and the detailed exposition,
and is to be analyzed through its conclusion and its doubt.
With profound wisdom like the ocean—
peaceful, sublime, subtle, and very difficult to see;
hidden, beyond the sphere of logic, and inconceivable—
The Well-Restrained One, the Resonance of the Dhamma,
thoroughly mastered that Yāmaka in its various methods and without exception;
it was overflowing with the high waves of diverse methods.
Adorned with the jewels of the interpretable and definitive meanings,
and further enriched by hundreds of internal turns of the Dhamma,
it is filled with the waters of the sections of the True Dhamma.
How can the Teacher [explain] the great ocean of the *Paṭṭhāna*,
which is a vast port with the fourfold twenty-three conditions as its boundary?

The Sage, whose wisdom is free from attachment, stirred and examined [the Dhamma] with the mountain of knowledge by means of the matrix (mātikā) established through such terms as "cause" (hetu), "condition" (paccaya), and so forth.
The twenty-fourfold "Known" (Ñeyya) is difficult to understand,
consisting of the indicated and the indications themselves, along with their elaborations;
based upon this, [one should know] the twenty-two-fold "Threefold" (Tika).
The *Paṭṭhāna* contains the essence of the [Abhidhamma] Pitaka;
it is based upon name-and-form, and likewise treats the dyads in their entirety.
The *Paṭṭhāna* contains the essence of the [Abhidhamma] Pitaka; it is based upon name-and-form.
Having inserted the twenty-two triplets into the pairs,
one who knows the *Paṭṭhāna* [should know] the "Pair-and-Triplet" [section];
there are one hundred pairs for the twenty-two triplets.
Having inserted this "triad-of-three" starting point,
and having formed twenty-two triads within the triads themselves,
one should apply the "triad-of-triad" method according to the *Paṭṭhāna* manual.
Having likewise arranged the hundred dyads within the dyads themselves,
and the dyad-dyad within the *mantāgati* section of the *Paṭṭhāna*,
thus I shall produce and insert [the conditions] in the direct order.
I shall also insert the six methods for the inverse;
having thus inserted the inverse-analogies,
as well as the six analogies-inverses.
Having thoroughly mastered the great ocean of the profound *Paṭṭhāna* with the Mount Meru of knowledge,
as he was thus contemplating it together with its objective bases, his skin—
Your complexion is serene, and your blood has become clear;
at that moment, the four elements of color ceased within a space of eight handspans.
Except for the power of resolve, from his body there issued forth rays of six colors that streamed out like snakes; [he was like] the moss,
the Kālindī river, and the Lord of Lakṣmī.
The radiance of peace, resembling the color of a blue lotus,
issued forth intensely from her hair, eyes, eyebrows,
and nose; this entire blue luster adorned her like ornaments.
With their splendor filling the remaining directions,
they appeared as if draped in dark blue woolen cloths, as they filled the world-systems.
They flowed like the powder of blue sapphires;
they completely covered the world with a mixture of yellow orpiment and saffron powders combined with liquid gold.
By the power of those golden-hued rays that issued forth from his skin, which was like refined gold,
he appeared as if anointing Mount Sineru.
The king was like water submerged in the great ocean,
while his eight conceived world-elephants became as if fashioned from polished gold and other precious materials.
Like the sprinkling of lac-dye, like the scattering of vermilion powder,
so were the rays reddened by the glow of twilight.
Having gone forth, they ran about, covered in flesh and blood;
by their power, the entire earth became impassable,
as if submerged in the great ocean.
All the grasses in the three worlds became as if perfectly fashioned from the colors of lotuses, jasmine,
*sogandhika* lilies, and moonlight.
White as the waves of the camphor-ocean,
with teeth and tusks made formidable by bones,
they whiten the quarters of the sky with their brilliant, pure radiance.
By their means, the bride of the earth was as if clothed and draped in white garments,
made beautiful by the sprinkling of streams of milk.
The splendor and radiance of the Buddha’s glory streamed forth,
anointing all directions and the entire world-system with saffron-colored paste.
Emerging from here and there, they flowed with the brilliance of madder,
like crushed coral and sandalwood,
by means of the five essential juices of the blue and other elements.
Radiant with light, as if filling the entire world with their splendor, they emerged and adorned the whole world with colors, flowers, and the seven kinds of jewels.
Those rays pervaded the earth,
the water that supports the world, the fire, and the wind,
as well as the space beneath the roots and the space above them.
They seized the world in all directions without limit; then the gods, along with the Devadūma tree,
the groves, the celestial palaces, the ornaments, the moon, the sun,
and the multitude of stars, [were likewise taken].
They were known by their mere shapes;
even today, those [trees] that have emerged from them still run wild.
Having gone from there to the trees with thick, dark-blue branches—
Perceiving the Nigrodha tree as a goat-herd’s shelter,
the Teacher sat at its foot,
experiencing the supreme bliss born of liberation for seven days.
Descending from that celestial mansion at that very moment,
having run through successive existences for the sake of the perfections such as giving,
he attained the accomplishment of uncommon knowledge.
"Thinking, 'I shall not form any further volitional constructions,' he,
seeking to withdraw, does not perceive even this much:
that for so long a time he has been free from stain, though his nature was stainless."
Agitated by grief, he sat upon the ground,
scratching sixteen lines with his fingernails while facing away;
why is he not seen now, nor has he departed?

Seeing his father sitting there with a very dejected face, writing letters out of grief, they looked on in distress, wondering, "Where has he gone? and thinking, "He seems to be drawing these lines out of sorrow."
Having gone there, Tanhā, Arati, and Ragā—the daughters of Vasavatti—quickly asked him:
"What, dear father? What, dear father? Why do you meditate here?"
Who was your rival, and by whom were you defeated,
that you— though the legitimate son of King Śuddhodana—
having reached the state of supreme enlightenment, have applied ink to your face?
"The Evil One said, 'The bonds of Māra have been severed by me; therefore I grieve.
Having brought that Māra-killer, like a well-trained elephant,"
"Having bound us tightly with the snares of passion and the like, we shall show you our strength; behold it, father!
Do not grieve, do not despair," so said the daughters.
She who has entered the arena of the battle of love,
who bears the bow of her knitted brows and is intoxicated by it, and who,
having fixed the arrows of her sidelong glances upon it, lets them fly without fail.
She pierces the arrows of the enemy of Kāma,
the foe of Māra; her mass of hair is dark blue like seaweed,
and the crescent moon adorns the circle of her beautiful forehead.
Her eyes were like blue lotuses; she wore swinging golden earrings, and her forehead was adorned with the radiance of a mass of flowers upon her hair;
she was like a vine of the wind-god entwined with blossoming jasmine.
Her row of teeth was like young shoots, her lower lip was as red as a *pāṭala* flower,
her nose bore the likeness of a golden flute—
the dwelling place of the sport of Kandarpa— and her face was as pure as a lotus.
Her beautiful arms were like streaks of lightning;
she possessed a circle of swans as her gracefully swaying girdle,
and her neck was lovely with its embrace of golden [ornaments].
Her fingers were as tender as the petals of a *lāvaṇṇa* flower;
her broad hips reached down to the banks of the river of play,
where she was adorned by a fresh, clinging girdle.
The circle of her navel is like the soot from the smoke of the fire of the pride of Kandarpa; her thighs and shanks are full,
and her rows of nails are like buds.
There, where the passionless Victor dwelt, the women of Māra— whose bodies were like the colors of a fading sunset and who were afflicted by the intoxication of the wine of lust— arrived.
Those beautiful women, with eyes like the goddess Indirā reflected in the golden mirror of Aṅgīrasa’s face,
were there to engage in the amorous play of Kandarpa.
"Kāla, O Yamī, you say as you wish;
we have been employed by you as your attendants, and now we have come here at the command of the Mind-Born One."
"O Kāla, this supreme enjoyment of kissing the lotus-like faces of women— what do you desire from it? O Puṇṇaka,
[this] is like a full water-pot in the temple of asceticism."
Why does he not prepare these full breasts for us— the auspicious vessel for the outpouring of the consecration of the God of Love—
whose dark nipples stand erect like upward-pointing banners?
O Earthly Sage, your lower lip is not inferior to a blooming lotus,
nor are your eyes like bees upon a cluster of lotuses; rather, they fall only upon us.
"Where are the arrows of Kandarpa, where is compassion, and where is asceticism?
You are young, my lord, and we too are young;
the season has arrived in this delightful forest."
The gentle breeze blows; why do you delay?
You are like the bodiless Ananga, free from passion;
even these divine garments and ornaments [are yours].
Together with Modesty, our limbs grow limp; yet, O stainless one,
your mind remains firm through its wondrous power over the bodiless Love.
Having spoken words that were agreeable to the ear and heart-reaching with a sweet, divine voice,
he addressed those men who were afflicted by desire.
The daughters of Māra, conceiving various high and low thoughts,
fashioned a hundred individual displays of conflict by means of the charms of maidens and other such allurements, and presented them.
"O sir, we shall serve at your feet," saying this, they strove to please him;
these verses were spoken by the Great Sage in the Dhammapada.
We were unable to agitate them after describing those various modes of amorous dalliance;
with empty hands, they returned to their father.
Then, having gone there, he stayed at the foot of the tree known as Mucalinda, which possessed the coils of the Mucalinda serpent;
he was perfectly situated within the fragrant chamber formed by the rows of its coils.
For seven days he dwelt in supreme jhāna;
having prepared a cross-legged seat at the root of the Rājāyatana tree, he sat there for seven days.
Having come from there, the Teacher, who severs the bonds of existence, partook of the bliss born of liberation.
While dwelling alone, the Teacher, delighting in the welfare of others, remained for a period of seven days.
Whatever duty there was to be performed as food, whether constant or occasional, high or low,
he did not fail to perform it while experiencing the unblemished bliss born of meditation and the Path.
To him, the Lord of the Devas gave tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, and security from fear in Magadha.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Exposition of the Blessed One’s Passing of the Seven Days, in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda— a source of joy to the hearts of all poets—
and containing the introductory narrative. At the root,
while the Blessed One sat having wiped his face in the shade of the branches of the Rājāyatana tree, which was like a necklace of pearls...
Two brothers, merchants, traveling for the sake of trade from their own country toward the Middle Country, arrived at that place.
Having seen the Buddha, whose splendor was peerless, they were stirred by faith.
"Having prepared honey-like sweet nectar, churned milk, and honey-cakes,
Venerable Sir, please accept our alms and partake of them.
Having spoken thus, those two groups of people stood with palms joined in reverence.
"All Buddhas do not take food from the palms of their hands; rather, they accept it when one has intended it"—this is what the Blessed One said.
Recalling this movement of the mind, I placed [the food] upon a stone plate of appropriate size.
Then the Four Great Kings, Kuvera and the others, brought a foot-measure of food;
having combined it into one and resolved upon four bowls, they offered it.
Having partaken of the meal, the Lord of the World expressed his appreciation for the food.
They went for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma;
thus those two merchants were born in this world as the very first lay followers by means of the two-fold formula.
"Give these two a pair of fine garments," they requested.
In the temple of his form, with palms adorned by webs of lines,
he offered a handful of hair that touched the playful grace of a dark-blue sapphire casket upon his head,
possessing the beauty of moss and the petals of a blue lotus.
Having reached their country and placed those relics within it,
while the Blessed One was still living, they established the Great Thūpa,
which amazed the hosts of forest deities and gods, at the place called Ajapāla.
The Conqueror departed from there, leaving Nigrodha behind;
thus he clearly demonstrated the profundity of the Dhamma, thinking:
"This Dhamma, realized by myself, is difficult to understand and hard to see."
Knowing the Blessed One’s mind to be free from desire,
Mahābrahmā approached and requested him to teach what he himself had realized;
having accepted the Brahmā’s earnest entreaty, that refuge of the world—
"I would indeed teach this first, incomparable Dhamma, so difficult to see;
whom shall I approach?"— thus he remembered, and being self-mastered,
he saw the passing away of Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta, who were indeed capable of understanding it.
Reflecting on those wise ones who had become sages, he thought:
"Where now are those monks of the fivefold group who were well-versed in the Dhamma?
Having learned that they were at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī during the month of Āsāḷhī, [he set out].
On the fifteenth day of the month, the Sage entered Bārāṇasī.
On the way, while on his journey, he saw the Ājīvaka ascetic Upaka approaching; at that moment, [he reflected] upon his own Buddhahood.
Having explained this to dispel their doubt, she, through her perception, [knew] them from afar.
Having become weary, the group—though formerly divided—lived together in harmony.
Knowing the mental transformation of those [monks], she sent forth a specific *samphappalāpa* (frivolous speech).
Then the man-lion, his mind filled with loving-kindness (*mettā*), being self-controlled,
bowed to the Protector who had arrived with palms joined in the gesture of the ten nails;
having gone out to meet him on that mountain slope and having cleared the seat, he invited him to sit.
Having thus persuaded them with the words, "O friends,
you must protect me first," the Sage, together with eighteen billion and ninety million Brahmās, adorned himself with his own omniscience.
At Bārāṇasī, on the Deer Park, the Victor, the benefactor of others,
having turned the Wheel of Dhamma upon the Buddha-seat prepared for him,
[taught] eighteen koṭis of beings headed by the ascetic named Koṇḍañña.
On the first day, the Elder Brahmā firmly established him in the first fruit [of the path];
on the following day, this earth-bride trembled violently at the conclusion of the *Kampitthāyaka* [Sutta].
Thus was the sequence of days assigned by Vappa Thera.
Those stream-enterers and others who had attained mastery, having exerted themselves with zeal,
were free from distress when the Elder explained the emptiness of the Suttanta at the time of his discourse; they sent him forth.
Having seen that the son of the Yasa family had become disenchanted with all sense objects and had departed from his home,
the Teacher summoned him; and on the day following that night,
at the conclusion of the night, [he conferred] upon him the first fruit of delight.
He ordained the upper stratum [of disciples], causing them to attain the fruits of the path;
having ordained the people consisting of the son of a noble family, his devoted followers,
and friends, he enabled more than fifty-four of them to reach the fruits of the path.
When thus sixty-one of those whose taints were exhausted had arisen on earth,
at the end of the rains, the Sage dispatched those monks as wanderers through the quarters.
As he himself proceeded toward Aruvela like a lion, that great hero—
Seeing thirty men from the Kappāsika forest settlement,
he ordained them after having disciplined them; those monks of the Bhaddavaggiya group wandered on alms-round, partaking of the flavor of the fruit of the Path.
Then the Leader, the Conqueror, who has disentangled the matted locks,
went to the Aruvela forest; having displayed there that excellent miracle which removes doubt in manifold ways,
he ordained those three eminent brothers with their matted locks.
Having caused the matted hair to be cut off— both internal and external—
he ordained them and made those many jaṭilas free from their tangles.
Together with those one thousand great ones whose taints were exhausted, he was peerless.
Shaking off the dust from every direction, beautiful with its six-colored rays of light,
he entered the city of Rājagaha, recollecting the King’s words;
there he dwelt in the presence of the Sugata at the Laṭṭhivanuyyāna park.
Having heard that account, so auspicious to hear, spoken by the park-keeper, the Lord of Men, having approached with twelve hundred thousand [followers],
honored him at his footstool of lotuses with palms joined in reverence. He was the King of Magadha.
Having abandoned his long-habituated views, Kassapa and the others became masters;
then, seeing the Blessed One practicing the Dhamma there,
the king, free from doubt, drank the most sweet nectar of the Dhamma.
Together with eleven hundred thousand, he attained the fruit of the stream-entry;
having found relief through the disappearance of his distress,
this great lay devotee requests that the Saṅgha, headed by the Sugata, accept alms from him.
Having made his request and bowed down to the two lotus-like feet,
he who was named Bimbisāra, together with his retinue,
rose up and departed from the city of Rājagaha at dawn, accompanied by eighteen koṭis.
On the second day, the city-dwellers gathered in heaps in the Laṭṭhivana grove to see the Buddha of incomparable glory;
however, due to the congestion, there was no space for even a single monk to enter, O long-lived one.
Having reflected thus, Sakka, who had become a young brahmin at that time, generated a sensation of heat upon his seat; then, having crossed over the Path,
he recited the three stanzas concerning the subject matter in the presence [of the Buddha].
"May the Blessed One accept this praise; let there be no lack of food for him.
Having given this gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Sugata, [he established] Rājagaha as the city of the lord of the earth, with the exception of the three sacred sites.
"Venerable sir, how shall I dwell here?
At whatever time I might wish to approach you, even at an improper time—thus he announced his intention. [The Buddha replied:
"In this place called Veḷudāya, which has dense shade and is free from the wind..."
Not far from my garden, which surpassed the groves of the gods,
that king offered water to the Conqueror— who was adorned with webbed hands—
as he performed worship, using a golden pitcher that resounded like a bee.
With the slopes of the Lokāloka mountain as her hips, the Vindhya forest as her eyes,
the Gaṅgā as the glances from the corners of her eyes, the Danaka mountain peaks as her arms,
and the three peaks as her breasts, she whose garment is the ocean proclaims aloud as if rejoicing in merit.
"Excellent! At that moment, Vasumatī’s daughter-in-law trembled with joy.
Having accepted that most beautiful grove, the Teacher preached the Dhamma and, rising from his seat, departed surrounded by the monks.
At that time, those two who were firm friends, seeking the supreme nectar,
wandered through various villages, market towns, and cities.
As he was wandering from house to house there for alms, they reviled him.
Seeing the Elder, who was perfectly self-controlled, the Brahmin named Apatisso,
having found the opportunity, followed his footsteps; hearing a single verse-quarter,
he became a stream-enterer, unraveling the triple bond of the "I" and "mine."
Having heard that deathless and sweet verse spoken by Sāriputta,
Moggallāna— whose fetters had been destroyed— likewise went forth;
both those men, having gone forth, led the wanderers [to the truth].
Having reached the fourfold Ārāma, they gratified the Teacher,
whose goal is the Deathless. Within seven days, having mastered the Great Elements,
Moggallāna dwelt in the remaining three paths and their fruits.
Having exerted effort for half a month and having heard the Sutta spoken by another, he attained mastery over the Dhamma; he was that General of the Dhamma.
At one time, the Lord of the Dhamma [spoke] both of these disciples of mine.
"The foremost, the auspicious pair"— thus did the Sage declare,
having recognized their prior conduct as worthy of the highest place;
he established them, illuminating the entire assembly like the moon shining upon a grove of kunda flowers.
Having heard that my son, King Suddhodana,
has now become a Buddha and, after departing from here, has been dwelling for a long time near Rājagaha,
delivering the entire multitude of people from the wilderness of saṃsāra.
"May you dwell turning the Wheel of the True Dharma which bestows peace.
"I am now old, aged, and advanced in years," he said, "and while still living, I wish to see my son; so speak [to him]."
Having spoken thus, he dispatched one minister there, saying:
"Bring my son within the range of your vision.
Having gone, the minister [beheld] the Victor teaching the Dhamma to the fourfold assembly.
Having seen this, he stood to one side there with his retinue,
palms joined in reverence. Having heard the most sweet Dhamma and attained the fruit of the supreme path,
he went forth and caused the lotus-heart of the king to close its petals.
Eight times more the king dispatched eight other ministers along with their retinues;
likewise, those ministers went forth as wanderers and attained the fruits [of the path], yet they did not return to the king’s presence.
Thus, even they failed to satisfy the king’s mind.
Those whose fetters were completely severed did not fail to propitiate him with their well-sharpened wisdom.
"The time of my death is difficult to discern, dear ones; I am now old.
Therefore, am I still capable of bringing my son within the range of my sight?"
Having spoken thus, the king dispatched his minister Dinnokāsa, together with his retinue,
to that place where Saccaddasena had uttered words that brought grief to Kapuna.
Arriving at the monastery surrounded by his people, he approached the one who had spoken those words.
Having heard the gradual discourse on the Four Noble Truths from Thiramati, the minister went forth,
became one whose fear of existence was destroyed, and having exhausted the taints,
he attained here the foremost place among those who bring beauty to their families.
From the time the Fully Enlightened One arrived at Kasi-patana in Varanasi until he received his royal alms-offering, five months and twenty-one days had passed;
when the winter season had ended, it was springtime.
The young mango sprouts, like women of the grove, were now adorning themselves with the sound of *bhusa*;
knowing the time had come for the Teacher who knows the right moment,
the powerful Kāludāyin thought, "Now is the time to go to the city of Kapila."
Praising him, the kinsmen sang various verses in very sweet tones, sufficient to make him set the time for his departure;
meanwhile, a cool, fragrant breeze now blows very gently.
The forest trees were strewn with flowers and crowded with swarms of intoxicated bees;
the Ganges and its ponds, with their pure and graceful beauty and blossoming lotuses and water-lilies,
were open and visible in every direction— by evening, at dawn, and throughout the day.
Venerable Sir, on the path there is a cluster of nine-petaled flame-like blossoms, radiant with its filaments;
it is covered in ash, yet the swarm of bees creates a dark gloom like chaff.
Even now, it shall consume the forest of full-blown mango trees belonging to those separated from their lovers.
Do forest fires still cause you even the slightest mental distress? For now,
these *asoka* trees on the road— blinded by passion, their branches lopped off and their leaves fallen— cause those who eat their fruit to grieve intensely.
Furthermore, even apart from the forest-dwelling women, those trees—
whose beauty is enhanced by hands as tender as young shoots and whose sprouts have grown lush—
have their cuckoos made intoxicated by drinking the juice of the fruits of the *cuta* tree that has fallen.
O Sage, today the women of the countryside, having formed a procession, are truly honoring you at your footstool with fresh lotuses that did not fade yesterday,
just as female Vetālikas might honor one with sweet songs.
Now, with their branches broken at the tips and bearing handfuls of flowers,
these trees, bending low as if prostrating, seem to announce your arrival, O Mother of the Earth;
they are like heaps of filaments, humming with bees and shaken by the wind, along the path.
O Venerable One, at the edge of your mouth, possessing the splendor of a golden conch,
the long-time dwelling place for the water of the *kalala* stage within,
the buds of the lotuses have opened and expanded as if they were once closed.
While you are now present as a refuge upon your auspicious throne,
abandon mental anguish as the sun rises, dwelling amidst the heat; [the birds],
with beaks adorned by lotuses and water-lilies as their provisions for the journey, [sing].
Now, as you fly along the path of the wind,
bending it, the sound of your tinkling bells as you move above the rows of swans is like a canopy covered with clusters of flowers.
The forest goddesses, having crossed the path,
honor the pair of her feet with handfuls of pollen shaken from the *kiñjalka* filaments—
like showers of parched grain— with their hands bearing the weight of ornaments of gems and gold.
The creeper, with its rows of branches adorned by swarms of bees and tender shoots,
has now fully ascended the wind-horse; the mine of desire,
emitting the humming of bees from its clusters of blossoms, is now joining them together.
The world, having lost its way, plunges into the snare of the minds of the multitude, though it was once radiant with the garlands of budding flowers such as the *campaka* and others;
for from King Suddhodana arose he who is the banner of the Solar Dynasty.
"Old and aged, your father longs to see you;
therefore, O Bhante, having entered Kapilavatthu—
the abode of beings ready for conversion— awaken the king’s heart, which is agitated by grief."
"Excellent! Having reached the domain of the Lord of Men, I shall rescue my father, my other kinsmen, and all others from the ocean of suffering.
Having spoken thus, he whose bimba-like lower lip was adorned with rays of light from his teeth—
Surrounded by the masters of the Dhamma, he departed from the royal palace;
having reached the upper chamber of the king, Āludāyi,
through his psychic power, announced that the meal had been eaten after seeing the king’s arrival there.
Taking a portion of the alms-food brought for the sake of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
he travels through the sky, consoling the family overwhelmed with grief;
day after day, while eating that [food], he goes from one league to another.
Summarizing [the account], impelled by his supreme compassion,
the Jina led twenty thousand of the most excellent monks whose taints were exhausted to Kapilavatthu,
the abode of Lakṣmī, and after staying for two months, he crossed over.
“Before the Blessed One has reached our foremost kinsman’s city, where shall we see him?”—
thus the Śākyas, their minds filled with the wonder of longing,
[went] to that grove of Nigrodha Sākka, a secluded and wind-swept park.
Thinking it suitable, they constructed a new dwelling there;
and having gone out to meet him with hands joined in reverence and strewn with fragrant flowers,
they welcomed the Great Sage as he approached, adorned by the majesty of the King’s power.
Having made the young princes the bearers of the spear-pole,
the king’s ministers led the most beautiful park into the city; [the prince] sat upon a couch like the moon,
surrounded by stars, atop the peak of the Eastern Mountain.
Seated upon the prepared Buddha-throne,
surrounded by various non-returners (anāgāmin) and those free from taints (anāsava),
this sorrowless Sage dispelled the darkness of grief for his father, awakening the lily-like minds of the Sakyans.
"This Siddhattha is extremely young; we are old.
He is our son-in-law, our grandson, and our younger brother," said the Sakyan youths, arrogant with pride, to the very young prince.
"Having approached, you should pay homage to the Jina; do not stand behind us.
Having reflected upon the entire assembly and understood their underlying disposition, [know that] these kṣatriyas are intoxicated with pride and drunk on the wine of worldly power."
Because they do not salute me with the sprouts of their hands joined at their heads,
thinking "I am worthy to be saluted," I have entered into meditative absorption (jhāna);
having attained supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), I am kissed by the rays of dust from my own feet.
The Sun-like Fully Enlightened One, shining upon the crest of their mountain-like crowns,
dispelled the incomparable darkness of pride by manifesting his peerless Twin Miracle,
just as he had awakened the Gaṇḍamba tree at its root with the lotus of his face.
Having seen that sublime miracle, the noble King Suddhodana,
bowing his head in a weight of joy, paid homage with his head at the lotus-feet;
his joined palms were touched by the dust of the soles adorned with the marks of the wheel.
He explained the splendor of the cluster of lotus buds among the royal princes;
like a sun surrounded by a mass of twilight clouds,
the golden-hued Victor descended from his auspicious seat upon the earth.
When their assembly was present, the lotus-eyed Lord, who delights in play,
rained down a shower of rain that possessed the luster of his own fingernails.
Having heard the account of his former life known as Vessantara, he then—
"Having approached and touched with their heads the crest-jewels at his feet,
may the Saṅgha, headed by the Sugata, accept our almsfood, O Bhante"—
thus did some [people] not offer this request on the first day.
Surrounded by those whose taints were exhausted, devoted to compassion for the world,
the Lord of the World, on the second day at dawn, went to the city of Kapila,
which was like a mine of jewels, in accordance with the customary practice of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Without abandoning his humble family status, he entered for alms;
wandering from house to house there for alms with senses calmed,
[he saw] that Teacher of incomparable glory, blazing with six-colored rays of light.
The citizens, having opened the lattice-work made of green gems, worshipped the one with lotus-like eyes that do not blink,
standing upon the palace, with their own lotus-like eyes; and having removed [the coverings],
they honored him who was perfumed by the fragrance of flowers.
With his hair and beard dyed soiled by the ochre robe,
wearing that coarse saffron garment, and holding his bowl with virtue,
the Noble One wanders about seeking alms in the city of Kapila like a wretched man.
Having heard that report, which was bitter to hear, Queen Bimbā— whose lips were like the bimba fruit—
beheld him walking along the street amidst a lattice of emerald stones;
he who moved with the gait of a rutting elephant, surrounded by his retinue, and was ever victorious.
Gazing with eyes like jewels, she filled them with tears;
intent on beholding him, she kissed that jewel of a son,
whose minor marks shone brightly and who was adorned with the halo of fathom-wide radiance.
He recited eight verses describing the incomparable beauty of his form,
from the soles of his feet up to the crown of his head; for a short while,
she moved with a languid gait, like a female black swan.
"O Great King, your son, distressed by the excessive weight of his fresh burden, has gone quickly and, having stumbled in his speech,
wanders through this city for alms, crying out, 'I am the king!'"
The king, who was like one surrounded by an army in his majesty and power,
having heard that, placed a fine cloth upon his shoulder,
covered himself with a new cloak, removed his crown, set aside his sword, and [fell] prostrate.
Overcome with shame, he went very quickly and stood at the head [of the procession].
"Even the storehouses in your father's family are empty; what do you think of this?
Why do you cause your father, born of the Bhānu lineage, to feel ashamed?"
"Venerable sir, since you have been invited by the Saṅgha of ascetics, do not go out for alms day after day; let one who speaks the truth give [the food] to you.
Your lineage is of ignoble descent; it should be the Solar Dynasty (Ādicca-vaṃsa)."
"May my lineage be a lineage of the Noble Ones, a lineage of the Fully Enlightened Ones.
Wandering through this lineage for the sake of alms, I shall dwell in the forest,
practicing that conduct which was practiced by the former Sugatas," so said the Victor.
Standing in the street, the King, who was already a stream-enterer, heard the verse beginning with "Arise!
which is easy to understand; having heard that sweet Dharma of the verse through his attentive listening, he said, "I shall practice the Dharma," and so forth.
Having heard of the conduct of the one named Dhammapāla, who followed the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma and attained the second path,
the heroless, the King [heard of] another conduct—
[that of the one] who attained the third path, which is free from harshness and shakes the abode of sensual desires.
He who, reclining on a white umbrella and a dark-blue couch, remained awake through the night and,
with a mind clear regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), comprehended their characteristics;
having dispelled all doubt and the accumulation of defilements, he attained peace.
Like a hero with a sword, he [the Buddha] conquered the five aggregates—
which are like enemies— with the sword of the supreme path; and being satisfied by drinking the nectar of the bliss of the fruit of that path,
he attained the glory of the sovereignty of Nibbāna, free from the fear of defilements.
Having ascended to the upper palace and taken a bowl,
the King then satisfied the Saṅgha, headed by the Sugata, with hard food and soft food;
thereafter, together with his retinue, he sat down on a low seat.
You spoke words that were consoling and full of joy; yet you,
like a swan submerged in the midst of the lake of the heart within the inner chamber of a woman—
your lotus-face withered as if scorched by the heat of grief.
She worshipped the Buddha with her hands joined in reverence and her head like a water-pot;
she moved forward, bowing low in the manner of a wind-blown haritālī creeper.
Within the inner chamber, she wiped away the tears from her eyes as she beheld the Jina.
Queen Bimbā, having dispatched her retinue to pay their respects,
stood there saying: "If my son, whose wealth is his virtue, has not arrived, he will surely not enter to see that work himself."
Accompanied by men at the king's command, he entered the inner chamber of Indirā’s palace,
which was perpetually shrouded in darkness pierced by the radiance of clusters of jewels;
having reached the foremost pair of ascetics, he sat upon an auspicious seat.
Seeing the Victor seated upon the peak of the Eastern Mountain like the young sun-garlanded one, that princess, with her broad chest slightly bent,
quickly approached him, divested of her garlands and ornaments of gold and gems.
I thought she was a lotus grove, as she bowed her head at my feet according to her desire, taking hold of both my ankles;
with the curls of her braided hair clinging to the interior lake of the palace.
Not sinking into the water agitated by the playful waves of her own creeper-like arms—
the water consisting of the stream of light radiating from the tips of the nails on the feet of the Lord—
she found relief and dispelled the heat born of long separation.
Having heard from you this non-hoarding of gold and gems,
this wearing of the saffron robes, this non-distribution of wealth and possessions,
this lack of delight in misconduct, and this refusal of high seats and couches—
The King said: "O you who manifest love and the arising of compassion,
having heard of her merit— which is surely the support for boundless virtues—
the Conqueror has come, revealing his deeds that were previously concealed by existence."
Having led the prince named Nanda—
who was being held by the hand as he entered his home— to the consecration festival on the following day,
he, together with the Blessed One, proceeded along with the five auspicious women.
Quickly opening the lattice and looking out onto the street, she said:
"Venerable sir, take the bowl; my word, and you shall not refuse it. But he did not give his reply.
Having ordained him, and having heard the words of her who was intoxicated by the wine of sensual objects, he caused Nanda— the prince of the lord of men— whose heart was filled with joy,
to desire the embrace of the divine Śacī, whose feet are like those of a peacock.
She established [her son] in the unsurpassed sovereignty of supreme bliss by the right method;
on the seventh day, Queen Bimbā embraced her own jewel of a son, Rāhula, who was devoted to pleasure and intent on play.
Having opened the jewel-encrusted lattice within the interior of the celestial palace,
she stood gazing at the Supreme among Men as he approached.
[The sky] was encircled by various mountain peaks and filled with the rainbows of the Lord of Devas.
"O King of the Golden Peak, proclaim him clearly: 'He who approaches like a walking mountain, surrounded by those whose taints are exhausted,
radiant with the splendor of gold— this, O Nārada, is your father.'"
These various treasures of hers arose through the power of her merit;
from the time she began to approach the merchant Kapaka, those treasures did not diminish.
Having adorned that jewel of a woman, who had a lifespan of only seven years, [he took her].
"Ask for it," he sent word to his father regarding the paternal wealth;
having generated intense affection for his father like a water-born lotus, the son said:
"I am your son, you are my father; even as a shadow, you are pleasant to me."
Having spoken these words, the Conqueror rose from his noble seat;
and having finished his meal, surrounded by his retinue, he began to depart. [The King said:
"O ascetic, give me my inheritance; I have need of wealth."
Repeatedly entreating the Conqueror who follows the gait of a lion king,
she adorned with her garland-like arm-creeper— long as the body of the lord of serpents, firm, beautifully red-fingered, and like the shadow of a lion— the Blessed One.
Having ordained Rāhula— who was born of his own wish, who follows after worldly existence,

and who follows the cycle of saṃsāra— with the thought, "I shall bestow upon him the treasure of noble wealth," the King of the True Dharma, whose son did not abandon him, reached the monastery and spoke this:
"Ordain him," he said to the gracious-faced Dhammasenāpati.
Having cut off his mass of hair, soft as the petal of a blue lotus,
Mahāmoggallāna donned it and covered himself with a brand-new saffron robe.
The Elder Mahākassapa, a proponent of ascetic practices, gave him the exhortation;
Sāriputta ordained that jewel of a youth, and he lived under his guidance.
At another time, the Elder Mahārāhula, desiring his training—
Having heard the *Vāda*, Rāhula attained even greater virtues;
having heard the *Kasutta*, he reached the position of one who is venerable among those venerable for their training, crossed over the three worlds, and attained the fruit of the supreme path. (Ka)
When that noble son of Suddhodana had gone forth,
the royal lineage’s banner plunged into the shoreless ocean of sorrow;
his mother and father gave him leave to go to his beloved son for the sake of his future destiny.
The lay followers requested the supreme boon, "May you grant us the going forth";
having granted the boon to the king with a noble mind, he rose from his seat after finishing his meal,
and emerging from the grove within the palace, he encountered a gentle breeze.
The Lord of the Six-Tusked Elephant retired to a cool, secluded spot on the shore of a lake,
where the tree-shadows were sparse and the breeze was refreshing.
At that time, there was also a great merchant born into a household of householders.
The faithful man named Sudatta, having reached the excellent city of Rājagaha and become a follower of the Buddha, heard that the Buddha was residing there; thus,
at dawn, Suddhodana arrived there through the gate opened by the immortals.
Having seen the handful of water-offerings cast upon the jeweled surface of the footstool,
which brought forth clarity of mind like a silver pitcher atop a crown,
he heard the Dhamma on that first day and attained the fruit of the initial path.
Having given a gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Sugata,
Sudattodhanī [said]: "Venerable Sirs, for the sake of our prosperity,
may you bestow upon us the city named Sāvatthī, which is powerful, prosperous, frequented by virtuous people, and free from the stains of misfortune."
May the Lord of Dhamma, whose horse is the shade of compassion, go quickly;
having found his breath, may he return to his own domain with his purpose accomplished.
Thus, that householder, for the sake of the Buddha, [saw] the great road entirely clear by day—
Having bestowed wealth that possessed the individual characteristics of beauty,
such as its splendor at night and so forth, he— possessing abundant riches—
had an excellent monastery built in the city of Daṭṭhabbasāra, which was like a second abode of the immortals.
Having purchased an even piece of land for eighteen koṭis,
having constructed abundant dwellings for eighteen koṭis,
and having performed a supreme festival of garden worship for eighteen koṭis—
Having prepared it, that householder brought the new palace to completion;
thus, having caused the excellent Jetavana monastery to be built,
the chief of merchants dispatched messengers for the arrival of the Great Hero.

Having heard that message, the Fully Enlightened One, possessing blazing supernormal power, departed from Rājagaha together with his retinue, honored by them with their hands joined in reverence at their heads.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Exposition of the Miscellaneous Deeds of the Blessed One, in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*— a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which serves as a cause for the joy of the hearts of all poets and provides a proximate introduction to the history of the Conqueror’s lineage.
At the auspicious festival of crossing over [the ocean of existence] by means of Indirā-Rāma, who is named Jetavana for the Teacher,
[he was] possessed of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

The chariot of the three realms of existence, with ignorance as its pole, craving and clinging as its axle-tree,

Ignorance (avijjā) is the non-knowing of the ten remaining phenomena beginning with volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), as well as of suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path.
Ignorance exists on three levels;
it is this that conceals the true nature of the Four Noble Truths,
for the duration of volitional formations that do not investigate thoroughly.
In the three realms of existence, by way of various methods,
the cause is the two types of volitionally constructed karma alone,
which serve as the respective causes for rebirth-linking consciousness in the sense-sphere realm.
Wholesome [kamma] leads to the form realm and the formless realm;
it is the cause for rebirth-linking in both.
Wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] are thus analyzed in three ways.
Accumulated in a previous existence according to its correspondence,
what else could there be for rebirth-linking other than the cause consisting of the resultant consciousness of the process of existence within the three realms?
The ripening of desire-forms consisting of the aggregate of origination occurs as rebirth-linking and during the course of existence,
each with its own respective name and form as the cause.
And likewise, according to their respective causes,
there are four types of immaterial results (arūpapāka),
each arising solely through the condition of its own specific level (bhūmi).
The mind accumulated in the non-percipient beings does not exist on earth merely for the sake of form;
both of these [types of mind] also arise from non-resultant consciousness.
In accordance with its nature, it prevails throughout the three realms of existence;
in good and bad destinies, within the sphere of sense-desire,
there arises for the six sense bases what is called name-and-form.
In the world, there exists name-and-form consisting of the three bases for one who is conscious of words and possesses a subtle form;
in the formless existence, there exists the arising of name-and-form.
It is merely a measure of the subtle mind-base (manāyatana);
thus, in the threefold existence, those respective bases arise from existence as their source, with contact as the cause.
In the same way, according to its sequence,
the form of existence arises through the six types of contact and feeling within the three kinds of existence;

The matted locks that have been plucked out become the cause for grasping again at both states of existence; through the nature of causality,

By means of that clear Dhamma, which is established through its connection with the fruit of power and arises in dependence upon its essence and profundity— this is what is performed.

The Dhamma-element, for the sake of understanding that which has been made free from the thicket of doubt by a mind of well-purified wisdom— possessing three connections, three divisions, and three sections— is [to be understood].
To the one with steadfast wisdom, whose fourfold assembly is rooted in two;

the Lord, whose entire spokes are joined to the wheel of the chariot of existence.

The entire world, including the gods, greatly honored him;
even Sahampati once honored him with a necklace of priceless gems as large as Mount Meru.
The many asuras and humans, according to their strength,
honored Yama; so too did Anāthapiṇḍika,
the householder, and the female lay follower Visākhā.
Together with his retinue, King Bimbisāra of Kosala, and King Aśoka,
the Lord of the Earth who bore the white umbrella,
the Universal Monarch of the Island.
Having renounced ninety-six billion Abhimahis equal to those of the Ten-Powered One,

who were vessels for the great respect and proper rites of worship,
likewise honored him with robes and other requisites worthy of such people.
The distinction of worship through the fourfold requisites:
he who is an ocean of virtues, the foremost among those worthy of offerings,
and who is worthy of receiving the hospitality of both the virtuous and the unvirtuous.
Thus the fame of the Blessed One’s poetic skill as an Arahant is renowned throughout the world; yet here,
people are greedy for the highest worldly honors.
These petty ascetics, arrogant in their own power and desiring fame,
do they not accumulate unwholesome deeds in secret out of fear of ill repute?
"Even a king who fears evil does not commit even the slightest wrong"—
thus it was said by the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The fame of the Arahant Bhūviviṣuta resounds;
his lust, hatred, and delusion are not yet stilled,
and his body, mind, and wisdom are neither firm nor well-cultivated.
Those who have failed in the noble practice,
who follow the ways of the ignoble and are the lowest of men—
may they well grasp the banner worthy of the Well-Gone One.
Even though the Blessed One’s fame as an Arhat, renowned throughout the world, is excellent and follows him closely,
it remains far from those who are devoid of faith.
In the same way, O wise one, the Sage dwelt together with persons devoid of hatred;
such indeed was the mindfulness of the Blessed One as a teacher.
The fame of the Arahant Bhūviviṣuta resounds;
he has destroyed all defiled states,
and his body, mind, and wisdom are constantly well-cultivated.
The wise one, who fulfills the noble path and guards against the ways of ignoble states,
remains far— by a hundred and ten times ten yojanas— from them.
Even those who dwell far away from the Victor are,
according to the Blessed One, not so very distant,
for the fame of his renown as an *arahant* resounds throughout the earth.
In the same way, the Sage also attained a state of non-remoteness toward such true persons;
thus it was for the Blessed One, the one who has reached the end of existence.
The fame of the Arahants, who have transcended the world, resounds:
"O people, abandon evil states!
The Arahants declare that they have abandoned those things which cause harm and bring no benefit."
Thus the Blessed One is worthy of the title "Arahant," a fame and renown spread throughout the world;
he is free from that which is censurable and should be shunned by the Noble Ones.
Because among the most exalted worldlings (parama-puthujjana),
there is no report of fame or renown for this Blessed One as "Arahant" or "World-Famed."
Moreover, there has never been a time when those who ought to be secluded were not rebuked by the Blessed One;
such is the Blessed One’s manner of seclusion.
The fame of his name as an Arahant resounds throughout the world;
that which is called "going" does not exist for him,
nor does the secret wandering through the three realms of existence.
Thus, for the Blessed One who has gone to the further shore,
there is a world-renowned report of his fame as an Arhat,
possessing unsurpassed virtue, mind, and wisdom.
‘One who has attained the knowledge of liberation through supreme liberation,
a vessel for incomparable qualities, unshakable,
peerless, unequaled, and unsurpassed.’”
He who is praised for his abundant form perfected by wholesome power and for his manifold virtues— thus may he be praised,
even as the Blessed One is praised.
The cry of fame, "An arahant born in the world," has arisen.
For this reason and for that reason as well,
the Blessed One is the banner of the Gotama clan.
The sound of the fame of the Worthy One (*Arahaṃ*) resounds throughout the world of beings, including those dwelling in water,

oil, and cloth. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Subject Matter Concerning the Designation of the Name 'Arahaṃ' for the Blessed One," within the *Jinavaṃsadīpa* (Lamp of the Conqueror’s Lineage), composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda as a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, and situated at the beginning [of the work].
Because he has rightly and personally awakened to the truth of all phenomena through the power of his wisdom,
the title "Sammāsambuddha" (Perfectly Enlightened One) has been proclaimed for him.
The world-system of Āsikityā (Sālinī);
and those phenomena which are to be directly known, those to be fully understood,
those to be developed, and those to be realized.
He awakened to the truth rightly, therefore he is known as the Buddha;
he is celebrated in the world as the Perfectly Awakened One (Sammāsambuddha).
Therein, that which is to be directly known is precisely the Four Noble Truths.
Suffering is indeed a truth that must be fully understood;
the truth of the path is what must be developed;
the truth of cessation is a reality that must be realized.
Phenomena arising on the side of craving that have come into being,
which are not to be abandoned by the paths— these phenomena,
together with the pairs of suffering such as birth and so forth, are fivefold.
The foot, the feet, and the trunk may be the truth of suffering;
that craving which is divided into craving for sense-pleasures and so forth,
being the cause of sufferings, is the second truth.
The non-existence of bondage therein is cessation;
and the truth which is the relinquishing of craving through direct knowledge—
these are the factors of the Noble Eightfold Path, beginning with right view.
The truth of the path that leads to the attainment of Nibbāna—
because he has fully awakened to these phenomena as well,
he is renowned in the world as the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha).
"This suffering is in the eye; its arising has craving as its cause.

the path is wisdom, the means for awakening. Thus it is said of it.
Having thus extracted each word individually and having established them among the true phenomena,
he who is the upholder of truth and the seer of truth is the Buddha.
He awakened rightly and by himself through sharp wisdom;
thus he became renowned in the world as the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha).
[He understood] the six doors and their six objects.
Of the six classes of consciousness, the sixfold diversity of cognitions,
the six perceptions, the six volitions,
and the six contacts beginning with applied thought;

Thus, by means of the complete and personal awakening to the truths through the removal of the six veils, beginning with form— that is, the removal of the groups of craving— he was therefore [called the Buddha].

the eighteen elements (dhātus), and the twelve bases beginning with the eye (cakkhu).

[he attained] the four meditations on form and the formless—
Of the jhānas, the recollections, the ten [bases of] mindfulness,

he [knew] all phenomena— past, future, and present—
as well as Nibbāna and the teachings of complete designation.
Having personally realized it for himself and not through another's teaching,
he was renowned in the world as the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha);
all that is to be known is his knowledge— how could it be otherwise?
When knowledge and the objects of knowledge— the two categories of phenomena—
had reached their ultimate limit through the attainment of the final stage of knowable things,
he became renowned in the world as the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha).

Because he has rightly and personally awakened through the knowledge of the path to the total exhaustion of the latent tendencies of the defilements along with the sleep of delusion, he is therefore called a Sammasambuddha.
He became renowned in the world as the Perfectly Enlightened One;
the Lord of Beings, his self impelled by the perfections,
sat cross-legged at the foot of the Bodhi tree, free from attachment.
Having attained beauty through union with the rays of the sun,
as if it were itself fully awakened,
she was peerless and unsurpassed in her excellence.
Having awakened by the light of the Path and attained the splendor of the knowledge of omniscience,
he was therefore renowned as the "Perfectly Enlightened One."
Thus, because he has perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena,

The fame [of this work] resounded throughout the world. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the illumination of the subject matter concerning the designation of the name "Bhagavā,

the Fully Enlightened One," within the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*— a cause for granting joy to the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, as a proximate introduction to the *Santikeka-nidāna*.

that Blessed One is perfected in true knowledge and conduct."

perfected in true knowledge and conduct,

or the swift flight of a hawk seizing its prey,
so too was the arrow of the Teacher, the exceedingly heroic Sarabhaṅga. (1)
When an arrow is shot, does it miss the target?
In the same way, among past existences,
one who is neither attached nor repelled—

He for whom there was nothing shared with others—
he is the Victor who has abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance,
endowed with true knowledge by means of that first [jhāna].
Just as the sound of a bronze bowl struck by a staff spreads far and wide, so too does his fame spread;
[he discerns] the various modes of conduct, such as the inferior and the superior.
To beings as they arise and pass away,
according to their karma, in their various destinies,
and to forms that are beyond the range of the eye of faith;
With the knowledge known as the divine eye, which is not shared by others,
with its clear radiance and its divine apprehension of light.
By means of that second true knowledge, the Teacher— unshaken, endowed with clear vision, and having transcended the sphere of death and rebirth— knows as a Conqueror.
Thus his fame resounded like the ringing sound of golden bells; and [he taught] suffering,
the origin of suffering, and its cessation.
And the path that brings about the cessation of suffering—
these four truths he, the Self-Existent One,
proclaimed according to their true nature by means of his knowledge.
Whatever taints there are, whatever is the origin of the taints,
their destruction, and whatever is the means for the cessation of the taints—
all that the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) has fully understood through his knowledge.
By that strength through which one is liberated from the taints—
one for whom birth is exhausted, who has lived the holy life,
and who has done what was to be done— this is the supreme conduct.
And he did not dwell with knowledge limited to the future,
but through his knowledge he dwelt having directly realized it;
the Self-Become One, for the exhaustion of all taints.
Endowed with that third [knowledge],
his fame spread abroad like the sound of a deep, resonant drum-roll.
For the Tathāgata who possesses the three kinds of knowledge previously mentioned,
there arises from them fame and a physical image.
The mirror of the mind of the virtuous shines forth;
that which consists of the four great elements and was born from the hands of mother and father.
This body, which is composed even of a morsel of food and a bit of gruel,
is a phenomenon subject to impermanence, destruction, and dissolution;
it has been experienced within the limited realm of sense-sphere existence.
In that very state of existence, within the division of the foot,
there is the name of the various categories of feeling,
perception, formations, and consciousness, which are dependent upon it.
That which is clear, like the color of a gem-staff—
into that I have looked with the eye of knowledge, as one would look at a thread wound therein.
By means of that, I have examined formless matter.
The one with clear vision knows that which is called "name" as dependent upon that [form];
and "form" is characterized by being broken by cold and so forth,
while "name" is characterized by not decaying.
Beyond that, neither an experiencer nor a doer,
nor a self possessing a personal identity, exists in the ultimate sense;
they proceed by way of mutual dependence.
They do not go separately like those with crippled limbs,
but rather name-and-form proceed here by depending upon one another, as it were.
"Of one who defines": this refers to the view that name-and-form is by nature devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul,
through the purification of wrong views.
Views arise as what is termed purification;
ignorance, clinging, and desire for existence are the causes for the arising of form and the formless, which is conceit.
In the *Pakavatti*, it is stated that "matter arises from the four causes,
beginning with the physical basis (*vatthu*)," which is its name;
[this principle] is everywhere, in all things, and at all times the same.
Thus, by means of that wisdom,
he discerned the conditions that produce those [states],
so that they were not seen as causeless nor as having an impermanent cause.
"Was I indeed? Was I not indeed?"— thus,
for one who has purified doubt by crossing over doubt regarding the distinctions of the past and so forth, there is the purity of having crossed over doubt.
By means of that wisdom which has been fully developed,
he discerned that the aggregates— distinguished by such categories as the past and so forth—
are impermanent phenomena in the sense of their total exhaustion.
