having thoroughly mastered name-and-form by means of these ninefold aggregates and the seven groups of fear, [taught the Dhamma].
When, through his wisdom, he performed the investigation of the arising and passing away of kinsmen in fifty ways,
by means of that youthful insight, [he attained the fruit].
The ten defilements became manifest;
by means of the eye of knowledge, he then perceived the three characteristics in those very phenomena.
Just as one who travels along a road purified by insight proceeds after having clearly distinguished the right and wrong paths, so too [should one proceed].
Having entered the path of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) through the mind,
there arises that which is called the purity of discerning what is the path and what is not the path—
a wisdom sharp in its analytical investigation.
Immediately thereafter, he reached the further shore of investigation and examination through full understanding and total destruction—
that which is endowed with the nine knowledges for the sake of accomplishment.
One who desires purity and longs for purification,
if they do not attend closely to those phenomena that are concealed by the density of attachment due to their continuity and habitual practice, [will fail to attain it].
When he again comprehends name-and-form by means of its arising and passing away within the three characteristics, at that time,
from the perspective of its arising, dissolution, and persistence—
The knowledge of dissolution, which arises for one who practices insight after having turned [the mind] away,
and which occurs at the breaking up of formations— this possesses smoothness,
various benefits, and the potential for further development.
As he contemplates the breaking up [of formations],
fear arises for him like that of wild beasts and the like;

Then, that knowledge of fear regarding the three states of existence arose for him;
thereafter, the phenomena consisting of the aggregates and sense-bases appeared to him like vultures and other scavengers with drawn swords.
When they had attained mastery over that which is fraught with calamity and danger, they perceived its peril,
just as golden swans perceive the cage.
Having become disenchanted with the three kinds of existence—
the dangers of which have been seen— the sole eye of the world attained that intense knowledge of disenchantment which serves as the cleansing of defilements.
Just as beings enter a palace from the outside,
those desiring liberation [should emerge] from the three realms of existence for one who desires the complete release from all conditioned formations.
And the knowledge that desired to release arose for him who was constantly meditating upon the aggregates as impermanent,
suffering, foul, and non-self.
The wisdom of reflective discernment that accomplishes the means for liberation from formations is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.
This heap of conditioned phenomena is twofold;
thus it is fourfold, manifold,
and even sixfold for the wise one who frequently practices insight.
That which is called insight that has reached its peak,
as well as the conforming [insight] leading to emergence,
is like a rope in the ocean [pulling up] the pillar of a well.
She took the three characteristics as her object of meditation;
she became weary of the nature of conditioned phenomena,
which are like a mass of sinews and bones fallen into a fire.
Like one who has released his children,
the great Seer’s equanimity toward formations is directed toward the aggregate of knowledge of the higher faculties.
The application of the three characteristics, the inclinations and tendencies,
and the various types of insight-knowledge—
whatever has been explained here by way of summary;
By means of that very knowledge pertaining to insight-wisdom, he has conquered Māra;
thus the creeper of his fame has grown.
He attained expansion within the husk of the world,
just as one might draw a blade of muñja grass from its sheath,
or as one would extract a serpent from its basket.
Possessing all limbs and minor parts,
with the excellence of the sense faculties, mind-made,
and measured from this body— having fashioned another body—
Possessing great power, he was worthy of those with psychic powers;
having attained mastery over the mind and perfected his skill,
he acted for the benefit of those who were to be trained.
Possessing great psychic power,
he was endowed with that knowledge known as the mind-made body;
thus his fame and renown spread far and wide.
He deafened the entire world. He who,
being one, becomes many, and having been many, becomes one again.
The one of great psychic power, standing in the conduct of those possessed of psychic powers, can manifest disappearance or invisibility,
just as [a form appears] upon a supportless surface of the earth.
O Lord of Power, you who possess supernormal might,
you pass through mountains, house walls,
and ramparts as if through open space, without even touching them.
He performs the miracle of diving and resurfacing upon the surface of the earth as if on the surface of water,
moving gracefully through the water without being broken by it.
Just as one who has prepared his way travels across the earth,
or as a bird soars through the sky, so too does he proceed,
having assumed the cross-legged posture of great majesty.
He who, with his hand, touches and rubs the orbs of the sun and moon, which possess great power,
even as far as the Brahma-world with his physical body;
He of great power brings [the mind] under his control,
just as a goldsmith fashions whatever particular ornament he desires according to his wish.
The Victor, who at any time experiences various kinds of supernormal powers according to his wish,
is likewise endowed with that very science (vijjā).
His fame has spread abroad, just as the path traveled by a person on a journey becomes an object of clear perception for the ear.
One may hear various sounds here and there— of kettledrums, conchs, drums, lutes, and so forth;
both from afar and nearby, whether human or divine.
Both sounds, whether subtle or loud,
pure or produced by humans—
those the Protector hears with his divine ear.
"Endowed with" means: by that science known as the divine ear, which has conquered its enemies, he has emerged;
he whose praises are sung by poets—
The word "siloka" is indeed the word "siloka";
likewise, a mind with lust is a mind without lust,
and a mind with hatred is a mind without hatred.
The mind with delusion and the mind without delusion;
the mind that is contracted and the mind that is distracted; the mind that is exalted and the mind that is not exalted.
The mind with outflows and the mind without outflows, the concentrated mind and the unconcentrated mind, the liberated mind and the unliberated mind.
Just as one fond of adornment gazes at their own face reflected in a mirror,
so too should one direct one's mind toward other persons with clarity.
He by whom the liberated mind is known—
endowed with that science called "penetration of others' minds"—
is a treasury of compassion.
In the womb of the three worlds, his white fame,
born of that [merit], spread forth like the splendor of a canopy;
by means of the three sciences and these eight kinds [of qualities]—
The Tathāgata has indeed attained true knowledge; his body,
radiant with fame, shines like the moon emerging from a cloud,
illuminating those who are ready to be trained.
He who moves about, a treasury of compassion,
adorned with the well-restrained Pātimokkha and the ornament of virtue so called;
One whose wealth is austerity, preeminent among those possessing virtue—
[he should avoid] flattery, seeking gain, acting as a messenger,
and sending letters on the day of the offering at the Veḷuvana.
Thus, by means of buffoonery,
by speaking falsehoods like bean-soup,
and by frequenting improper places—
Why indeed would he violate the Pātimokkha?
Having abandoned improper conduct and unsuitable resort,
he should always practice right conduct and proper resort.
Even toward immeasurable things,
the all-seeing one perceives fear in blameworthy states;
having attained the virtue established by the supreme path and its fruition—
"He trains with reverence for the training;
he wanders toward the secure direction"—
by means of that practice of the higher training for liberation, he protects himself.
Exalted is the lineage of his conduct,
the succession of glory belonging to the Kinsman of the Sun;
[it consists of] the sixfold sense-bases, beginning with the beautiful form-base.
Having made [objects] the domain of his eyes and other senses,
the Protector does not grasp at their signs or secondary characteristics;
thus he possesses restraint over the sense faculties.
Seeing him dwelling with states such as lust because he did not restrain the six doors beginning with the eye,
they would surely overcome him by means of the restraint of mindfulness.
He practiced for the sake of that restraint;
by means of that conduct,
he who had conquered his senses moved toward the state of security through the restraint of the senses.
The fame and renown of that Lord of the Three Worlds spreads far and wide;
for those who desire gain, honor, and renown—
Some in this world, being equal to those with evil desires who are intent on gain,
reject the four requisites and then make use of them [inappropriately].
By means of whispering to others, by such acts as remaining stationary in the four postures,

one’s own welfare through the planting of merit,

By means of hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth, and by seeking gain through gain,

By explaining the treatises on signs and so forth,
one does not violate the virtue of livelihood;

Neither for sport, nor for intoxication,
nor for the sake of physical beauty,

In order to eliminate the ancient hunger for the supreme conduct of exertion in the process [of practice],

Tilokanātha indeed wanders through the world toward the direction of safety.
His fame has spread abroad;
by day through sitting and walking meditation,

With a pure interior, through two modes of conduct,

The Sage, in his middle age,

through that perfected conduct of pure faith, he was established in confidence toward full enlightenment.

like one who loathes filth, he shuns evil."
Because he wanders through the world with that noble conduct of moral shame, the sound of his fame has risen up high,
reaching as far as the realm of Khemā.
By means of that conduct characterized as moral dread (*ottappa*),
which has the characteristic of causing one to tremble at the unliberated from evil,
one wanders through the world toward the direction of security.
The fame of that wise one has spread abroad through his practice of the Dhamma by means of strength and truth, which is not shared by others.
He whose fame and virtue are preeminent wanders through the world like the moon;
by his firm strength and heroic exertion, he is thus called Samubbhava.
Because he wanders with heroism through that very conduct,
he wanders toward the auspicious goal;
thus his origin was given as "Samubbhava," and his medicinal herb was "Yasodhī."
Because he is exceedingly brave in recollecting past deeds,
and because he moves toward the state of security through the practice of truth, he is the Teacher. Thus it is said of him.
His fame spread far and wide through that noble conduct of wisdom, which possessed a profound knowledge not shared by others.
The continuity of his fame spread abroad as he wandered toward the state of security,
which brings happiness in this very life.
The Blessed One, the Buddha, is one who has escaped through his conduct,
who obtains the fourfold jhāna at will,
and who obtains it without difficulty.
With those four form-jhānas,
which are obtained at will, the Protector traverses the auspicious directions in the world.
His fame has spread abroad and continues to grow;
he is endowed with these threefold eightfold sciences and these fivefold fourfold practices.
The body of glory, purified by true knowledge and conduct,
shines forth as long as the world endures.
Thus ends the *Jinavaṃsadīpa* (Lamp of the Conqueror’s Lineage), composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which serves as the primary cause for bestowing joy upon the hearts of all poets.
The twenty-first chapter, the Nidāna, in the *Santike*, is the illumination of the referent for the designation "the Blessed One, perfected in knowledge and conduct.
Furthermore, regarding that venerable Gotama, this excellent report of his fame has spread abroad: "In this way, the Blessed One is a Sugata.
He is called a Sugata because of his beautiful going (*sugamana*).
They say that going is "gone," which is most beautiful;
one who has gone by the noble path toward the auspicious direction has gone, free from both haste and delay.
"Thus indeed is the Sugata, he may be called the Sugata;
the teachers here proclaim that going which is unsurpassed,
the bestowing of non-existence, and beautiful."
Because he has gone by means of that which is to be gone by with certainty, from whence [he came],
he is thus called the Sugata;
the Sage is one whose sole purpose is to conceal the three circles.
With a golden knife, he neatly trimmed his inner robe into a perfect circle,
cutting it like a nine-petaled lotus.
Surrounding him with a supreme golden garland,
he binds it around his hand like a lotus;
the Sage possesses the splendor of steady lightning.
The binding of the corpse of one who has mastered the arts;
like a fresh woolen cloth from Ratana,
upon the cetiya of solid gold, [is] a mass of glory.
The Sage, whose excellent body is adorned with a beautiful webbed membrane,
wears a saffron robe as ruddy as the glow of the rising sun.
With his palms possessing the luster of blue sapphires,
he adorned [the ground] with lotus petals,
just as a lake adorns itself with bees upon its lotuses.
He proceeds like a truly moving Mount Meru entwined with the beautiful bow of the mind’s lake;
his body is adorned with the ornaments of a recluse.
"Thus indeed is the Sugata, may he be the Sugata!
Like the elephant of the gods from the Nandana grove,
or like the monkey [Hanuman] from the cave of jewels to Mount Yugandhara."
Like a noble swan emerging from a divine lake filled with fresh lotuses,
he emerged auspiciously from the forest cave and the ascetic grove.
Having gone forth from his home,
he possesses a form beyond compare, with unsurpassed splendor and great majesty;
thus indeed is he the Sugata, truly the Sugata.
As if by the excellent sprinkling of the golden essence of the immeasurable rays radiating forth,
the earth and sky proceed as if turned tawny-gold.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
like a noble elephant surrounded by elephants,
he himself is free from all stains of evil.
He who is served by those free from stain,
and who possesses even a fraction of the splendor of the Unequaled Buddha— it is for this reason that he is called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
He who has overcome the delusion of both men and gods and follows the beautiful path that leads away from it—
thus indeed is he a Sugata, a Sugata.
Illuminating the ground with the radiance emanating from his body in the front, back, right, and left,
he moves upon the earth like a jewel measured by the fathom.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata,
a Sugata who wanders on his journey through towns, villages,
and cities, one whose conduct is governed by compassion.
"May he bring about the wish of immeasurable beings"—
thus indeed may that Sugata be truly called a Sugata;
(he who is like) the kumuda, the paṅkaja, the campaka, and the mālatī.
With his form touched by a rain of flowers,
he moves with even greater beauty, possessing radiant supernormal power;
thus indeed is he the Sugata, truly the Sugata.
On the great highway strewn with fragrant powders of tagara, saffron, and red sandalwood,
he moves with splendor like a scent-elephant.
Thus may he be a Sugata, a Sugata indeed;
one whose excellent qualities are praised with hundreds of verses,
accompanied by the songs of the fourth heaven and the hymns of the virtuous.
He moves with the graceful gait of a swan;
thus he is called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One;
he is the vessel for the eyes of gods, humans, and others.
The nectar-like essence of the playful beauty of his sublime form,
and his prowess that strides with the majesty of a lion’s stretch—
thus indeed may he be called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
Unable to endure the weight of the glory of the lotus-like feet,
as if she were a woman of the earth longing for him,
the earth trembles, quakes, and shakes as he walks there.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata:
one who has compassion for minute creatures, for gnats, flies,
stinging insects, mosquitoes, beetles, and moths.
He who walks without harming others is indeed called "Sugata"; he is truly a Sugata,
marked with the excellent wheel upon his right [foot].
If he who walks first with a gait as swift as a golden lotus were to set it down [first],
then indeed he would be a Sugata, a "Well-Gone One."
He who, unstained by passions,
touches the surface of the earth with feet as soft as lotuses,
wanders over the ground having shaken off all impurities.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
like the surface of a drum when struck, his path is difficult to traverse because of the lotus-like feet he has set forth.
Because he has made the places that were low and high level,
he may truly be called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One;
upon the head of the mud-born lotus of the earth and the waters.
With lotus-like feet whose tender soles are set down,
he walks with a beautiful grace like that of golden dust;
thus indeed is he the Sugata, truly the Sugata.
Even pebbles, gravel, shards,
potsherds, and thorns give way from the path for the Best of Bipeds.
"Thus indeed is the Sugata, the Sugata he may be:
you think your own footprint is too far away to lift up,
yet too near to set down."
He walks without jarring his ankles or knees;
thus he is called "Well-Gone," for he is indeed Well-Gone—
swift yet composed, with his faculties fully stilled.
He does not walk, yet he walks with a radiance blazing;
on ground both level and uneven, he is unequaled, walking with evenness.
Thus he is the Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
Without looking up, down, or in the intermediate directions,
nor in the four cardinal directions,
he who walks mindfully observes only a distance of a yoke’s length before him.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata:
one whose stride mocks the graceful gait of the lion,
the lord of beasts, with its three-fold bound mane.
He walks with the soles of his feet touching the ground;
thus he is the Sugata, truly the Sugata,
the Bull among Men, by virtue of his incomparable radiance.
With valor unconquered by King Vasabha,
he proceeds, engendering great joy among the people;
thus indeed may he be called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
The sun’s rays shine forth,
and a breeze fragrant with the scent of flowers blows;
he moves through the midst of that stainless path.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata:
before him, the clouds scatter drops of water,
and gods and men scatter flowers.
When he went along the road attended by kings,
it was said: "He is indeed a Sugata, a Sugata!"—
the immortals bearing radiant fly-whisks and parasols.
He goes, honored, revered, esteemed,
and respected even by gods and men;
thus indeed he is a Sugata, a truly Well-Gone One.
If he proceeds with a canopy of flowers borne over his head, highly honored by the sounds of lions, elephants, horses, deer, and birds;
"Truly, he is the Sugata, the Sugata indeed!
When the elephant-like Conqueror moves,
he glides with grace upon the beautiful, smooth path of the gateway arches."
Even the ornaments on the hands of beings [shine]—
thus he is the Sugata, truly the Sugata;
there arises a wondrous, marvelous, and auspicious [splendor].
Because the three worlds are incessantly filled with the play of festivals and festivities,
he is indeed "Well-Gone" (Sugata) upon the path of the Well-Gone; thus may he be called Sugata.
He has gone to the unconditioned element, the unsurpassed,
the most beautiful state, free from taints,
and devoid of birth, aging, and death— Śiva.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata:
like the sound of a drum or a kettledrum, unconfined,
reaching from the sky up to the peak of existence.
He honors the Conqueror’s conch by means of the lotus that blossoms from his navel,
which is the very ground for the adornment of perfect enlightenment.
Where Vijayabodhi now shines,
like a cluster of lalita-piñja flowers,
in a place that is immovable and beyond the reach of others.
Though he had previously reached that most beautiful place,
which was as fragile as a bubble and like the heart of a young woman of the earth, he arrived there once again.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
for even that which is called the "basis of enlightenment" is here the noble knowledge, supreme and unsurpassed.
Even though his knowledge was unobstructed,
it did not transcend the entire range of the knowable;
for he had fulfilled the perfections in previous births.
Because he was devoted to the peace of the conditions for strength and had reached that beautiful place even then,
he may truly be called the Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
Because the Sugata has reached the state where the defilements,
once abandoned by means of the fourfold Noble Path, do not return,
he is therefore called "One Who Does Not Return."
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata:
from his excellent resolve and his perfect progress,
beginning from that time until his attendance upon the seat of victory.
By fulfilling the thirty perfections,
he may truly be called the Sugata;
for he has abandoned both the views of existence and non-existence.
He who, having gone without following [others],
brings about welfare through a most excellent practice—
it is for this reason that he is called the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata).
Having entered the midst of the assembly like a lion, he, free from fear,
utters his lion’s roar with beautiful and eloquent speech.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata,
a Sugata: with a fragrant lotus-face,
through the power of well-spoken words arising from virtuous conduct.
He speaks in the assembly of the Dhamma while dwelling in seclusion;
thus he may be called the Sugata,
the one who brings delight with a voice like the song of the cuckoo.
He speaks words that are more acute, sweeter, and full of flavor,
with a delightful resonance in the midst of the assembly;
thus he is the Sugata, truly the Sugata.
He who speaks, having purified himself from all verbal defilements,
having broken through attachments and doubts,
speaks with truth and according to reality.
Thus indeed is the Sugata, the Sugata;
his speech is firm and never fails;
he speaks with confidence, unwavering and immovable.
One who always possesses the vision of the Four Noble Truths and has reached the further shore—
such a one may truly be called a Sugata;
he is devoted to compassion for people who are both united and divided.
When one speaks with an intention that is truly free from grasping,
and the other receives those words accordingly,
in this way he may be called a Sugata, a Well-Gone One.
Since he speaks words that are pleasing, exceedingly delicate,
pleasant to hear, easy to understand, and heart-stirring—
words that are flawless and free from any flaw in their delivery.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
having abandoned association with women who delight in the arts of love,
the wise one of excellent mind knows the proper time for the appropriate occasion.
He speaks of the occurrence of phenomena in their true nature, not otherwise;
thus he is the Sugata, truly the Sugata.
He always speaks as one who has mastered the meaning of all that is to be known.

Because he has spoken that which is for the welfare of the world, for the benefit of the world, which removes mental distress, which has reached the ultimate goal, and which provides for both [this life and the next],
thus indeed is he the Sugata; he may truly be called the Sugata.
It speaks of liberation from all conditioned phenomena within the unconditioned element,
as well as that which is dependent upon the noble paths and fruits.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
for he is a proponent of discipline who disciplines the people,
being intent on the purpose of discipline and devoted to self-restraint.
How can one who speaks based on the Vinaya say,
"Thus indeed is the Sugata,
he is the Sugata," when [the truth] is always deposited within the treasury of the heart?
He who speaks with a sweet voice, possessing excellent speech that is well-composed and measured,
such a one may truly be called "Well-Gone" (Sugata).
The Sage, whose lotus-face was free from fear,
further expounded the very same words,
proclaiming the eightfold path of practice.
Thus indeed may he be a Sugata, a Sugata;
[whether] speech that is not false or even false, whether it be purposeless,
or whether it be pleasant or unpleasant to those who hear it.
The Tathāgatas never speak thus:
"He is indeed a Sugata, he may be a Sugata";
rather, they speak of what is beneficial and pleasant to those who listen.
When those who know the proper occasion speak words that lead to their own true welfare,
even in the course of ordinary conversation,
it is for this reason that he is called "the Well-Gone One" (Sugata).
Addressing the people each in their own language,
the Tathāgata— the banner of the Gotama clan— who speaks words of welcome,
spoke in the Magadhi tongue at the assembly for the sake of their satisfaction.
By that [teaching], he became widely renowned as the Sugata throughout the three worlds.
[He taught] the world, the origin of the world,
the cessation of the world, and the means for liberation from the world.
Because he has rightly gone by means of the four clear realizations, the Lord is therefore the Sugata. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter,

the illumination of the subject matter regarding the designation of the Blessed One as "Sugata," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*— a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, a source of joy to the hearts of all poets, and a proximate cause for [the attainment of] the goal.
Furthermore, sirs, this excellent report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad: "In such a way, the Blessed One is a knower of the world.
Of him, whose soles of the feet are marked with the excellent wheel and who possesses the beautiful characteristics of a Great Man—
Even unto the peak of existence, the cry "Knower of the World!
arose as a single verse:
"The cessation of the root of characteristics, the cessation of cessation."
Because he penetrated all the remaining worldly views by means of the path,
the Sage who benefits the three worlds is therefore called "Lokavidū" (Knower of the World).
Right here in this world, within the mere frame of a body,
he realized the cessation of the world’s causes and the practice that brings about the cessation of the world.
Therefore he is called "Knower of the World";
he who has crossed to the further shore of the great ocean of the world—
the world being divided into the conditioned world and the receptacle world.
Thus the Blessed One knew everything without exception;
therefore he is called the "Knower of the World" (Lokavidū).
For he [knew] the nature of the craving for existence and non-existence...
Because he has awakened to the nature of the mind— which is characterized by patience in accordance with knowledge— and because he understands all beings,
he is therefore called "Knower of the World."
When the conditions were met for its manifestation,
he— who had shattered the world— penetrated the sevenfold underlying tendencies of people.
Therefore, he is called "Knower of the World" because of the mixture of lust, hatred,
delusion, faith, wisdom, and thoughts.
Thus he penetrated the conduct of those who understand;
therefore he is called "Knower of the World" by virtue of his inclination toward the inferior and the sublime.
He understood the two-fold inclination of beings;
therefore, he who knows the world’s language for the sake of the people is called "Knower of the World."
He who has little dust in his eyes, whose evil is small,
whose evil is slight, and whose dust in his eyes is minimal— because of this,
he has awakened to this world which is difficult to penetrate.
Therefore he is called "Knower of the World.
By means of the radiance of knowledge regarding the faculties—
both their prior and subsequent states— he [knows] the world of sharp faculties.
Thus, because he has penetrated the world of dull faculties,
he is called "Knower of the World" (Lokavidū); therefore,
the foundation of the turning and unturning of the cycle of existence is not good.
The Blessed One has entered into the assembly of the virtuous;
he knows both this world and the other world.
Therefore, he is called "the Knower of the World."
Since he knew the entire collection of beings,
it was easy for him to make known even that which is difficult— the fixed destiny of those who are well-praised and those who are censured.
Therefore he is called "Knower of the World," for he has penetrated the state of liberation,
having attained release from the obstructions of karma,
defilements, and their results.
Because he knows those who are capable of being trained and those who are incapable of being trained,
he is called the Knower of the World; therefore,
[he is] the one whose speech is not fruitless, the Unsurpassed, the Infinite.
Because he has personally realized through the power of knowledge that is free from the seven obscurations,
he is therefore called "Knower of the World."
In this world, that Sage, according to the manner already described, penetrated the manifold nature of the seven classes of beings,
like a bee in a lotus forest of sentient beings.
Therefore he is called "Knower of the World," for he has penetrated the world of the conditioned as established by causal relations,
seeing it as unconditioned.
Although it is of a single kind,
it is called "the Knower of the World" because the world has been planted [in it]; therefore,
all form is so called by virtue of its characteristic of being susceptible to change.
Because he understood the four names according to their characteristics and the two-fold world,
the Lord of Sages is therefore called "Lokavidū" (Knower of the World).
The Blessed One, the benefactor of the world, has thoroughly analyzed the threefold experience of pleasure, pain, and equanimity, and has thus penetrated the three worlds.
Therefore, he is called "Knower of the World" (lokavidū).
By way of his kinsmen, the Sage is fivefold;
by way of his retinue, he is fourfold in the world.
He who resembles a lamp for the world has penetrated [reality] and is therefore called the Knower of the World (Lokavidū);
he is the teacher of non-duality regarding what is known as the six sense-bases.
The Victor has known the world in its sixfold aspects,
and he has known the world as the sevenfold station of mind;
therefore, he is called the "Knower of the World."
Since he, the Sage of the Śākyas, understood the eightfold nature of the world, beginning with gain,
while dwelling in his new residence.
Therefore, he is called the "Knower of the World"; as such,
by way of the differentiation of the twelve bases,
he is the Lamp of the Three Worlds.
He who has known the world, who knows the three characteristics,
is therefore called "Knower of the World" (Lokavidū),
because he has analyzed [the world] thoroughly by way of its constituent elements (dhātu).
He has penetrated the world, which consists of eighteen realms, by breaking through the conditioned world;
therefore, he is called "Knower of the World."
Thus he knew the world— including jewels,
gold, silver, pearls, conch shells, coral, stones, and gravel—
as bound by factors beyond the reach of the senses.
Therefore, he is called the "Knower of the World" (Lokavidū).
[This is] by way of the distinctions of trees, creepers, fruits, sprouts,
leaves, flowers, and various types of colors.
Thus he knew the world of subtle intervals;
therefore he is called "Knower of the World.
As much as there is of this mass of aggregates—
Whatever has come down to this world of vessels,
he has penetrated that entirely;
therefore, he is called "Knower of the World."
Thus the Blessed One [described] the measurements of the Himālaya,
the measurements of the eight great hells and so forth,
and the measurements of the palaces of the nāgas and supaṇṇas.
The measure of the worlds of Brahmā, the Suras, and the Asuras;
the measure of dust, water, wind, and earth;
the measure of islands, rivers, and oceans.
The measure of Mount Meru, the peaks of the earth,
the wish-fulfilling trees, the sun, and the moon—
the entire collection of phenomena conditioned by causes.
Because he has penetrated the entire receptacle world—
including all that is above, below, and across—
he is therefore called "Knower of the World."
The maker of light for the world, the ornament of the three worlds,
awakened to this world of beings by way of the underlying tendencies, the abodes, and so forth; likewise,
he awakened to the world of formations and the world of space by way of nutriment, measure, and so forth.
Therefore, the Conqueror, who has reached the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*), is called "the Knower of the World" (*lokavidū*).

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Designation 'Knower of the World' for the Blessed One," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*—composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which is the primary cause for granting joy to the hearts of all poets—and within the "Proximate Introduction.
Furthermore, such a glorious report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad: "Indeed, that Blessed One is the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
Because there was no other person with a multitude of virtues equal to himself,
that Sage, by way of compounding and derivation, [was so named].
The peerless moon, with a face like a lovely lotus;
for thus that Man-Lion, by his perfection in virtue and these qualities,
surpasses the world together with its gods.
Through concentration, excellent wisdom, and liberation,
as well as through the perfection of the qualities of the vision of liberation—
therefore, no further perfection of higher virtue is found.
Who here could be his equal in the qualities of mastery over concentration and the rest? Who could possibly exist as one superior to him?
Yet even he is surpassed by this peerless one of great wisdom.
O Sage, you are incomparable among sages who are themselves unequal;
since you are equal to those who are unequaled,
you are thus the peerless Tathāgata, with no second anywhere in this world.
Because of his non-existence [in the future], the Tathāgata is without a second;
since even a likeness of him does not exist,
he is then peerless even in the attainment of the incomparable.
Since there was no companion who had penetrated awakening,
the Sage remained peerless and without a companion,
even though his physical body was captivatingly beautiful.
There is no person on earth who is equal to him in virtues,
nor is there anyone who can even conceive of a division of his teachings; indeed,
there is no counterpart to him in the world except for himself.
Because of the accomplishment of the supreme enlightenment,
which is the exclusive domain of no other, I am indeed the Self-Become One (Svayaṃbhū),
the Peerless One; it is not fitting for me to give a promise without [the fulfillment of] my own [task].
He is "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed";
he tames those persons who are to be tamed and has them well-tamed, and he causes those persons who are not yet tamed to remember [the training].
Since the Victor is skilled in the means of discipline,
he is called the "Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed," just as a charioteer [controls] horses with a soft rein.
The Tathāgata, through discourse on the higher realms and the Dhamma,
tames and reminds others accordingly; thus is the Tathāgata called the "Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed."
Just as a charioteer by means of harsh methods subdues and guides a horse,
so too does the Tathāgata subdue and guide beings according to their needs.
He is the "Unsurpassed One," the charioteer who subdues men.
Just as a charioteer subdues [a horse] by means of both gentleness and severity, so does the Tathāgata.
Even though he has left behind those who revile him and does not instruct those who follow him,
he is the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed;
like an elephant rushing forward when urged by its trainer.
It was only the directions, beginning with the east, that were set in motion by the Conqueror,
the unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed,
who has reached the further shore of the human realm.
Seated upon some place for reclining or sitting, you,
moving with extreme agility through the eight directions,
rushed swiftly toward the unsurpassed quarter.
He is also called "The Peerless One," the Charioteer who tames men.
Having become established in the training of higher virtue,
the Sage, being a master, taught through the training of higher mind.
He tames those individuals capable of being tamed as is appropriate;
thus he is called the "Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed.
When the Sage’s mind is concentrated through the training in higher consciousness,
Having instructed even a recluse in insight meditation,
he tames those worthy of being awakened according to their needs;
thus he is also called the "Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed."
In order that they may attain successive higher realizations,
the Leader of the World tames and disciplines the non-noble and the trainee persons respectively.
He is the "Unsurpassed One," the charioteer who tames men;
having subdued his own kinsmen, he, whose face is like the moon,
disciplined the lords of Kosala, Magadha, and other realms.
The Guide, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, [instructed] many kṣatriya men;
[he was like] a lion to the elephant of false views, [and he subdued] Kūṭadanta.
Since the Lord of the Jinas, having instructed the wise Brahmin Surādibhūsurapuri, disciplined him,
he is therefore called "The Unsurpassed" as well as "The Charioteer who Subdues Men."
The Leader extensively disciplined that eminent householder scholar Upāli, who was difficult to approach,
because he was capable of receiving the higher ordination.
The Peerless One, the Charioteer who tames men;
he who calls even the view of untruth "Truth," the Leader of the Nigaṇṭhas who has no other teacher.
The Jina, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, [taught] Vīna, Tappa, Bhūti, Digambara, and others;
the Lion among Jinas [taught] Sabhiya and Subhadda.
He who was skilled in piercing the darkness with discourse on the True Dhamma,
who trained even those ascetics both within and without,
and who is called the Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed; ()
Since I have disentangled the matted locks of the matted-hair ascetics,
such as the brahmin Uruvelakassapa and Gayādikassapa; O Lady, I am a monk.
He is the Peerless One, the Charioteer who subdues men;
the Sage, supreme in abandonment, restraint, and discipline,
amidst many kshatriyas and ascetics within the Teaching.
Like a charioteer who guides his horses from one stage to the next,
he is the "Unsurpassed One," the trainer of men to be tamed; he [is free] from those seats of human blood and flesh.
Having subdued the night-stalker with his pendulous belly,
along with the most terrible mānava and many rakkhasas,
he is indeed the unsurpassed charioteer of those to be tamed by men.
Vināyaka, who is well-disciplined, [subdued] the one named Rāhu,
the lord of the Masuras; likewise, he subdued the lords of the gods,
beginning with the Lord of the Suras, as well as the Asuras.
He is the unsurpassed charioteer who subdues men;
he is compassionate toward all beings,
including Pajāpati and even the one called Baka, who held empty views.
He is the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, who has trained those who were not yet trained even by means of whips and goads,
seated upon a dust-free, stainless seat at the edge of the forest.

a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda as a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, serving as an introduction to the proximate cause [of the Buddha].
But why has this fair report concerning the venerable Gotama spread abroad, saying: "The Blessed One is indeed a Teacher of gods and men"?
[It is like crossing] a wilderness, harsh and thorny, waterless, a path to be traversed with difficulty—a wilderness where the king of beasts, the elephant, and the great lion sport.

Because he instructs this world— including its brahmins, gods, humans, ascetics, and priests—

Furthermore, such a glorious report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One a Buddha"— he who,

Because he possesses the power of awakening those who are to be awakened, because of his own excellent wisdom, because he is not to be led by others due to his own Buddhahood,

The sound of the song of his praises rose up through the abodes of the three Buddha-fields;
for he had attained the supreme path with an intellect that had utterly uprooted passion,
as well as hatred and delusion, along with the entire thicket of their latent tendencies.
Thus, because he has destroyed the taints and relinquished the acquisitions,
this title "Buddha" is uttered and celebrated with high praise by the wise even until today;

One who has not crossed over the flood of defilements and sloth, awakened by another,

This [work] awakens the minds of the wise, like white water-lilies, but what [awakening] could it bring to the lowest of men? Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter,

titled "The Illumination of the Subject Matter through the Designation of the Blessed One’s Name," in the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*— a work composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which serves as a source of joy for the hearts of all poets and is a primary cause for the granting of blessings.
Herein, how are the Buddha’s qualities, though boundless, comprised in two ways: through his own attainment of welfare and through his practice for the benefit of others?
Of these, his own attainment of welfare consists in being a Wheel-turner of the True Dhamma.
It is twofold according to the distinction between the perfection of abandonment and the perfection of knowledge;
likewise, the majesty of the physical body is included therein as twofold;
and the practice for the benefit of others is also twofold, according to the distinction between application and disposition.
The practice of one who is indifferent to gain, honor, and fame,
for the sake of the pacification of suffering, is a teaching that leads to liberation;
his intention remains even toward those who are enemies, such as Devadatta and others.
With a constant disposition toward the beneficial and a heart of loving-kindness for my husband,
I daily attended to those who were to be awakened but whose faculties were yet unripened,
beginning with the discernment of the time when their faculty of wisdom and the others had reached maturity.
Out of compassion for those beginning with the recipients of religious gifts,
you accomplished the welfare of others through the practice of benefiting them;
and also by way of manifesting those specific virtues of theirs, [you acted].
How is the inclusion of terms such as "arahant" and so forth in the Pāḷi [to be understood]?
Therein, by this term "arahant," what is indicated is the perfection of abandonment,
which is the perfection of one's own welfare.
By the phrase “the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the Knower of the World,” the perfection of his own knowledge is illustrated;
by the phrase “endowed with clear vision and conduct,” his own perfection of virtue is shown.
All attainment of welfare, beginning with true knowledge and conduct,
is expressed by the term "Sugata," starting from his initial aspiration: namely,
the perfection of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the charioteer who tames those who can be tamed,
has explained the practice for the sake of others through the analysis of word-components;
by means of these word-components, he is revealed as the Buddha, the Blessed One.
The attainment of one’s own welfare, the practice for the welfare of others,
and the threefold qualities of a Buddha—
these are summarized by the terms "Arahant" and "Sammāsambuddha," which denote the destruction of the causes of suffering and the benefit of sentient beings.
By the phrases "endowed with true knowledge and conduct" and "knower of the world," the qualities comprised by the fourfold perfection of the axle are extolled; however,
by the two terms "charioteer of men to be tamed" and "Teacher," [the remaining two are indicated].
The qualities are described by way of the perfection of the sevenfold assistance;
both sets of Buddha-qualities are elucidated by this term "Buddha" through the distinction between the attainment of the fruits and the attainment of the sevenfold assistance.
The Sugata, the Blessed One, the Kinsman of the Sun, has revealed through two verses the perfection of cause and effect for one devoted to the goal;
he is more steadfast and solid than the lofty and noble Mount Meru of sublime virtues.
Even the King of Mountains appeared small before the King of Conquerors;
compared to that ocean of his gradual, profound,
and perfect qualities, this [other] ocean seems like a mere drop.
The dust of the earth does not equal even a hundredth part of the Teacher’s ground of qualities— steadfast, immovable, firm in resolve, and well-established;
it is as if thousands of world-systems were crowded together [in comparison].
By the power of the radiance of his virtues, the Teacher— who is free from the bonds of the sun— is perceived through a mass of qualities that is infinite and boundless;
thus, even though space is limitless, it appears as if it had a limit.
Thus, the qualities of the Buddha are infinite, boundless, inconceivable, ineffable, and beyond comparison—oh, how marvelous and wonderful!

Thus ends the ninth chapter, which briefly illuminates the qualities of the Arhat and others, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda as a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, serving as a lamp for the lineage of the Conquerors. May it endure for a long time.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.
On the Gijjhakūṭa mountain, cool with the breeze from the chowries of waterfalls cascading from its peak-clasping slopes,
Wandering at times as one who bears a body as yellow as the Haricandana tree, the Compassionate One dwelt there,
presiding over the entire community of monks.
"In this royal capital named Rājagaha,
honor the excellent circle of the assembly,
gladdening the Sage and subduing the blameless one," he said.
Having now assembled the community of ascetics,
that king of ascetics, whose lotus-feet were honored by beautiful hands joined in reverence, spoke to them.
"Consider this, O Venerable One, as the time for what must now be done.
Then the Sugata, having gone further from there,
was like the morning sun scattering its rays at the break of dawn.
The Sun descended from the peak of the Eastern Mountain like a celestial coral tree to the excellent Maṇḍalamāḷa hall;
seated there upon the top of that palace, he sat.
Like the king of beasts upon the peak of the Golden Mountain, the King of Sages,
confident amidst his assemblies,
proclaimed the qualities that lead to non-decline.
Having departed from that city,
the Blessed One was dwelling at Ambalaṭṭhikā,
where mango trees were adorned with fresh sprouts.
With a beautiful form, lovely in its minor marks;
thus concentration is brought forth by virtue,
and wisdom is brought forth by the mind, both bearing fruit.
"Success! Having thus set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he then went to Nālandā together with the Saṅgha;
there, in the mango grove, he stayed as long as he desired.
Approaching him as he dwelt there, the Elder Naga Sāriputta,
with his head bowed like a cluster of *mañjarī* flowers and palms joined in reverence,
paid homage at the moon-like feet of Canda.
Having approached and extolling the Blessed One— who is free from attachment and possesses abundant wisdom—
the one who resembles a lion by the river spoke these fearless words:
And the Blessed One approved that speech;
having stayed there, he delivered a discourse connected with higher virtue, mind, and wisdom.
Then that wise Sage, preceded by the community of ascetics,
went from there to Pāṭaligāma; the Muni [arrived] at the upāsakas of Pāṭaligāma.
In this dwelling beautifully constructed out of compassion,
he gave the nectar-essence of the Dhamma to those who were drinking it with hands cupped in reverence.
Not long after those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma had departed,
the Blessed One, seeing that the dwelling was empty of people and without others...
Having entered, he made the lion’s posture;
there in that city of the lord of Magadha, the king of the earth, were Sunīdha and Vassakāra.
At that time, having consulted with the gods of the Thirty-three, the ministers completed it;
having beheld it with his divine eye.
The Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"This shall become a noble site, a place of trade;
it is the road to the city named Pāṭaliputta."
Due to the occurrence of internal dissension,
just as from fire, there may sometimes be obstacles to the city known as Pāṭaliputta because of its origin from the river Dakā.
The Sage spoke thus to the Sage of Videha;
on that very day, Sunītha and Vassakāra approached the Blessed One.
With their heads touched by the crowns of the Conquerors' feet,
they shone for a moment as if they had been anointed,
by virtue of the steadfast and essential quality of the King of Dharma.
Their neck-bones standing like the staffs of bows,
both of them together invited the Sugata for a meal on that very day.
Having granted him his consent,
they served the Blessed One together with his company with the prepared, exquisite foods.
Then the Blessed One, having washed his hands,
ate at the hands of Sunīdha and Vassakāra,
who were residing in Kamalāvasa, once he had removed his bowl.
Having drunk deeply of the drink of Dhamma, they rejoiced,
their inner selves overflowing with rapture;
thus did those people follow the King of Dhamma.
As he proceeded from there, protected by the monks,
he traversed the broad expanse of the earth to the wide city gate.
Thus, this gate known as Gotama,
touched by the feet of the Buddha Gotama, is exceedingly glorious;
through it one descends to that place where [the waters] are drinkable even for crows.
To the sage named Gaṅgā, who flows with lofty waves—
a deep river whose garlands of ripples are tossed by the force of the heavy wind— ;
That which was fragile and subject to dissolution,

Beholding the people together with his disciples,

Narasārathi went toward Koṭigāma by way of Bhumikantā,
where there was no space between the villages of Makuṭa and Ākāra.
With her thighs raised and her feet placed upon her lap, she said:
"I am one who has awakened to the true Dhamma;
for me, there is no further rebirth. Thus she spoke.
There, in the rainy-season retreat at Movadi,
the Sage, having come from the village named Nātika, addressed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with a discourse connected to the Three Trainings.
Having answered the questions asked by Ānanda,
he elucidated the method known as the Mirror of Dhamma for the purpose of reviewing one's destiny.
The Great Sage, who established the qualities of the Arahants and others,
resided there in the Giñjakā Hall,
dwelling as the compiler of the Three Piṭakas.
The Sugata, together with the community of monks, further delivered discourses on higher morality and other topics,
and then set out for the city of Vesālī, the foremost among cities.
While dwelling in that mango grove,
he taught the Dhamma, supreme in mindfulness and wisdom, to me,
Ambapālī— the scent-elephant of the Conqueror.
Having now heard [the news] in the mango grove,
the courtesan mounted her excellent carriage,
her burden of devotion greatly increased by the weight of her breasts.
Then the courtesan sat with palms joined in reverence,
her body trembling as if burdened by the weight of thick, swelling breasts,
her voice as sweet as the cry of the karavika bird.
The Teacher spoke the sweet Dhamma to her;
having accepted the invitation for a meal, they expressed their confidence with sounds like the ringing of bells.
Having circumambulated the Lord of Sages clockwise,
that lady, like a female swan, went to her palace;
she was adorned with fresh garments of blue, yellow, and red—
Well-dressed and well-robed in garments dyed with white and madder,
they ascended auspicious and excellent vehicles like the sons of the gods.
Then the Licchavi kings and princes, having approached and paid homage to the King of Dharma on the banks of the Sindhu river,
which was bound by the rays of his nails, [spoke].
Seated there, they rested from the fatigue of the journey;
their crests, bee-patterned garlands,
and sparse clusters of *licchavi* flower buds shimmered.
The fragrant rice, though broken and unable to stand upright,
has been made fruitful by the one who wields the sword against the wicked.
Those people, whose invitations had become fruitless,
set out from that city after mounting their chariots, even though they were covered in dust from the feet of Virajaṅgha.
Early in the morning, the Great Sage, together with his Saṅgha, descended from the gateway that was like the eye of the world to the spotless dwelling of the courtesan.
The one whose lotus feet are stepped upon by the crowns of kings departed;
at the conclusion of the meal and the company,
the courtesan sat down with palms joined and [heard] the Dhamma.
Having fully understood, she of perfected faith gave the mango grove to the Sugata and his disciples;
the Sage, having accepted the mango grove, [bestowed it upon her].
Having dwelt there, O King, teaching these doctrines concerning supreme virtue, mind,
and wisdom, he went to the village of Beḷuva.
"I dwell here, monks; you are my companions in the ascetic life.
Come, let us enter the rains retreat together."
The Sage, having arrived from the vicinity of Vesālī, spoke thus at Beḷuva:
"Victory over the power of Māra!
Now that the Rains have begun, a terrible disease has come upon me."
And there arose in him, at the time of death,
piercing bodily pains, exceedingly intense;
yet he was one who had reached the further shore of patience through endurance.
Then the Blessed One, like a scale in the face of pleasure and pain, being untroubled in nature,
endured it with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Without regard for the community of monks,
and without having made an announcement of my presence here,
I am now free from craving and have attained the state of Nibbāna without residue.
If I should attain the state of final Nibbāna,
having exerted myself with vigor and cast off this powerful affliction that cannot be easily removed.
Having established the Blessed One’s life-faculty upon a distinction worthy of reflection,
the Blessed One then applied himself to concentration.
Having stilled his painful feeling,
he entered into great insight;
for feelings do not arise again once they have been extinguished.
Having come from the Ravi Bandhu monastery,
she sat down well-adorned upon a beautifully prepared seat in the open courtyard of Bahichāyā.
Overcome by illness, he sat down quickly; there, the ascetic Ananda,
who had conquered birth, old age, and disease, approached him.
There, having seen me, he said, "Is it endurable? Are you at ease?
because of your severe illness, O Bhante.
"My state of being is like a pillar struck down;
all the directions do not appear to me,
nor do the teachings manifest," he said.
Moreover, this disciple of mine has no stain upon his heart;
having realized the state of nothingness,
the Blessed One has passed away without remainder.
"Venerable sir, may I attain the state of parinibbāna.
Having thus made a distinction between what is internal and external,
is it not indeed the Dhamma that has been proclaimed by Ānanda?
There is no "teacher's fist" among the Tathāgatas.
Tell me, what does this Saṅgha expect from me?
Now I am one who has spent eighty years [in the religious life].
The body of the Tathāgata is utterly decayed;
like a cart worn out by age,
it functions with a creaking that is held together by repairs.
When, through the cessation of sensations accompanied by signs,
one enters and dwells in the concentration born of liberation,
at that time one's personal existence [is stilled].
Even that which is subject to decay is exceedingly peaceful; therefore,
from this moment forth, make yourselves islands unto yourselves, relying on the Dhamma as your lamp, and do not seek refuge in anything else.
"The Blessed One said that they alone are the seventh [type of person]:
the ascetics who have developed their body, mind, and wisdom;
having completed the rains retreat, they return there again."
Then Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, having approached the great monastery of Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, the Blessed One.
Having performed various transformations through his supernormal powers,
the elephant-sage, granted leave by the Sage,
said, "This is my final sight of you."
Surrounded by five hundred followers, like a second Teacher,
he bowed down, circumambulated the Blessed One to the right, and approached the mother’s house.
When Janindo lay down upon his bed in the lower chamber,
he then attained parinibbāna, and there was an earthquake;
then the Naga-like Elder named Kolita—
Having thus prepared the opportunity, he attained final Nibbāna;
then, having caused the distribution of his bodily relics,
the Sage had cetiyas erected for them.
The Sage, his form being drunk in by the eyes of the people,
having reached the city of Vesālī in due course,
was well-clad and well-robed as he entered among the families.
Wander for alms like an elephant moving with deliberate grace;
the Blessed One, having finished his morning meal,
desires to spend the day in seclusion, Ānanda.
Then, having said, "Take a seat," he went to the Cāpāla shrine known as the Caitya;
thereupon the Blessed One sat down.
The chief attendant of that [monk], having departed from him,
spoke thus and sat with palms joined:
"Udena’s cetiya is also beautiful."
Furthermore, he said: "The four bases of spiritual power (iddhipāda) of the Sugata— these qualities have been well-developed, well-practiced, and repeatedly cultivated by the monk."
The Sage might remain for an eon if he so chose;
yet, with a mind permeated by compassion,
having conquered Māra, he did so only three times.
While the Sage was performing the utterance of the sign of vast radiance with straightforwardness, another person,
as if his mind were possessed by defilements, [acted otherwise].
With his mind distracted by Kharamāra,
he did not penetrate that [truth], nor did he even request,
"May the Blessed One remain for the full span of my life."
"O Vāja, you who desire [the goal], for whom it is always the time for giving—
Aṇḍaka, you who are intent on asceticism! Having spoken thus,
[he remained] for a moment under the control of Vasavatti.
He sat not far away at the foot of a tree;
the Blessed One, the kinsman who brings others to awakening, approached the place where his negligent kinsmen were.
With his body not bent by pride,
which was like a serpent that had consumed its own tail,
he was once known as "Ajapāla" (the Goat-herd).
At the foot of the banyan tree in Uruvelā,
have you accomplished what was to be done? The promise made by you is inscribed and persists upon the canvas of my mind.
"O Ascetic, by your teaching alone have they crossed over;
now they are upholders of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma,
devoted to the practice, and possessed of great learning."
Well-prepared, highly confident, and disciplined;
having refuted the doctrines of opposing disputants,
they [proclaim] with righteousness and with miracles.
They speak and cause others to speak of the Dhamma;
then, having said, "May you attain final Nibbāna," he who has completed all the duties of a Buddha [passed away].
When the Sage had thus spoken three times,
he who has no abiding place in the realms of existence uttered the verse beginning with "Analā" (in the Upacchandaka meter) as a refutation of that [position].
May he dwell free from anxiety until the end of three months;
may the lamp of the Dharma-king, who illuminates the light of truth and destroys the darkness of evil,
remain for forty-five years in this abode of the three worlds, having rightly extinguished all craving.
"Today he will attain Parinibbāna, casting off the force of his life-faculties," he said.
Thus, at the Cāpāla Shrine, as he cast off the force of his life-faculties with mindfulness and clear comprehension,
there was an earthquake, a sharp sound like the beating of drums, and a deep resonance.
The clouds, struck by hundreds of arms like streaks of lightning, thundered like drums;
the world, plunged into the darkness of sorrow, fell into a terrifying state that caused the hair to stand on end.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Lord’s Relinquishing of the Life-Faculty," in the *Santika Nidāna*, a lamp for the lineage of the Conquerors composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which serves as the primary cause for bringing joy to the hearts of all poets.
Having gone to where the Blessed One dwells with Ānanda,
he sat down before the lotus-feet of the highly honored One with hands joined in salutation, his head bound in happiness;
"Venerable Sir, my mindfulness is dried up, my hair stands on end, and I am overcome by terror."
"Since you have been born, O daughter-in-law of Vasumati, why do you tremble?
he asked. "Perhaps because of the powerful wind blowing below in the air, the winds that shake the waters, the earth, and the ground of dust."
Just as when the earth trembles, some ascetics and brahmins who have plunged into the midst of the surging garland of restless waves think, "This is the place where the earth is shaking, O Ānanda!"—
even so, some ascetics and brahmins [perceive] the immeasurable.
Those who have cultivated the perception of water as subtle earth and have attained mastery through the development of higher knowledge, they are the gainers of meditative attainments;
even this trembling of the earth becomes for them a state of earthquake.
When he enters the womb, he is mindful and clearly comprehending;
when he emerges from the womb in his final existence, then too,
that man of noble power either awakens to full enlightenment or causes the earth to tremble.
These phenomena, O ascetic, are the cause of a great earthquake:
when the Buddha, the eye of the world, having become enlightened, sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma for the sake of those who understand,
and when he relinquishes the force of the life-formations.
When the earth shook as it touched the element of Nibbāna at the cessation of the aggregates,
these were the causes for that great earthquake, O Ānanda.
With hearts purified by that [experience], they gladdened the Elder Ānanda.
Having comforted him and expanded his teaching further and further, he said:
"Ānanda, once I dwelt at the bank of the river Nerañjarā,
at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, where the rain-clouds had ceased their pouring."
Having arrived there, may the Blessed One touch the Nibbāna-element within his body—
thus spoke the Evil One, whose heart was defiled by envy and deceit;

"O most beautiful lady, you shall sit here at this Cāpāla shrine on the full moon day of Āsāḷha;

"For while I was proclaiming [the Dhamma], being diligent, mindful, and possessed of equal wisdom, my monk has been abandoned by me, as have the phenomena of the life-constituent, by the one who is like a conqueror of Māra.
When this was said, the Elder Ānanda, whose feet were like the moon among lotuses—

"Ānanda, the Blessed One has declared that a bhikkhu is one whose mental formations have subsided— one who,
even for the sake of protecting his life, would not utter a word such as that which a stump split by lightning might produce."
Having spoken thus, the Sugata, who travels like a lordly scent-elephant,

"Quickly summon the assembly of recluses who speak thus;

"Formations are characterized by their nature of arising"; thus [he reflected].

In the forenoon, the Teacher, whose feet were firm, arrived with his robes covering his limbs, having reached the place where he had been seated upon a seat supported by the tips of his hands like tender sprouts.

he will appear at the seat of enlightenment as a perfectly adorned mass, assuming a created form of the Buddha that is beyond compare.
In the physical form composed of relics, which blazes with garlands of fresh lotus-fiber nets produced by the power of the Buddha,
not even a trace of anything else is seen beyond that extent.
Having performed this, the parinibbāna of the elements will surely come to pass.
O wise ones, out of devotion, remember again and again this *Buddhāpadāna*,
which is pure with the virtues of the Maras, Indras, and others.
The mind, when it has become upright after being overwhelmed by defilements,
will surely attain purity like well-refined gold;
even the states of applied thought and sustained reflection are purified by the radiance of the mind.
Then, with the accumulation of the Teacher’s qualities as their object, there arises abundant joy, as well as tranquility of body and mind,
bliss through the absence of distress, and concentration.
Because of its profundity, it is a state of seclusion from which the ocean of qualities dependent upon it has been drawn forth;
one should cultivate this absorption so that one may attain the access concentration.
The yogi who practices the noble factors that lead to that [liberation],
being devoted to taking refuge in that Teacher of most beautiful conduct,
remains possessed of reverence for the Teacher and respect for his companions.
One who has reached maturity through the faculty of faith and the rest,
abounding in rapture and joy, attains a wholesome outflow;
his very person becomes like a shrine hall for the Teacher.
One who is worthy of honor, who endures fear, terror, and suffering,
and who is modest and fearful, gains the perception of living together with those who share his virtue;
such a person may become a partaker in the splendor of heaven and liberation.
In the excellent village of Lakkhapati in Laṅkā,
by the Lord of Rāma, adorned with the ornaments of virtue,
renowned for his pure and extensive wisdom, the creeper—
By the Elder named Saṅghananda, a noble teacher of venerable status,
who was born in Gāmuba, skilled in moving among assemblies,
and endowed with the four analytical knowledges.
Having removed the poison of envy and established his own vision as a protection, he who was nourished by growth—
disregarding even his own life for the sake of Tambapaṇṇi—
O Lord, please take possession of this island three times over,
and honor the tooth-relic of the Conqueror with a costly casket studded with pearls and gems,
and adorned with the songs of the Siddhas.
Having taken as his preceptor the master of Vajira-nāma monastery,
who was reverent toward the training, self-controlled, and bore the seal of being the teacher of the King of Kings,
he received full ordination in the Dhamma.
May the delightful kingdom of Maramma be protected by the King Meṇḍu, who attained his position through his father’s lineage,
and who, having gained confidence in his own wisdom regarding the tip of a blade of kusa grass,
has increased [the prosperity] of the realm.
The pupil of the King of the Saṅgha—
who was renowned as Ñeyyadhammābhivaṃsa and who mastered the entire scriptural tradition—
was named Saṃjayuttabhāṇakakumārabhivaṃsa.
Relying upon that most steadfast bull among elders,
who bears the insignia of the King of Kings and the Garuḍa, and who is honored for his excellent practice,
he attained proficiency in the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Born by birth into a noble family in the most delightful city named Moraṭu, the essence of fortune,
he was endowed with the quality of an age measuring thirty-eight years.
By that sovereign of Rāma, named Abhayakaruṇāratanābhivāna, who was born in Gaṇvācaka and whose domain was the village of Pāsāṇadūrapura.
By this [work], which illuminates the perfectly purified qualities of the Buddha and is intended for the purpose of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra,
may the wise ascetic produce joy and gladness.
By the poet named Nanda, this body of a narrative was composed,
illuminating the pure life-story (*apadāna*) of the qualities of Jinarāja,
the Kinsman of the Sun, among the elephants of poets.
The *Saddānusāsani*, the *Itihāsa*, the *Nighaṇṭu*, the *Chando*,
the *Laṅkārasāra*, and the profound discourse on the *Abhidhamma*—
these thirty-two works bestow the bliss of both heaven and liberation.
Accompanied by its commentary, employing words in their proper form,
filled with two thousand verses, and undisturbed by the lamp of the Conqueror’s lineage—
this supreme crest-jewel among compositions has been completed in its entirety.
On the auspicious full-moon day of the month of Māgha,
two thousand sixty-four years have passed since the Tathāgata attained Parinibbāna without hindrance.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Occurrence of the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One’s Relics," within the *Jinavaṃsadīpa*, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda— a source of joy to the hearts of all poets— and containing the introductory narrative.
The third section, consisting mostly of proximate origins, is concluded.
